docs.title: KeyLease
docs.text:
A Soroban protocol on Stellar that turns metered API/RPC access into time-bound, escrowed micro-leases.

KeyLease replaces long-lived static API keys with leases: expiring on-chain authorizations backed by a SEP-41 micropayment held in Soroban escrow. Providers publish a price instead of a secret; consumers pay only for the calls they use; the Stellar ledger holds the truth about every lease.

  • Repository: keylease-core — the Soroban contracts
  • License: MIT

docs.title: The Stellar loop
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Consumer
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry (Soroban)
    participant T as SEP-41 token (SAC / custom)
    participant P as Provider
    participant I as Indexer / RPC

    C->>R: create_lease(consumer, service_id, calls, duration)
    R->>T: transfer(rate × calls → escrow)
    R-->>I: lease_created
    R-->>C: lease_id
    P->>R: get_lease(lease_id) / read the event stream
    P-->>P: verify expiry + quota, serve the call
    P->>R: settle_lease(provider, lease_id, verified_calls)
    R-->>I: lease_settlement_proposed (funds still locked)
    opt consumer disputes the reported count
        C->>R: challenge_settlement(consumer, lease_id, evidence_hash)
        R-->>I: lease_challenged
    end
    P->>R: finalize_settlement(lease_id) (after the 24h window)
    R->>T: payout used × rate → provider
    R->>T: refund the remainder → consumer
    R-->>I: lease_settled

docs.title: Status
docs.text: ⚠️ Pre-1.0 and not independently audited. Suitable for Stellar Testnet and limited-value evaluation. See Deployments for the contract-id registry and Security for the current limitations.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: KeyLease is one Soroban contract and the Stellar ledger it runs on. There is no second source of truth: services, leases, escrow balances and lifecycle history all live on-chain, and the contract exposes them through entry points and contract events.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Actors
        DEV["Consumer<br/>Stellar account or contract"]
        PROV["Provider<br/>Stellar account or contract"]
        IDX["Indexer / RPC client"]
    end

    subgraph "Stellar ledger"
        REG[["KeyLeaseRegistry<br/>services · leases · escrow"]]
        TOK[["SEP-41 token<br/>native SAC or custom"]]
        EV[["Contract events<br/>lease_created · lease_transferred · settlement_proposed · challenged · lease_settled · lease_revoked"]]
    end

    DEV -- "create_lease (auth: consumer)" --> REG
    PROV -- "register_service · settle_lease (auth: provider)" --> REG
    REG -- "transfer / refund" --> TOK
    REG -. "typed events" .-> EV
    EV -. "subscribe" .-> IDX
    IDX -. "verify + meter" .-> PROV

docs.title: KeyLeaseRegistry
docs.text:
A pure Rust Soroban contract. It is the only component that can move value.

Module Role lib.rs Entry points, contractmeta!, upgrade, lifecycle documentation. types.rs Service, Lease, ServiceStats, LeaseStatus, Settlement, SettlementState. storage.rs DataKey layout, instance/persistent split, duration-aware TTL policy. events.rs Typed #[contractevent] payloads for every transition. errors.rs Stable error codes (part of the ABI).

The registry is deliberately small. It does not know what an HTTP request is, what the endpoint does, or who is calling it. It knows service_id, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit and — once a provider settles — the proposed payout/refund split and any consumer challenge against it.

docs.title: SEP-41 token
docs.text:
The registry holds no privileged token logic. It calls the standard SEP-41 transfer on the token configured by the admin:

  • the native Stellar Asset Contract wraps XLM (the usual Testnet choice),
  • any custom SEP-41 asset works without a contract change,
  • contracts/mock_token exists only for tests and local sandboxes.

The token boundary is a cross-contract call, so the money paths follow checks-effects-interactions and are tested against a re-entrant token.

docs.title: Consumers of the ledger
docs.text:
There is no privileged off-chain service. Anyone can observe the protocol using standard Stellar tooling:

Consumer How it reads the protocol Provider request path get_lease over Soroban RPC (cached for a short TTL), or a local projection built from the event stream. Accounting / dashboards stellar events, Horizon or an indexer subscribing to lease_created / lease_transferred / lease_settlement_proposed / lease_challenged / lease_cancelled / lease_settled / lease_revoked. CLI tooling stellar contract invoke for writes and reads (reads need any funded --source-account).

See Integration for the concrete verification pipeline.

docs.title: Data flow: one metered call
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Consumer
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry
    participant T as SEP-41 token
    participant P as Provider service
    participant U as Upstream API

    C->>R: create_lease(consumer, service_id, calls, duration)
    R->>T: transfer(consumer → registry, rate × calls)
    R-->>C: lease_id + lease_created event
    C->>P: request + Stellar-signed proof of consumer address
    P->>R: get_lease(lease_id)   (TTL-cached)
    R-->>P: Lease { allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, settled, ... }
    alt lease active, unexpired, quota remains
        P->>U: forwarded request
        U-->>P: response
        P-->>C: response + x-keylease-calls-remaining
    else invalid / expired / quota exhausted
        P-->>C: 401 / 403 / 429
    end
    P->>R: settle_lease(provider, lease_id, verified_calls)
    R-->>P: lease_settlement_proposed event (funds still locked)
    Note over C,R: 24h consumer challenge window
    C->>R: challenge_settlement(consumer, lease_id, evidence_hash)  (optional)
    R-->>P: lease_challenged event (payout frozen)  (optional)
    alt no challenge, or consumer cancelled
        P->>R: finalize_settlement(lease_id)
    else challenge active
        R->>R: resolve_challenge(admin, lease_id, upheld)
    end
    R->>T: payout + refund
    R-->>P: lease_settled event

Settlement is drawn as one arrow there because the request path is the subject. The two transfer legs are itemised below.

docs.title: The money paths in order
docs.text:
The component diagram says who may talk to whom; it does not say in what order value moves. The order is the security property. There are exactly three paths that move tokens, only one of them moves twice, and in every one of them the lease is written to storage before the token is called — so a token that tries to re-enter the registry during the transfer sees the final state, not the state before the money moved.

Each step below is labelled with the authorization that opened it and the state it wrote, because a reader auditing escrow needs both, not just the arrows.

docs.title: 1. create_lease — one transfer, into escrow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Consumer
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry
    participant T as SEP-41 token

    C->>R: create_lease(consumer, service_id, requested_calls, duration_secs)
    Note over C,R: AUTH — consumer.require_auth()
    Note over R: CHECKS — requested_calls and duration_secs both non-zero,<br/>duration_secs ≤ MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS,<br/>service exists and is_active, deposit = rate × calls (checked),<br/>deposit ≤ MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT, token configured
    Note over R: STATE WRITE — LeaseCount += 1, Lease(lease_id) saved with<br/>settled = false, expires_at and locked_deposit, lease, service<br/>and instance TTL extended
    R->>T: TRANSFER IN — transfer(consumer → registry, rate_per_call × requested_calls)
    Note over R: EVENT — lease_created, topic lease_id, payload { schema_version,<br/>service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit }
    R-->>C: lease_id

Nothing can be claimed before the STATE WRITE step exists: the escrow transfer and the lease record are the same transaction, so either both are visible on-chain or neither is. A consumer that cannot fund the deposit never gets a lease id.

docs.title: 2. settle_lease → finalize_settlement — two transfers, out of escrow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant P as Provider
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry
    participant T as SEP-41 token
    participant C as Consumer

    P->>R: settle_lease(provider, lease_id, verified_calls)
    Note over P,R: AUTH — provider.require_auth()
    Note over R: CHECKS — lease not settled, verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls,<br/>caller owns the service, and (expired OR verified_calls == allocated_calls)
    Note over R: STATE WRITE — Lease(lease_id).used_calls = verified_calls and<br/>settled = true, plus Settlement(lease_id) = Pending
    Note over R: EVENT — lease_settlement_proposed, topic lease_id, payload includes<br/>payout, refund and challengeable_until. No token call yet.
    Note over C,R: 24h consumer challenge window; an admin may resolve a challenge
    R->>R: finalize_settlement(lease_id) (permissionless, after the window)
    Note over R: STATE WRITE — Settlement.state = Finalized and ServiceStats updated,<br/>persisted BEFORE any token call
    R->>T: TRANSFER OUT 1 — transfer(registry → provider, payout)
    T-->>P: payout
    R->>T: TRANSFER OUT 2 — transfer(registry → consumer, refund)
    T-->>C: refund
    Note over R: EVENT — lease_settled, topic lease_id, payload { schema_version,<br/>provider, verified_calls, payout, refund }
    R-->>P: ok

payout + refund == locked_deposit always, and a leg of zero is skipped rather than emitted as a transfer. The STATE WRITE above the two arrows is what makes the pair atomic against a malicious token: after a re-entrant call the settlement already reads Finalized, so a second payout fails with SettlementFinalized (29) instead of paying twice. test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice holds that line. A challenged settlement is frozen until the admin resolves it; an upheld challenge pays the consumer the full deposit instead.

docs.title: 3. revoke_expired_lease — one transfer, after the grace window
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Consumer
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry
    participant T as SEP-41 token

    C->>R: revoke_expired_lease(consumer, lease_id)
    Note over C,R: AUTH — consumer.require_auth()
    Note over R: CHECKS — caller is lease.consumer, not settled,<br/>now ≥ expires_at, and now ≥ expires_at + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS
    Note over R: STATE WRITE — Lease(lease_id).settled = true, persisted<br/>BEFORE the refund transfer
    R->>T: TRANSFER OUT — transfer(registry → consumer, locked_deposit)
    Note over R: EVENT — lease_revoked, topic lease_id, payload { schema_version,<br/>consumer, refund }
    R-->>C: ok

The provider is deliberately absent from this diagram: it has no role in a revocation and no way to veto one. It can only pre-empt it, by settling first — which is exactly what the 24-hour grace window before this point is for. Nothing in the contract closes the settlement door when the window ends, so a lease in Expired is still a race, and the consumer wins it by acting after the deadline.

The refund is the full locked_deposit, not the unused remainder: the provider that never settled earned nothing. used_calls stays at 0 on this path, which keeps the accounting unambiguous — a revoked lease is a lease that was never paid for.

Path Who authenticates State written first Token transfers out create_lease consumer Lease(lease_id), LeaseCount — (one transfer in) transfer_lease current consumer Lease.consumer, pending cancel request cleared — settle_lease → finalize_settlement provider, then anyone after the challenge window used_calls, settled = true, then Settlement.state = Finalized payout + refund revoke_expired_lease consumer (must be the lease's) settled = true full locked_deposit

Read the deadlines and the worked numbers in How the protocol works.

docs.title: Why the contract is minimal
docs.text:
Every line of on-chain code is attack surface for escrowed funds. endpoint_hash is a commitment precisely so the contract never has to reason about off-chain credentials. Usage reporting is a single settlement call rather than one transaction per API call, which keeps the protocol affordable for small allotments.

Off-chain enforcement is replaceable. A provider can read leases directly over RPC, run an indexer, or write their own middleware. The protocol does not depend on any of those being alive: if a proxy is down, providers can still settle with stellar contract invoke, and consumers can still revoke.

Trust flows one way. Off-chain code trusts the ledger for lease state. The contract trusts nobody: every mutating entry point authenticates the actor it claims to represent, and the consumer always has an exit.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Key Storage TTL policy Admin, Token instance extended on every state change (≈30 days) SchemaVersion instance stamped by init, rewritten by migrate; see Storage schema migrations PendingAdmin instance single admin hand-over awaiting acceptance; shares the instance TTL ServiceCount, LeaseCount instance same as instance Service(u64) persistent extended on save and by bump_service (≈30 days) Lease(u64) persistent extended for the lease's remaining term plus the 24h grace window and a one-day read buffer, or by bump_lease Settlement(u64) persistent extended on save and read to the standard ~30-day horizon; keyed by lease id ServiceStats(u64) persistent extended on settlement only (≈30 days); derived data, so aging out loses a convenience counter, not money LeaseRevoked(u64) persistent written when a consumer reclaims, given the same horizon as its lease in that transaction, so a readable lease always has a readable marker CancelRequest(u64) persistent pending early-cancellation request; standard ~30-day TTL, removed on withdraw/reject/approve

docs.title: What extends a TTL, and what does not
docs.text:
An extension moves the entry's liveUntilLedgerSeq, which the host books as a rent bump and bills the caller for across the whole extended horizon. Only these calls extend anything: init, set_token, upgrade, register_service, set_service_active, create_lease, settle_lease, revoke_expired_lease, bump_service and bump_lease — and, since PR #152, set_token only when it actually changes the configured token. Every read-only view — get_service, get_lease, lease_status, remaining_calls, locked_balance, service_stats — is pure, so a simulation of a view costs instructions and no rent. In particular lease_status consulting the revocation marker and service_stats reading the settlement counters both extend nothing: each of those entries is sized by the write that created it, and a marker is never left alive longer than the lease it describes. At the ledger where an extension is due, get_lease estimates at 113 stroops (all instructions) against 48,798 for bump_lease, of which 48,684 is persistent rent.

Because reads stopped bumping, state that is only ever looked at has to be kept alive deliberately, and create_lease therefore extends the service it leases from: an actively leased service never goes stale under its own leases.

create_lease caps duration_secs at MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days), so the TTL extension is bounded and a locked deposit can never outlive its entry. Only the time a lease can be acted on is paid for, so Soroban rent does not dominate short leases.

Three bounds sit on top of each other, and each one is deliberately below the next:

Bound Ledgers Set by longest lease's policy ask (30-day term + 24h grace + 1-day buffer) 552,960 MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS contract ceiling for any single extension 1,555,200 (90 days) MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS network maxEntryTtl 6,312,000 Stellar protocol

The ceiling is above every horizon a valid lease can produce, so it never truncates one; what it bounds is an entry whose expires_at was not produced by today's create_lease — one migrated in by an upgrade, or one created after the duration cap is raised. Each extension also takes the minimum of that ceiling and env.storage().max_ttl(), so a network that lowers maxEntryTtl is followed rather than contradicted.

docs.title: Command-line helper
docs.text:
The helper under examples/consumer/ validates the configured service before every operation and keeps signing in the Stellar CLI keystore:

cp .env.example .env
# Set KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID, KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID, KEYLEASE_NETWORK,
# KEYLEASE_CONSUMER_IDENTITY, KEYLEASE_REQUESTED_CALLS and KEYLEASE_DURATION_SECS.

./examples/consumer/keylease-consumer.sh create --env .env
./examples/consumer/keylease-consumer.sh status --lease-id 1 --env .env
./examples/consumer/keylease-consumer.sh revoke --lease-id 1 --env .env

create first calls get_service, then create_lease, and prints lease_id and lease_expiry. status calls get_lease. revoke applies the contract's expiry plus 24-hour grace window by calling revoke_expired_lease; it does not bypass that window. The script never accepts or writes a secret seed.

You want metered access to an API or RPC endpoint without a permanent static key. This guide walks through buying, using and reclaiming a lease with Stellar.

docs.title: The deal you are getting
docs.text:
• You prepay rate_per_call × requested_calls into Soroban escrow.
  • You get an on-chain authorization that expires after duration_secs.
  • You pay only for the calls you use: unused balance is refunded at settlement.
  • If the provider never settles, you reclaim the entire deposit 24 hours after expiry — no support ticket, no trust required.

Your Stellar account is your identity. There is no API key to copy into a .env file and no separate credential service.

docs.title: 1. Pick a service
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account <funded-account> \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

Returns the provider, rate_per_call, is_active and endpoint_hash. Confirm the endpoint_hash matches the endpoint descriptor the provider published off-chain before you escrow anything.

docs.title: Rate units: base units, not XLM
docs.text:
rate_per_call is an integer in the escrow token's smallest unit. It is not a whole-token amount and not necessarily XLM. The registry never converts it, so the human-readable price depends entirely on the token's decimals.

For the native SAC, XLM has 7 decimals: 1 XLM = 10,000,000 stroops. The demo service's rate_per_call = 1_000_000 therefore means:

1,000,000 stroops / 10,000,000 stroops per XLM = 0.1 XLM per call
500 calls -> 1,000,000 × 500 = 500,000,000 stroops = 50 XLM

For a custom SEP-41 token, use its decimals(): the same 1,000,000 is 1.0 token at 6 decimals and 0.000000000001 token at 18 decimals. Check the token's decimals before you create the lease — assuming 7 when the token has 6 makes this lease ten times more expensive than you expect. See Rate units and stroops for the conversion table.

docs.title: 2. Fund your account
docs.text:
Any SEP-41 token the registry is configured with can be escrowed. On Testnet the native asset's SAC is the usual choice, and Friendbot funds accounts with 10,000 fake XLM.

# Testnet only: create + fund in one step
stellar keys generate consumer --network testnet --fund

# or fund an address you already have
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address consumer)"

docs.title: 3. Create the lease
docs.text:
export REGISTRY=<your registry contract id>
export CONSUMER=$(stellar keys address consumer)

# optional: price it first. quote_lease is a view — no auth, no transfer — and
# it runs the same validation as create_lease, so these are the numbers the next
# transaction locks.
stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  -- quote_lease \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer $CONSUMER \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

This escrows rate_per_call × 500 and prints the new lease_id. The transaction emits lease_created { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, rate_per_call }; keep the transaction hash as proof of purchase.

Choose your numbers deliberately. If your lease expires while you still have unused calls, those calls are not usable — remaining_calls drops to 0 at expires_at. The maximum duration is 30 days (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS). Under-buy with a generous duration, then renew, rather than over-buying with a short one.

rate_per_call × requested_calls also has a ceiling: MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT (1,000,000,000,000 base units, so 100,000 of a seven-decimal token). A lease above it reverts with DepositTooLarge before the token is called, so an over-typed call count cannot escrow the wrong amount even when your balance would cover it.

Order of arguments matters. consumer is the first argument. This is the exact ABI; older documentation that shows service first is wrong.

Someone else can arrange it for you. create_lease_for mints the identical lease with a sponsor as the courier: the sponsor signs and pays the Soroban transaction fee, you sign and your balance is escrowed, and you keep the refund and revoke rights.

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account sponsor --network testnet --send=yes \
  --sign $CONSUMER_SECRET_KEY \
  -- create_lease_for \
     --delegate $SPONSOR --consumer $CONSUMER \
     --service_id 1 --requested_calls 500 --duration_secs 3600

Your signature is mandatory: a sponsor cannot lock your deposit on its own.

docs.title: 4. Use the access
docs.text:
Tell the provider which lease backs your requests. Because the lease records your Stellar address, the provider authenticates you with a Stellar signature (SEP-10 challenge–response, or an equivalent signed challenge) and checks that you are lease.consumer. No bearer token is issued by KeyLease, and none is needed.

Concretely, for a provider that follows Integration:

  1. complete the provider's Stellar challenge with your account,
  2. send requests with your lease_id (path, query or header, as the provider documents) or let the provider resolve it from your authenticated address,
  3. read x-keylease-calls-remaining if the provider exposes it.

If you can sign for the account that owns the lease, you can use it — there is no separate credential to store or rotate. If you rotate that account, create a new lease from the new one.

docs.title: 5. Watch the lease
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- remaining_calls --lease_id 1

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- lease_status --lease_id 1

lease_status is 0 (Active), 1 (Expired), 2 (Settled) or 3 (Revoked — you reclaimed the deposit, so the provider earned nothing and used_calls stays 0). A lease becomes Settled as soon as the provider proposes a settlement; read get_settlement to see whether the payout is still in the challenge window or has been released. Only a finalized settlement is counted in service_stats.

docs.title: Hand the lease to another account
docs.text:
You can transfer an unsettled lease to any Stellar address. The recipient gets the remaining access and the refund right; your account loses both.

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- transfer_lease \
     --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1 --new_consumer <NEW_ADDRESS>

This is a direct assignment — the recipient does not need to accept — and it emits lease_transferred { lease_id, from, to }. A settled or revoked lease cannot be transferred, and neither can a lease whose settlement is pending under a challenge window. An expired, unsettled lease can still be transferred: you are selling the refund claim, not access.

docs.title: End the lease early
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- request_early_cancel --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1

The provider either approves — reporting the calls it actually served — or rejects the request. On approval you are refunded rate × unused_calls immediately and the lease ends; on rejection the lease keeps running exactly as before. You can withdraw a pending request with withdraw_early_cancel. Early cancellation is only available before expires_at; after expiry, use the revoke path below.

docs.title: 6. Get your money back
docs.text:
Normal path — automatic. When the provider settles, the unused balance is returned to you once the challenge window closes. Nothing to claim.

A settlement is a two-phase flow: settle_lease only proposes the split and locks the funds for 24 hours. If you disagree with the reported call count, you can dispute it inside that window with a 32-byte evidence hash:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- challenge_settlement \
     --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1 \
     --evidence_hash <sha256-of-your-evidence>

The challenge freezes the payout until the registry admin resolves it. If the dispute is upheld you get the entire deposit back; if it is rejected the original proposal is released. You can withdraw a challenge with cancel_challenge; the settlement returns to pending and the original deadline is unchanged.

Otherwise the payout can be released by anyone after the window closes:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- finalize_settlement --lease_id 1

Provider went dark. After expires_at + 24 hours, reclaim everything:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- revoke_expired_lease --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1

This refunds the full locked_deposit and emits lease_revoked { lease_id, consumer, refund }. It works for a lease that was never used and for one that was partially used but never settled.

docs.title: Why you must wait 24 hours
docs.text: That window is reserved for the provider to settle legitimately. It is the provider's guarantee, and your refund is the counterweight. It is a fixed constant in the contract (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400).

docs.title: Refund decision table
docs.text: Lease state What happens Provider proposes a settlement Funds stay locked; you have 24h to challenge You challenge inside 24h Payout frozen until the admin resolves it Dispute upheld You get the entire deposit back Dispute rejected or no challenge locked_deposit − used × rate returns to you at finalization Provider proposes verified_calls = 0 You get the entire deposit back Provider never settles, now ≥ expiry + 24h You revoke and get the entire deposit Provider never settles, inside the 24h window Nothing yet — wait You transferred the lease The new consumer receives all later refunds You request early cancel and the provider approves rate × unused_calls, immediately You request early cancel and the provider rejects Lease continues; nothing moves

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
Creating a lease and revoking one are two Soroban transactions (network fees plus the escrow transfer). There is no per-call on-chain cost — the provider settles with a single call count. Check the current fee with stellar network settings or your RPC provider.

create_lease also pays storage rent for keeping the lease entry alive through its term, the 24-hour grace window and a one-day buffer. Rent depends on duration, not call count, so a short lease with a larger allotment is cheaper per call than a long lease with a tiny one. The network enforces a minimum persistent TTL (≈7 days on Testnet), so a very short lease still pays that floor.
