docs.title: Types
docs.text:
pub struct Service {
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub provider: Address,
    pub rate_per_call: i128,
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
}

pub struct PendingUpgrade {
    pub new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>,
    pub execute_after: u64, // ledger timestamp
}

pub struct Lease {
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub consumer: Address,
    pub allocated_calls: u32,
    pub used_calls: u32,
    pub created_at: u64,       // ledger timestamp of create_lease
    pub expires_at: u64,       // created_at + duration_secs
    pub locked_deposit: i128,
    pub settled: bool,
}

// `Settled` means no further lease transition is possible (revoked, or a
// settlement was proposed); use `get_settlement` for the payout state.
pub enum LeaseStatus { Active = 0, Expired = 1, Settled = 2 }

/// Returned by `quote_lease`; the two fields mirror the `Lease` they predict.
pub struct LeaseQuote {
    pub locked_deposit: i128,
    pub expires_at: u64,
}

/// Returned by `services_for_provider`.
pub struct ProviderServicePage {
    pub service_ids: Vec<u64>,
    /// Index entries consumed; pass back as `after`.
    pub next: u32,
    /// `true` once the index is exhausted.
    pub done: bool,
}

pub enum SettlementState { Pending = 0, Challenged = 1, Finalized = 2 }

pub struct Settlement {
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub consumer: Address,
    pub provider: Address,
    pub verified_calls: u32,
    pub payout: i128,
    pub refund: i128,
    pub proposed_at: u64,
    pub challengeable_until: u64,
    pub state: SettlementState,
    pub challenge_evidence: BytesN<32>, // all zeroes when no challenge is active
    pub challenged_at: u64,            // 0 when no challenge is active
}

pub struct CancelRequest {
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub requested_at: u64,
}

pub struct ServicePage {
    pub services: Vec<Service>,
    pub next_start: u64,
    pub done: bool,
}

pub struct LeasePage {
    pub leases: Vec<Lease>,
    pub next_start: u64,
    pub done: bool,
}

pub struct PendingAdminTransfer {
    pub proposed_by: Address,
    pub new_admin: Address,
    pub proposed_at: u64,
    pub expires_at: u64,
}
}

Lease is stored on-chain and its field layout is frozen — appending a field breaks decoding of leases written by an older version. Revoked therefore derives from a separate LeaseRevoked(lease_id) marker rather than a revoked: bool on the struct, and ServiceStats lives under its own key for the same reason.

docs.title: created_at and upgrade compatibility
docs.text: created_at was appended to Lease after the type had already been published, so a lease written by an earlier release is stored without it. get_lease reads such an entry through a legacy shape and reports created_at = 0, meaning the creation time is unknown; everything else about the lease is unchanged, so it can still be settled or revoked, and the next write stores the current shape.

docs.title: Storage layout
docs.text:
pub enum DataKey {
    Admin,                     // instance
    Token,                     // instance
    ServiceCount,              // instance
    LeaseCount,                // instance
    Service(u64),              // persistent
    Lease(u64),                // persistent
    ServiceAttestor(u64),      // persistent: optional attestor key per service
    PendingUpgrade,            // instance (appended)
    ProviderServices(Address), // persistent: service ids, oldest first
    Settlement(u64),           // persistent: proposed split, keyed by lease id
    CancelRequest(u64),        // persistent: pending early-cancellation request
    SchemaVersion,             // instance, u32: see SCHEMA_VERSION
    PendingAdmin,              // instance: proposed admin hand-over
}

TTL policy for the two appended keys: neither is user-controlled, and each stays readable at least as long as the entity it describes. Only writes extend them — reads never do, in line with get_service and get_lease. ServiceStats(id) is bumped with the same LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD / LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND policy as Service(id) and is rewritten (and re-extended) on every settlement; an entry that sees no settlement for that horizon ages out and reads back as ServiceStats::zero(). LeaseRevoked(id) is written when the lease closes and given the same horizon the lease entry itself receives in that transaction, so any ledger view that can still read a lease can read its revocation marker — and lease_status never pays rent to keep either one alive.

#[contracttype] enums encode as a SCV_VEC whose first element is an SCV_SYMBOL variant name — so DataKey::Lease(7) is the wire key Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)]. This matters if you read contract data directly with getContractData; see the developer guide.

docs.title: Storage classes and TTL policies
docs.text:
Soroban expires storage: every key below has a lifetime, and when it runs out the host deletes the entry. Two operations keep an entry alive — a save on a write path (save_service, save_lease, the instance writes) and an explicit bump (bump_service, bump_lease, documented under Storage maintenance). Reads do neither. That split is deliberate and it is priced: an extension bills the caller for rent across the whole extended horizon, so a view that bumped what it read would turn a free lookup into a large fee. test_bump_lease_is_where_the_rent_lives pins the difference — the pure read costs 113 stroops, bump_lease costs 48,798, of which 48,684 is the rent for the horizon it just bought.

The numbers come from contracts/registry/src/storage.rs:

Constant Ledgers Wall clock at 5s blocks LEDGER_CLOSE_SECS — 5 seconds LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD 17_280 1 day — below this remaining life, a save or a bump extends the entry LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND 518_400 30 days — the horizon instance and Service entries are extended to MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS 1_555_200 90 days — the ceiling every extension in this module is clamped to

The last row is a policy bound rather than a network constant. ttl_ceiling returns min(MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS, env.storage().max_ttl()), so no call can ask for more than 90 days of lifetime and no call can contradict a network that publishes a smaller maxEntryTtl (6,312,000 ledgers on Pubnet and Testnet). Because create_lease caps a lease at 30 days, the clamp never truncates a well-formed lease; what it bounds is an entry whose expires_at says something else — one migrated in by an upgrade, or created after a future raise of MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS.

Key Class Holds Extended by TTL policy If it is never extended Admin Instance Address of the protocol admin init, set_token (only when the token actually changes; a repeat call is a no-op), register_service, create_lease — each via extend_instance_ttl extend to 30 days, clamped, when less than 1 day is left The whole contract instance entry is evicted: the id stops resolving, and admin, token and both counters are gone with it. Token Instance SEP-41 escrow token Address as Admin as Admin as Admin. Reads answer TokenNotSet, writes answer NotInitialized long before eviction, so a missing value is a bug report, not a normal state. ServiceCount Instance u64, next service id as Admin as Admin as Admin. It resets to 0 on a fresh instance, which is why id monotonicity is only guaranteed within one live instance. LeaseCount Instance u64, next lease id as Admin as Admin as ServiceCount. Service(u64) Persistent Service struct (provider, rate, endpoint hash, active) save_service — so register_service and set_service_active; create_lease via extend_service_ttl; and bump_service. Not get_service, settle_lease (which reads the service), or any view extend to 30 days, clamped, when less than 1 day is left The entry is dropped and every call naming that id answers ServiceNotFound (4) — including settle_lease on leases that are still live. Nothing resurrects it: re-registering mints a new id, so the old leases are orphaned. The defence is bump_service, which needs no authorisation and is paid for by whoever calls it. Lease(u64) Persistent Lease struct (allotted and used calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, settled) save_lease — so create_lease, settle_lease, revoke_expired_lease; and bump_lease. Not the get_lease, lease_status, remaining_calls, locked_balance views lease-specific: see the next section The entry is dropped and get_lease answers LeaseNotFound (6). Settlement and the consumer's refund path both begin by reading the lease, so an evicted lease can be neither settled nor refunded. bump_lease prevents that while the entry still exists and can do nothing after it is gone.

A registry that is deployed and then left unused is not kept alive by reads: settle_lease, revoke_expired_lease, upgrade, bump_service, bump_lease and every view leave the instance horizon alone. Instance eviction is a redeploy event, and Networks treats it as one.

docs.title: The lease-specific extension
docs.text:
save_lease and extend_lease_ttl (the body of bump_lease) do not use the generic 30-day horizon. Both call storage::lease_ttl_extend, which sizes the entry to the time the lease can actually be acted on:

ledgers = (remaining_term_secs + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS) / LEDGER_CLOSE_SECS
          + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD
          then clamped to ttl_ceiling

remaining_term_secs is expires_at - now, saturating at zero, so the result covers the lease term, then the 24-hour provider settlement window, then one extra day of buffer for the consumer's revoke_expired_lease call. Worked examples:

Lease Extension Entry lives 1 hour, fresh 35_280 ledgers ~2 days 7 days, fresh 155_520 ledgers ~9 days 30 days (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS), fresh 552_960 ledgers ~32 days already expired 34_560 ledgers 2 days — the grace window plus the buffer expires_at far past any legitimate term 1_555_200 ledgers 90 days — the clamp, not the term

The fourth row is why bump_lease is safe to expose permissionlessly: once a lease's horizon is in the past the ask stops shrinking. An expired lease is extended about two days at a time, never by its original term, so bumping the tail of a lease is a small explicit payment rather than an accidental re-buy of months of rent.

Three properties make this safe rather than merely cheap:

  • Bounded. create_lease rejects durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (DurationTooLong, 16) and every ask passes through ttl_ceiling, so a caller cannot inflate the extension and rent stays predictable. bump_lease takes only a lease_id: the horizon comes from the lease's own expires_at, never from the caller.
  • Never shorter than the money is locked. The entry outlives expires_at + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS, which is the last moment anyone can claim against the lease. A deposit cannot outlive the record that authorises paying it — the invariant docs/security.md states as "every lease has a consumer path to a full refund, for its entire TTL".
  • Only ever forward. Soroban's extend_ttl raises liveUntilLedgerSeq and cannot lower it, so a bump can never shorten a lease somebody already paid for (test_bump_lease_cannot_shorten_a_live_lease).

One asymmetry is worth stating plainly: keeping an entry alive is not the same as being able to read it. bump_lease refuses a settled lease with LeaseAlreadySettled (7) because its funds have already moved and extending it would only grow state, and bump_service answers ServiceNotFound (4) for an unknown id so that nobody pays rent for an entry that was never there.

The old behaviour — extending every lease to the generic 30-day horizon on every read — charged a one-hour lease thirty days of Soroban rent, and made the read path expensive. That is why the calculation is per-lease, and why reads no longer do it.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text:
Codes are part of the ABI. New variants are appended; existing numbers are never reused.

This table is pinned by ERROR_ABI in contracts/registry/src/test.rs: inserting a variant in the middle, renumbering one, or appending one without recording it there fails cargo test. Add a new code by appending it to Error, to ERROR_ABI and to this table together.

Code Variant Meaning 1 AlreadyInitialized init called twice 2 NotInitialized registry has no admin 3 Unauthorized caller is not the required actor 4 ServiceNotFound no service with that id 5 ServiceInactive service is paused 6 LeaseNotFound no lease with that id 7 LeaseAlreadySettled lease already settled or revoked 8 LeaseNotSettleable not expired and not fully consumed 9 LeaseNotExpired revoke before expiry 10 RevokeWindowNotElapsed revoke inside the 24h grace window 11 InvalidCalls zero calls, or more than allocated 12 InvalidDuration zero duration 13 InvalidRate non-positive rate 14 TokenNotSet escrow token not configured 15 Overflow checked arithmetic failed 16 DurationTooLong lease duration above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS 17 DepositTooLarge deposit above MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT 18 AttestorNotConfigured settle_lease_attested on a service with no attestor 19 AttestationRequired plain settle_lease on a service that requires one 20 AttestationMismatch attestation does not match the lease, service or calls 21 AttestationStale attestation's valid_until has passed 22 NoPendingUpgrade cancel_upgrade/execute_upgrade with no proposal 23 UpgradeDelayNotElapsed execute_upgrade before execute_after 24 InvalidLimit page size outside 1..=MAX_PAGE_SIZE 25 CancellationNotRequested no pending early-cancellation request 26 CancellationAlreadyRequested a request is already pending 27 LeaseExpired early cancellation requires now < expires_at 28 SettlementNotFound no settlement proposed for that lease 29 SettlementFinalized settlement already released funds 30 ChallengeWindowClosed challenge filed at or after challengeable_until 31 SettlementChallenged settlement is already under an active challenge 32 NoActiveChallenge nothing to cancel or resolve 33 ChallengeWindowStillOpen finalize attempted before the window closes 34 InvalidEvidence challenge evidence hash is all zeroes 35 LeaseNotTransferable lease already settled or revoked 36 InvalidConsumer transfer target is the current consumer 37 RateTooHigh published rate_per_call above MAX_RATE_PER_CALL 38 SchemaMigrationRequired stored schema older than this Wasm; admin must run migrate 39 SchemaVersionUnsupported stored schema newer than this Wasm, or no migration path 40 NoPendingAdminTransfer accept_admin / cancel_admin_transfer with no proposal 41 AdminTransferExpired accept_admin at or after expires_at 42 InvalidAdmin propose_admin named the current admin 43 InvalidEndpointHash endpoint_hash is all zeroes and commits to nothing 44 ContractPaused new commitments refused while admin emergency pause is active

docs.title: Invoking with the Stellar CLI
docs.text:
# register a service
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  -- register_service \
     --provider $PROVIDER \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 \
     --endpoint_hash 0707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707

# list a provider's services, one page at a time (read-only)
# pass `next` back as --after until the response reports done: true
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  -- services_for_provider \
     --provider $PROVIDER \
     --after 0 \
     --limit 100

# quote before you buy (read-only: no auth, no transfer)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  -- quote_lease \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

# create a lease
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  -- create_lease \
     --consumer $CONSUMER \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

# early cancellation: consumer asks, provider consents
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  -- request_early_cancel --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  -- approve_early_cancel --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320
# create a lease for someone else: the delegate pays the fee, the consumer's
# balance is debited, and both must sign
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account delegate --network testnet \
  --sign $CONSUMER_SECRET_KEY \
  -- create_lease_for \
     --delegate $DELEGATE \
     --consumer $CONSUMER \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

# lifetime revenue reported for one service
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --network testnet \
  -- service_stats --service_id 1

# propose a settlement (opens the 24h challenge window)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  -- settle_lease --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

# finalize after the 24h challenge window (anyone may call this)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  -- finalize_settlement --lease_id 1

# the consumer can dispute inside the window
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  -- challenge_settlement --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1 --evidence_hash <64_HEX_CHARS>

# the admin resolves the dispute
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet \
  -- resolve_challenge --admin $ADMIN --lease_id 1 --upheld true

# upgrade (after `stellar contract upload`)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet \
  -- upgrade --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash <64_HEX_CHARS>

# page the catalogue (a read view, but the CLI still needs a fee payer)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account reader --network testnet \
  -- get_services --start 1 --limit 100

docs.title: MockToken (test only)
docs.text:
contracts/mock_token implements a minimal SEP-41 surface — init, mint, transfer, transfer_from, approve, allowance, balance, decimals (7), name, symbol, admin — with an unlimited mint: the admin chooses every amount, and the only ceiling is i128, where a mint or a recipient credit returns Overflow (7) instead of trapping.

It exists so local sandboxes do not depend on a live SAC, but it must never be deployed to a network holding value. The registry's own tests escrow against the real Stellar Asset Contract (register_stellar_asset_contract_v2).

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deploying KeyLease is a short, strictly ordered sequence of stellar contract commands against a Stellar network. Steps 2–5 each depend on the previous one, so the whole thing is scripted:

SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

To create and fund the identity as well (Testnet only):

KEYLEASE_GENERATE_KEY=1 SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

The script never deploys mock_token. That token has an unlimited mint and is for tests and local sandboxes only.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
--dry-run resolves every default, validates every input and prints each command with the values it would send, then exits. It builds nothing, signs nothing and makes no network call:

./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --dry-run
ADMIN=G... PROVIDER=G... TOKEN=C... ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --dry-run

Values that only exist after a real deployment — the contract id, the service id, the Wasm hash — are printed as <placeholders>. Input that a real run would reject fails here first: a malformed ENDPOINT_HASH, a non-numeric RATE_PER_CALL, or a missing or malformed REGISTRY in an upgrade mode. The same flag works for every mode, so --upgrade --dry-run shows the upload and proposal without queueing anything.

docs.title: Mainnet guard
docs.text:
NETWORK is user-controlled, so a typo or an exported variable can point the script at mainnet. Mainnet deployment is deferred until the contract is audited (see Mainnet), so the script refuses NETWORK=mainnet unless KEYLEASE_ALLOW_MAINNET=1 is exported for that invocation:

KEYLEASE_ALLOW_MAINNET=1 NETWORK=mainnet ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --dry-run

In every mode the script prints a banner with the resolved network, mode and signing identity before the first send, adds a MAINNET — real XLM is at risk line when the opt-in is set, and repeats the network in the final summary.

docs.title: What the script does
docs.text:
1. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
2. stellar contract deploy   <registry wasm>  -> REGISTRY contract id
3. stellar contract invoke -- init            --admin  <ADMIN>
4. stellar contract invoke -- set_token       --admin <ADMIN> --token <TOKEN>
5. stellar contract invoke -- register_service --provider <P> \
                              --rate_per_call <R> --endpoint_hash <H>

Then it re-reads get_service to confirm the write landed, and prints a block you can paste into .env. In deploy mode that block is nine lines:

KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID=C...
KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID=1
KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS=C...
KEYLEASE_NETWORK=testnet
KEYLEASE_RPC_URL=https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org
KEYLEASE_ADMIN=G...
KEYLEASE_PROVIDER=G...
KEYLEASE_RATE_PER_CALL=1000000
KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH=<64 hex chars>

In --upgrade mode it prints only the two lines that change — KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID (unchanged, echoed back for confirmation) and KEYLEASE_NETWORK — plus the new version() and Wasm hash, which are not env entries.

docs.title: Mapping printed values to your env file
docs.text:
Two sets of names are in play and mixing them up is the usual way a deployment goes sideways. The variables in Configuration are inputs: you set them before running the script, they carry no KEYLEASE_ prefix, and SOURCE_ACCOUNT is the only one that touches a key. The KEYLEASE_* lines the script prints are outputs: they describe what now exists on the ledger, and they are what your client, indexer or CI reads afterwards.

Printed as .env entry What it actually is In .env? KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID the deployed KeyLeaseRegistry id; the script asserts it matches ^C[A-Z0-9]{55}$ public KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID the decimal u64 returned by register_service; monotonic from 1 public KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS the SEP-41 escrow token set by set_token — for native this is the network's SAC id, so it is the same string on every Testnet deployment public KEYLEASE_NETWORK KEYLEASE_NETWORK the CLI network name; also the --network argument for every later invocation public KEYLEASE_RPC_URL KEYLEASE_RPC_URL Testnet only: the script hardcodes https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org and prints the placeholder <your <network> RPC url> for anything else. Replace the placeholder — do not paste it public KEYLEASE_ADMIN KEYLEASE_ADMIN address authorized for set_token and upgrade; defaults to the address of SOURCE_ACCOUNT public address, secret seed elsewhere KEYLEASE_PROVIDER KEYLEASE_PROVIDER owner of the demo service; defaults to KEYLEASE_ADMIN public KEYLEASE_RATE_PER_CALL KEYLEASE_RATE_PER_CALL stroops per call, and already on-chain in service_registered public KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH the 32-byte commitment actually stored, lowercased by the script; default sha256("<PROVIDER>:<SERVICE_NAME>") public digest, not the descriptor

Nothing in that table is a secret. Every one of those values is either on the ledger already — visible through get_service, get_token or the service_registered event — or an address that is by definition public. So the rule is simple:

Never commit Where it belongs instead The seed of any identity used here (SOURCE_ACCOUNT, admin, provider, consumer) the stellar CLI keystore, or an OS secret manager The off-chain endpoint descriptor behind KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH your own config; only the digest goes on-chain, and a committed descriptor is one an attacker can re-derive to confirm they guessed your service .env itself, and anything you add to it later — database URLs, webhook signing secrets a secret manager; .env is gitignored, .env.example is the committed template and carries no values

Four entries in .env.example are not printed by the script, so pasting the output leaves them empty:

  • KEYLEASE_NETWORK_PASSPHRASE — the signing string for the network; the script passes --network, which reads its own CLI config, so it never needs the passphrase and never prints it. Take it from Networks.
  • SOURCE_ACCOUNT — an input, not an output.
  • KEYLEASE_GENERATE_KEY — an input, and Testnet-only.
  • KEYLEASE_CONSUMER — a consumer you fund after the deploy; the script has no reason to know it.

docs.title: The minimum env for a read
docs.text:
After cp .env.example .env, three entries are enough to read a deployment:

KEYLEASE_NETWORK=testnet
KEYLEASE_RPC_URL=https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org
KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID=C...

Read views require no authorization and submit nothing, so no funds move and no escrow token is involved: KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS, KEYLEASE_RATE_PER_CALL, KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH, KEYLEASE_ADMIN and KEYLEASE_PROVIDER are all unread. KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID matters only as the thing you name — it is an argument to get_service, the way lease_id is to get_lease — and KEYLEASE_CONSUMER is never needed for a read.

stellar contract invoke \
  --id "$KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID" --source-account "$SOURCE_ACCOUNT" \
  --network "$KEYLEASE_NETWORK" -- get_service --service_id "$KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID"

That call names one more variable, SOURCE_ACCOUNT: a local CLI identity to build the simulation against. It is an input from Configuration, not one of the printed outputs, and it is not a secret in the file either — only its address is ever written down here. A client that only reads can skip the CLI entirely and simulate directly, which needs no signing authority at all; see Integration. Note that the CLI resolves the endpoint from its own --network configuration, so KEYLEASE_RPC_URL is consumed by your own client and indexer rather than by the CLI.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Variable Default Meaning SOURCE_ACCOUNT keylease-admin stellar CLI identity used to sign NETWORK testnet network name from your CLI config REGISTRY_ALIAS keylease-registry contract alias saved locally ADMIN address of SOURCE_ACCOUNT registry admin PROVIDER ADMIN owner of the demo service TOKEN native SAC on NETWORK escrow token RATE_PER_CALL 1000000 0.1 XLM at 7 decimals ENDPOINT_HASH sha256("<PROVIDER>:keylease-demo") 32-byte commitment KEYLEASE_GENERATE_KEY unset 1 to generate + Friendbot-fund the identity KEYLEASE_ALLOW_MAINNET unset 1 to permit NETWORK=mainnet for this invocation

docs.title: Doing it manually
docs.text:
The script is the supported path, but the raw commands are:

# 0. identity
stellar keys generate keylease-admin --network testnet --fund

# 1. build
rustup target add wasm32v1-none
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --package keylease-registry

# 2. deploy
REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet \
  --alias keylease-registry)

# 3. initialize
ADMIN=$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$ADMIN"

# 4. configure the escrow token (native SAC here)
TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token --admin "$ADMIN" --token "$TOKEN"

# 5. publish a service
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- register_service \
    --provider "$ADMIN" \
    --rate_per_call 1000000 \
    --endpoint_hash 0707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707

--send=yes is required for the state-changing invocations. Without it the CLI only simulates. The -- before the function name is required.

docs.title: Verifying a deployment
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- get_token
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- service_count

For a repeatable, pass/fail check, use the verification script. It reads the contract id from .env (or the environment), checks version, get_admin, get_token and a demo service, prints PASS/FAIL per check, and exits non-zero on mismatch:

./scripts/verify-deployment.sh --env-file .env
# Preview without network calls:
./scripts/verify-deployment.sh --env-file .env --dry-run

version is embedded by contractmeta!, so it proves which release is live. The contract id itself is in the registry: see Deployments, and the explorer link for that network in Networks.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
The contract is upgradeable in place through the Soroban deployer; the contract id, storage and balances are preserved. Because the old storage carries over, the steps must run in order and the result must be checked, so they are scripted:

./scripts/upgrade.sh --contract-id C... --admin keylease-admin

Both flags are required and have no defaults: the script will not guess which contract to replace or which key signs for it. --admin is a stellar CLI identity; its address is passed to upgrade --admin and must equal the live get_admin, which the script checks before it sends anything.

docs.title: What the upgrade script does
docs.text:
0. get_admin, version                     -> confirm the signer is the admin, record the live version
1. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --package keylease-registry
2. stellar contract upload  <registry wasm> -> Wasm hash (must equal sha256 of the built file)
3. stellar contract invoke -- upgrade      --admin <ADMIN> --new_wasm_hash <HASH>
4. stellar contract invoke -- version      -> must equal [workspace.package] version in Cargo.toml

It then prints the Wasm hash, the version before and after, and the stellar events command (with the contract_upgraded topic filter and the ledger it started from) to confirm the upgrade event. It exits non-zero when:

  • --contract-id or --admin is missing, or the id is not a C... contract id;
  • the identity is not the registry admin;
  • the live contract already reports the workspace version — bump [workspace.package] version first, or pass --allow-same-version to re-install the same release deliberately;
  • the uploaded hash differs from the local build;
  • version() after the upgrade does not equal the workspace version.
Flag Default Meaning --contract-id required (env CONTRACT_ID) registry contract to upgrade --admin required (env ADMIN_IDENTITY) stellar CLI identity of the registry admin --network testnet (env NETWORK) network name from your CLI config --allow-same-version off proceed when the live version already equals the workspace version --yes off skip the confirmation prompt (required on a non-interactive shell)

REGISTRY=C... SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --upgrade builds and uploads the Wasm and then queues it behind the contract's 24h time lock; --execute-upgrade installs the proposal once that delay has elapsed and --cancel-upgrade drops it.

docs.title: Upgrading manually
docs.text:
The raw commands the script wraps are:

# 1. upload the new Wasm and print its hash
WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet)

# 2. propose the upgrade (admin auth); read back the hash and execution ledger
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- propose_upgrade \
    --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH"
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --network testnet -- get_pending_upgrade

# 3. wait until ledger.timestamp() >= execute_after (24h), then install
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- execute_upgrade --admin $ADMIN

# 4. lift the post-upgrade stop (a no-op when the storage schema is unchanged)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- migrate --admin $ADMIN

# 5. confirm the new version and schema, and watch the events
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- schema_version
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

Guard rails for an upgrade: keep the storage layout unchanged unless you bump the storage schema and ship a migration (see Storage schema migrations), append error codes instead of renumbering, and keep event names and payload fields backwards-compatible. The execute_after timestamp and proposed hash are public via get_pending_upgrade and upgrade_proposed; announce them so clients can exit in time. Settle or revoke in-flight leases before changing token semantics. See Security and the design note.

docs.title: Storage schema migrations
docs.text:
The registry records which storage schema its data conforms to (schema_version(), stored under DataKey::SchemaVersion), and every Wasm knows which schema it was built for (code_schema_version(), and the storageSchemaVersion metadata on the uploaded Wasm). When the two differ, the registry is stopped: set_token, register_service, set_service_active, create_lease, settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease revert, and no value can move.

Stored vs. code State Error Way out equal running — — stored older stopped SchemaMigrationRequired (29) admin runs migrate stored newer (a downgrade) stopped SchemaVersionUnsupported (30) reinstall the newer Wasm; migrate refuses

propose_upgrade, cancel_upgrade, execute_upgrade, migrate, bump_service, bump_lease and every read-only view stay available while stopped, so a bad install can always be rolled back and entries can be kept alive during the window. A registry deployed before versioning reports schema 0. Its layout is identical to schema 1, and the first migrate after upgrading to a versioned Wasm only writes the stamp.

docs.title: Proposing a migration
docs.text:
A change that renames or retypes a DataKey variant, changes a stored struct's fields, or changes the meaning of a stored value must, in the same PR:

  1. Bump SCHEMA_VERSION in contracts/registry/src/storage.rs and the storageSchemaVersion metadata in lib.rs (a test fails if they diverge), and add a row to the version table in the SCHEMA_VERSION docs.
  2. Add the N-1 => … arm to storage::migrate_step. The arm must be bounded. It may rewrite instance storage, but it must never iterate over services or leases. Persistent entries are migrated lazily, by an accessor that reads both the old and the new shape and writes the new one on the next save.
  3. Add a test that seeds state in the old shape, asserts the registry is stopped with SchemaMigrationRequired, runs migrate, and asserts the old data reads back correctly and the registry runs again.
  4. Add a design note under docs/design/ and a release note that says the upgrade stops the registry until migrate runs.

Changes that old entries already satisfy, such as a new key that defaults when absent, do not need a bump.

docs.title: Reviewing a migration
docs.text:
The reviewer checks that the bump and the migrate_step arm are in the same PR, that the arm is bounded, that every old-shape value has exactly one new-shape meaning, and that the test above exists. Before installing, the reviewer confirms the uploaded artifact is the reviewed build:

stellar contract info meta --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm
# storageSchemaVersion must equal schema_version() + 1, or equal it when no
# migration is expected

docs.title: Executing a migration
docs.text:
1. Record the live state (step 2 of the checklist below), including schema_version.
  2. execute_upgrade, once the 24h delay after propose_upgrade has passed. From this transaction on the registry is stopped. Nothing can be created, settled or revoked, and no value moves.
  3. migrate --admin $ADMIN in the very next transaction, to keep the stop short. It runs every step from the stored version to the code's version and stamps the new version atomically, then emits schema_migrated.
  4. Verify that schema_version equals the new version and that pre-upgrade leases and services read back unchanged, then resume traffic.

If migrate fails, the registry stays stopped and nothing is written. Reinstall the previous Wasm hash with propose_upgrade and execute_upgrade, which is valid until migrate succeeds, because the stored data is still in the old schema. The upgrade time lock still applies, so a rollback keeps the registry stopped for at least 24 hours: rehearse the migration on Testnet first. After a successful migration, rolling back to the old Wasm leaves the registry stopped with SchemaVersionUnsupported, which is the intended outcome. The old code cannot read the new data, and it must not write over it.

scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --execute-upgrade runs execute_upgrade and migrate back to back and prints the resulting schema_version.

docs.title: Upgrading safety checklist
docs.text:
An upgrade replaces the code but keeps the contract id, so every stored entry written by the old Wasm is still there when the new Wasm runs. The new code does not get a clean slate — it gets your users' escrow. Work the checklist in order.

1. Invariants the new Wasm must preserve. These are the reasons the guard rails above exist; the full layout is in Storage layout.

Invariant Why an upgrade can silently break it DataKey variant names and arities: Admin, Token, ServiceCount, LeaseCount, Service(u64), Lease(u64) A #[contracttype] enum key encodes as Vec[Symbol("<variant>"), …], so renaming Lease to Leases orphans every existing entry. The registry then reads LeaseNotFound on leases that still hold escrow. Stored value shapes for Service and Lease Entries decode by field name and type. Renaming used_calls, retyping locked_deposit, or removing settled reinterprets or loses live records. Field presence, not field order, for structs Old entries are read by key, so adding a field is safe only if the accessor tolerates its absence in entries written before the upgrade. Error codes, append-only (1–30 today) Callers and indexers branch on the number; a reused code changes what a past transaction meant. Event names, topics and payload fields, append-only They are the indexing ABI. Dropping a #[topic] field shifts every subscriber's filter, including the base64 segments in Topics, payloads and filters. LeaseStatus discriminants (0/1/2/3) Returned by lease_status and cached by clients. Revoked = 3 was appended; reusing 2 for a reclaimed lease would rewrite what every cached Settled meant. The settled-before-token-call ordering in settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease It is the double-payout guard; reordering it behind a transfer reintroduces the re-entrancy bug the suite proves closed. The lease TTL policy covers term + 24 h grace + read buffer If a shorter policy evicts a lease entry while escrow is still locked, the consumer's revoke path disappears. MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS never lowered below an in-flight lease's term Existing leases stay settleable; lowering the cap for new leases is additive, lowering it retroactively is not.

2. Record the live state before you touch anything.

# version, counters and the exact Wasm you are replacing
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- service_count
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- lease_count
sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm

Keep the highest pre-upgrade lease_id and note the current ledger: it is the --start-ledger for the replay in step 5.

3. Upgrade. Upload, install, and keep the hash the deployer returned. ./scripts/upgrade.sh --contract-id $REGISTRY --admin keylease-admin runs this step and step 4 together; the raw commands are:

WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- upgrade --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH"

Then run migrate --admin $ADMIN (see Storage schema migrations); until it succeeds every state-changing call reverts.

4. Compare version() and schema_version(). The embedded metadata must move; a build that did not bump the workspace version installed new code that still reports the old one.

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract info meta --id $REGISTRY --network testnet

version must equal the release you intended, name must still be KeyLeaseRegistry, and schema_version must equal code_schema_version. Then re-read one lease and one service created before the upgrade and diff the field values against step 2 — identical expires_at, allocated_calls, locked_deposit and settled is what proves the stored shapes were not reinterpreted.

5. Replay the events across the boundary.

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger-from-step-2>

Expect exactly one contract_upgraded carrying the new_wasm_hash from step 3, with nothing else in that transaction, followed by a schema_migrated if the storage schema moved; the counters must be unchanged across it (service_count and lease_count before equals after — an upgrade mints no leases); and every lease_created before the upgrade must still have a terminal lease_settled or lease_revoked after it. If a pre-upgrade lease that was Active now reverts on settle_lease, stop: the new Wasm is not storage-safe.

6. Only then resume traffic, and record the outcome — the new version, Wasm hash and upgrade ledger — in Deployments, which ties a listed address to a revision.

Rollback. upgrade is symmetric: install the previous Wasm's hash the same way. It is only safe while the new build has written nothing the old one cannot read, so a new DataKey variant or new field is a one-way door the moment it is used. The schema stamp enforces this for versioned changes: once migrate has run, the old Wasm sees a newer schema and stays stopped (SchemaVersionUnsupported) instead of misreading the data.

docs.title: Multisig admin deployment and upgrades
docs.text: In production, operators should configure a cold or multi-signature account as the registry admin to prevent a single compromised key from executing unauthorized contract upgrades or token modifications.

docs.title: 1. Initialization with a multisig admin
docs.text:
Any funded account can build and deploy the contract Wasm. When initializing the registry, pass the multi-signature account address (G_MULTISIG...) as the --admin parameter:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account deployer \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$MULTISIG_ADMIN"

Once initialized, all functions requiring admin privileges (set_token and upgrade) call admin.require_auth(), delegating authorization enforcement to the Stellar host.

docs.title: 2. Multi-party upgrade workflow
docs.text:
Upgrades with a multisig admin are coordinated through transaction envelopes:

  1. Upload the new Wasm: Any account can upload the compiled bytecode to obtain its hash:
WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account deployer --network testnet)
  1. Construct the unsigned invocation transaction:
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" \
  --source-account "$MULTISIG_ADMIN" \
  --network testnet \
  --build-only \
  -- upgrade --admin "$MULTISIG_ADMIN" --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH" > upgrade_tx.xdr
  1. Collect signatures from signers: Each required co-signer signs the envelope until the cumulative signature weight meets or exceeds the admin account's threshold:
stellar tx sign --network testnet --source-account signer-alice upgrade_tx.xdr > signed_1.xdr
stellar tx sign --network testnet --source-account signer-bob signed_1.xdr > signed_threshold.xdr
  1. Submit the fully-signed transaction:
stellar tx send --network testnet signed_threshold.xdr

docs.title: Host-level auth guarantees
docs.text:
• What the contract enforces: The contract checks admin.require_auth(). If the accumulated signature weight does not meet the Stellar account's configured threshold, the host rejects the transaction before contract invocation occurs.
  • What the contract cannot enforce: The contract does not inspect individual signer identities, weights, or whether the signer set is 2-of-3 versus 1-of-1. Those rules live entirely within the Stellar account configuration.

docs.title: Post-deploy
docs.text:
1. Fund a consumer so create_lease can escrow a deposit.
  2. Point your client or indexer at the registry with KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID, KEYLEASE_RPC_URL and KEYLEASE_NETWORK.
  3. Subscribe to events, or read get_lease on demand — see Integration.
  4. Optionally run the smoke test after deployment to confirm the contract can escrow and settle a one-call lease on the selected network. It is opt-in and guarded to avoid accidental production runs:
KEYLEASE_SMOKE_TEST=1 \
CONSUMER_IDENTITY=keylease-consumer \
PROVIDER_IDENTITY=keylease-admin \
KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID=C... \
KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID=1 \
KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS=C... \
./scripts/smoke-test-deployment.sh --env-file .env

Use --dry-run to print the planned commands without sending transactions. Set KEYLEASE_SMOKE_VERIFIED_CALLS=0 or 1 to control settlement; 1 is the default. The script prints create/settle transaction output and exits non-zero on failure. Mainnet requires both KEYLEASE_NETWORK=mainnet and KEYLEASE_ALLOW_MAINNET=1.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: Testnet, Futurenet, Mainnet and local standalone differ only in RPC endpoint and passphrase; the full table, SAC addresses and reset schedule are in Networks.

docs.title: Mainnet
docs.text: Not yet. Mainnet deployment is deferred until the contract is audited — see Security and the known limitations listed there. The deploy script enforces this: NETWORK=mainnet is refused unless KEYLEASE_ALLOW_MAINNET=1 is set explicitly, and a --dry-run never sends anything even then.

docs.text:

  • Deployments — the address registry.
  • Integration — verifying leases from your service.
