docs.title: On-chain metadata
docs.text:
stellar contract info meta --id $REGISTRY --network testnet returns the contractmeta! embedded in the deployed Wasm:

name:        KeyLeaseRegistry
version:     0.2.1
repository:  https://github.com/KeyLease-Security/keylease-core
description: Time-bound micro-leases for API/RPC access, escrowed with SEP-41 tokens on Stellar.
rssdkver:    26.1.1

docs.title: Lifecycle verified on-chain
docs.text:
Two real leases were created and settled against the live contract. The escrow moved through the native Stellar Asset Contract.

Step Output create_lease (lease 1, 100 calls, 1h) ledger 5382801 — tx bea25af0…4b90; locked_deposit = 100000000 settle_lease (lease 1, 100 verified) ledger 5382802 — tx f34bff56…bde22; payout = 100000000, refund = 0 create_lease (lease 2, 10 calls, 60s) ledger 5382814 — tx ab4f69e2…0ca21; locked_deposit = 10000000 settle_lease (lease 2, 4 verified after expiry) ledger 5382835 — tx 7a6a939d…5a01; payout = 4000000, refund = 6000000

Both settlements emitted lease_settled; every create emitted lease_created. Those events are not retrievable, though: a public RPC serves a rolling window of ledgers, and this deployment predates the window it currently offers. The command that looks right on the table above is refused today:

stellar events --id CCEZYHUJUICXVPLH6UC2OFZL2RG23QQ7EMZOWE32WVQPT25DCTIAFH62 \
  --network testnet --start-ledger 5382788
# error: startLedger must be within the ledger range: 5698139 - 5819098

The window is stated in every JSON-RPC getEvents response as oldestLedger and latestLedger, so read it from the endpoint rather than assuming it: on the public Testnet RPC those two came back as 5698126 and 5819085, a span of 120,959 ledgers over 604,791 seconds — seven days at five seconds a ledger.

Two things follow for anyone verifying this record. The rows above stay checkable through the explorer links, and get_lease 1 still returns them on the deployed build (locked_deposit = 100000000, used_calls = 100, settled = true) — but a persistent entry has its own lifetime, and reads only keep it alive for as long as the deployed Wasm extends on read, so that proof decays too; see Storage lifetime. The event log is gone from the endpoint already, and re-running the deploy script will not reproduce either, since it stops after register_service and funds no lease. Use stellar events against the window it does serve to prove the contract is still publishing events. See Resuming where you left off.

docs.title: Deployment economics (Testnet)
docs.text: The Wasm upload reserves on-chain code rent (~3,557 XLM for this build at the current Testnet settings). Lease creation pays storage rent as part of the transaction resource fee: the host enforces a minimum persistent TTL (~7 days on Testnet), so the first lease (which also funded the contract's own SAC balance entry) cost ~20 XLM, a following 10-call lease cost ~5.6 XLM, and settlement is a few thousand stroops. Mainnet rent parameters differ; size allotments against real fees before quoting per-call prices.

docs.title: Mainnet
docs.text:
Field Value Status ⛔ not deployed Network mainnet Network passphrase Public Global Stellar Network ; September 2015 RPC third-party only, e.g. https://mainnet.sorobanrpc.com

Mainnet deployment is intentionally deferred until the contract is audited. See Security and SECURITY.md.

Before any mainnet transaction, follow the maintainer-approved Mainnet deployment and key-custody runbook. It defines the audit gate, multisig custody, exact deploy/verify/monitor/upgrade commands, expected outputs, and rollback procedure.

docs.title: Verifying a listed address
docs.text:
The registry can be checked without trusting this page: the Wasm carries contractmeta!, and the configured token and admin are public views.

stellar contract invoke --id <ID> --source-account <funded-account> --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id <ID> --source-account <funded-account> --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id <ID> --source-account <funded-account> --network testnet -- get_token

# lifecycle history, straight from the ledger
stellar events --id <ID> --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

For the same checks with clear pass/fail output, point the verification script at your .env (or export KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID and related values):

./scripts/verify-deployment.sh --env-file .env

The script checks version, get_admin, get_token and the configured demo service, exits non-zero on any mismatch, and supports --dry-run.

version() must match the release this page claims, get_admin() must be the documented admin, and escrow_token_set / service_registered events must appear at the recorded deployment ledger.

The deployed Wasm is reproducible from this tree — its hash matches stellar contract info hash. CI also builds the release Wasm twice from clean targets and compares hashes, failing if they differ:

cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm
# 5362d4cb866a0405f17d1adfe8179e63afaca8a7dc741df3c3b87ee0ab75146a

docs.title: Recording a deployment
docs.text:
1. Run ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh.
  2. Copy the printed values into the Testnet table above, including the contract version.
  3. Record the deployment ledger so stellar events can be replayed.
  4. Commit the change and tag the release so the addresses are tied to a specific revision.

docs.title: Recording a post-reset deployment
docs.text:
A Testnet reset (2–4 times a year, 17:00 UTC) wipes the ledger, so this table is stale from the moment it happens and a reader can be pointed at a contract id that no longer exists. The operator sequence is in Networks — After a Testnet reset; what changes here is only the record:

Field After a reset KeyLeaseRegistry new id — from the script output, never from memory. Contract version, Wasm hash Whatever this build produced. Unchanged only if you deployed the same commit. Contract created, init, set_token, register_service All new ledgers and tx links. The pre-reset history is gone, so replay starts at the new Contract created ledger. Escrow token (native SAC) unchanged — derived from the passphrase, which a reset does not alter. Re-derive it to prove it: stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native. Admin / provider / demo consumer unchanged addresses, but the accounts themselves were wiped and must be re-funded before they can sign. Demo service_id Back to 1. ServiceCount is instance storage and the instance is new, so ids restart rather than continue. Any consumer still holding an old id is calling a service that does not exist.

Two things to do before merging the update:

  1. Prove the old id is dead. stellar contract info fetch --id <OLD> --network testnet and … -- version must both fail; the event stream must answer empty. If version() replies, you are on the wrong RPC or the reset has not landed yet.
  2. Keep the superseded id in history, not in the table. The old id belongs in the commit that replaces it (git log -p docs/deployments.md), not in a "previous deployments" section — a second live-looking address on this page is exactly the fake-contract-id risk Security warns about.

docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text: How to build, test, upgrade and extend the KeyLease Soroban contracts.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Tool Version Notes Rust 1.84+ rustup install stable Wasm target wasm32v1-none rustup target add wasm32v1-none components rustfmt, clippy rustup component add rustfmt clippy Stellar CLI latest only needed to deploy, invoke, read events or upgrade on a network Node.js >= 20.11 only if you build your own JS client against Soroban RPC

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/KeyLease-Security/keylease-core
cd keylease-core
rustup target add wasm32v1-none

cargo build --all
cargo test --all

docs.title: The commands CI runs
docs.text:
These five are the definition of "green". Run all five before opening a PR.

cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --target wasm32v1-none --release --all -- -D warnings
cargo test --all
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all

CI also runs a cargo-deny dependency policy check (deny.toml), a shellcheck pass over every tracked shell script, a gitleaks secret scan, and a ClamAV malware scan over the checkout and the built Wasm artifacts. CI job names are Format, Shellcheck, Clippy, Test, Build (wasm32v1-none), SBOM (CycloneDX), Secret Scan, Dependency Policy and Malware Scan — these are the required status checks in branch protection.

SBOM (CycloneDX) generates a machine-readable inventory of the crates in the registry Wasm from Cargo.lock, stamps the workspace version and full commit SHA into its metadata, and uploads it as the sbom-cyclonedx workflow artifact. Consumers can download that artifact from the CI run for any commit to answer "which crates were compiled into this Wasm?" without rebuilding it.

The shell pass is not one of the four cargo commands, so run it separately:

git ls-files -z '*.sh' | xargs -0 shellcheck

It uses shellcheck's default severity, which includes style notes, and fails outright when no tracked script matches.

The script behaviour itself is covered by bats in tests/. The suite stubs gh, stellar, cargo and rustup on PATH (from tests/stubs), so it needs no network, credentials or Stellar toolchain:

bats tests

It covers argument parsing, the mainnet guard, --dry-run plans and the "CLI not found" branches of scripts/deploy-testnet.sh, scripts/create-issues.sh, scripts/setup-repo.sh and scripts/sandbox-local.sh.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text: Path Purpose contracts/registry/src/lib.rs Entry points, contractmeta!, upgrade, protocol lifecycle. contracts/registry/src/events.rs Typed #[contractevent] payloads. contracts/registry/src/types.rs Service, Lease, ServiceStats, LeaseStatus. contracts/registry/src/storage.rs DataKey layout, TTL policy, accessors. contracts/registry/src/errors.rs Stable Error codes (never reuse a number). contracts/registry/src/test.rs Lifecycle, SAC, events, upgrade and re-entrancy tests. contracts/mock_token/ Test/sandbox SEP-41 token. scripts/deploy-testnet.sh Sequential testnet deploy and upgrade. scripts/sandbox-local.sh Local-network sandbox: deploy, write .env.sandbox, tear down. scripts/check-no-std.sh Checks the release Wasm is built without std and crates forbid unsafe. scripts/create-issues.sh Batch Wave backlog creation. scripts/setup-repo.sh Topics, labels, branch protection. tests/ bats coverage for the shell scripts, with CLI stubs in tests/stubs.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
See .env.example for the full list.

Variable Used by Meaning KEYLEASE_NETWORK scripts, clients testnet / mainnet / futurenet / local KEYLEASE_RPC_URL scripts, clients Soroban RPC endpoint KEYLEASE_NETWORK_PASSPHRASE clients passphrase used to sign transactions KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID scripts, clients deployed KeyLeaseRegistry id KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID clients service a consumer acquires from KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS tooling SEP-41 / SAC escrow token KEYLEASE_ADMIN / KEYLEASE_PROVIDER / KEYLEASE_CONSUMER tooling Stellar addresses KEYLEASE_RATE_PER_CALL register_service stroops per call KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH register_service 64 hex chars (32 bytes)

Never commit secret seeds. .env is gitignored.

docs.title: Adding a new entry point
docs.text:
1. Add the variant(s) to errors.rs (append, never renumber).
  2. Add any new DataKey variants to storage.rs with a documented TTL policy.
  3. Implement the entry point in lib.rs, documenting auth + preconditions.
  4. Add a typed event in events.rs and publish it after the state is persisted.
  5. Add tests covering the happy path and each failure/refund path, plus the emitted event.
  6. Update the interface and event tables in README.md and docs/contract-reference.md.
  7. If the change adds or modifies exported functions, events, or error discriminants, update the ABI snapshot (see ABI snapshot).

docs.title: Code standards
docs.text:
• #![no_std] — no std in contract code; the target is wasm32v1-none.
  • All token math is checked; map failures to Error::Overflow.
  • Authenticate actors with require_auth() on the address you represent.
  • Follow checks-effects-interactions. Persist settled (or the equivalent) before any cross-contract call.
  • Guard money paths with the settled check first.
  • Bound storage. Every persistent key needs a TTL policy and, if user input controls its lifetime, an upper bound.
  • No unbounded loops over user-supplied collections.
  • Errors over panics.
  • Never reuse an error code.
  • Emit events for every state transition; never put secrets in one.

docs.title: Testing conventions
docs.text:
Use env.mock_all_auths() for happy paths and try_* client methods to assert specific errors:

assert_eq!(
    client.try_settle_lease(&provider, &lease_id, &11),
    Err(Ok(Error::InvalidCalls))
);

Event tests compare the emitted topics and payload with the event type generated by #[contractevent]:

assert_single_event(
    &env,
    &registry_id,
    &LeaseSettled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund },
);

The suite also deploys the real Stellar Asset Contract as the escrow token (env.register_stellar_asset_contract_v2), and installs a hostile SEP-41 token that re-enters settle_lease to prove the double-settlement guard holds. Keep both patterns when adding money paths.

Every security-sensitive change needs an adversarial test — an attempt to steal, strand, or double-spend.

docs.title: ABI snapshot
docs.text:
contracts/registry/abi_snapshot.json is a checked-in snapshot of the public contract ABI: exported functions, event specs, and error discriminants. The abi_snapshot test in contracts/registry/src/test_abi.rs compares the current contract surface against this file and fails on any drift.

To update the snapshot after a legitimate additive change:

UPDATE_ABI_SNAPSHOT=1 cargo test -p keylease-registry abi_snapshot -- --nocapture

Review the diff carefully — renames, removals, reordering, or discriminant changes are breaking ABI changes and should not be accepted without an explicit versioning decision.

docs.title: Releasing a version
docs.text: A release is four things: a version bump, a notes page, a check run and an annotated tag. Nothing in .github/workflows/ publishes a crate, builds a GitHub Release or cuts a tag — ci.yml only gates commits and docs.yml only builds and publishes the site — so the steps below are the whole process.

docs.title: 1. Bump the version
docs.text:
Cargo.toml carries the only version this repository reports. Both crates inherit it (version.workspace = true), so one edit covers the workspace — but two more files have to follow it.

File What changes Cargo.toml [workspace.package] version = "X.Y.Z" contracts/registry/Cargo.toml the version = "X.Y.Z" pin on the keylease-mock-token dev-dependency Cargo.lock the keylease-registry and keylease-mock-token entries — regenerate with cargo check --all and commit the diff

No other file carries a version string, because the version reaches the rest of the system through the build:

  • contractmeta!(key = "version", val = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")) embeds the new value in the Wasm, so stellar contract info meta reports it.
  • version() reads that same value, so the on-chain contract identifies itself after the upgrade — the check in Deployment.

Use the convention the existing releases already follow. 0.x.0 is a release that changes what the world sees — a new entry point, a new event, a new error code, new storage. 0.x.1 is a release that changes none of those (v0.2.1 only changed the lease TTL policy). Error codes are append-only, so a new code alone is never a major-version event.

docs.title: 2. Write the notes page
docs.text:
Add docs/releases/vX.Y.Z.md, then register it in both tables of contents — mkdocs.yml under nav: → Project: and docs/SUMMARY.md under ## Project. The newest page keeps the Release notes label and the previous ones are relabelled to their version:

  - Project:
      - Deployments: deployments.md
      - Release notes: releases/v0.2.2.md   # new
      - v0.2.1: releases/v0.2.1.md          # relabelled
      - v0.2.0: releases/v0.2.0.md
      - v0.1.0: releases/v0.1.0.md

Copy the shape from an existing page rather than inventing one:

Example What it shows v0.2.1 a behavior-only patch: the problem it solved, a short "What changed", compatibility stated as "no ABI, event, storage-key or error-code changes" v0.2.0 an additive release: new events and upgrade, a full "Interface at this tag" table, and an "Upgrading from v0.1.0" section v0.1.0 the first release, and the banner pattern a superseded page uses to point at the current interface

A notes page needs these sections, in this order:

  1. Heading and lead — # keylease-core vX.Y.Z then one paragraph saying what the release is and, when there is a reason, why it exists.
  2. Highlights or What changed — one bullet per user-visible change, each naming the entry point, constant or error code it touched.
  3. Contracts — the package → Wasm table.
  4. Interface at this tag — the entry points and their auth requirements, so the page stays readable after the reference moves on.
  5. Compatibility — Rust, soroban-sdk, Wasm target, the error-code range, and an explicit statement about storage keys and events.
  6. Upgrading from vX.Y.Z — required whenever a deployed network is running an older build; say whether upgrade is safe in place.
  7. Known limitations, Verification (the four commands), License.
  8. Artifacts — link the sbom-cyclonedx workflow artifact so consumers can see the crates compiled into the Wasm. It is generated from Cargo.lock by the CI run for the release's commit, with the workspace version and full commit in its CycloneDX metadata. Use this snippet, replacing the version and pointing at the CI run for the tag:
## Artifacts

- [CycloneDX SBOM (`sbom-cyclonedx`)](https://github.com/KeyLease-Security/keylease-core/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
  — crates compiled into this release's Wasm, generated from `Cargo.lock`
  by the CI run for its commit and stamped with the workspace version and
  commit.

Never put a secret, seed or raw credential in a notes page — including a deployer's secret key. Addresses and ledger numbers are fine and useful.

docs.title: 3. Run the checks a release is gated on
docs.text:
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --target wasm32v1-none --release --all -- -D warnings
cargo test --all
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
./scripts/check-no-std.sh --no-build
cargo deny check
./scripts/scan-malware.sh
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt && mkdocs build --strict

The first four are the CI jobs every commit must pass, and check-no-std.sh runs inside the Build (wasm32v1-none) job; cargo deny check and ./scripts/scan-malware.sh are the Dependency Policy and Malware Scan jobs run locally. mkdocs build --strict is the one that bites here, because the failure it catches is a page missing from nav: or an anchor that does not resolve. It is a pull-request gate as well as a main gate, but only for a PR that touches docs/**, mkdocs.yml or requirements-docs.txt — those paths run the Docs → Build preview job. A release branch that changes none of them, such as one that only bumps the version, gets no preview run at all, so execute the command above yourself before tagging.

docs.title: 4. Tag the release commit on main
docs.text:
Tag the merge-base commit on main that carries both the version bump and the notes page — not a branch tip that has not merged. v0.1.0 is an annotated tag, so stay annotated:

git fetch origin
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "keylease-core vX.Y.Z" origin/main
git push origin vX.Y.Z

The tag is what makes the recorded hashes meaningful: it is the revision anyone can rebuild from to reproduce the deployed Wasm.

docs.title: 5. Record the artifacts
docs.text:
Deploying is covered in Deployment; what a release must record is in Deployments, whose Recording a deployment steps this table feeds.

Artifact How to obtain it Where it is recorded Contract id stellar contract deploy prints it Testnet table, KeyLeaseRegistry Built Wasm digest sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm "Verifying a listed address" On-chain Wasm hash stellar contract upload prints it; stellar contract info hash --id $REGISTRY reads it back Testnet table, "Wasm hash" Version, as the chain sees it … -- version and stellar contract info meta --id $REGISTRY Testnet table + "On-chain metadata" (rssdkver included) Deploy-ledger trail ledger and tx hash for init, set_token, register_service, or the upgrade Testnet table rows Pre/post counters service_count, lease_count, get_service, get_lease release notes "Verified on-chain" bullet Signer addresses admin, provider, demo consumer, escrow token Testnet table Source revision the tag cut in step 4 Testnet table, "Deployed from" CycloneDX SBOM sbom-cyclonedx artifact of the tagged CI run release notes "Artifacts" link

The built digest and the on-chain hash are the same value only if the build is reproducible: check out the tag, run cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all and compare against stellar contract info hash. If they differ, the release is not verifiable from source — say so in the notes page rather than recording a hash you cannot reproduce.

docs.title: Upgrading a deployment
docs.text:
stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account admin --network testnet

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- propose_upgrade --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash <hash-from-upload>

# inspect the recorded hash and execution ledger timestamp
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --network testnet -- get_pending_upgrade

# after the 24h delay has elapsed (the contract rejects earlier calls)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- execute_upgrade --admin $ADMIN

# or abandon the proposal: -- cancel_upgrade --admin $ADMIN

Rules for upgrades:

  • Never change the DataKey layout or the meaning of stored values.
  • Append fields to a #[contracttype] struct; never reorder, rename or remove one. A struct decodes by unpacking the field names it declares, so a missing field makes existing entries undecodable. Lease.created_at is the worked example: it was appended, and storage::get_lease keeps a legacy fallback that reads pre-created_at entries and reports created_at = 0 (unknown) so settlement and refunds still work across the upgrade. Add the same fallback, or drain the affected entries, whenever you extend a stored type.
  • Never renumber or reuse an error code.
  • Keep event names and payload fields compatible; add new events for new transitions.
  • Bump the workspace version so version() and contractmeta! change.
  • Settle or revoke in-flight leases before changing token semantics.

docs.title: Reading contract state and events
docs.text:
Clients should prefer the read views and the event stream over raw storage:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger 123456

If you must read storage directly, #[contracttype] enums encode as an SCV_VEC whose first element is an SCV_SYMBOL with the variant name:

Logical key Wire key DataKey::Admin Symbol("Admin") DataKey::Lease(7) Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)] DataKey::Service(3) Vec[Symbol("Service"), u64(3)] DataKey::Settlement(7) Vec[Symbol("Settlement"), u64(7)] DataKey::CancelRequest(7) Vec[Symbol("CancelRequest"), u64(7)]

With @stellar/stellar-sdk:

import { xdr, nativeToScVal } from '@stellar/stellar-sdk';

// DataKey::Lease(leaseId)
xdr.ScVal.scvVec([
  xdr.ScVal.scvSymbol('Lease'),
  nativeToScVal(leaseId, { type: 'u64' }),
]);

getContractData returns a scvMap of the Lease struct fields. Decode it as { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, settled }. A proposed settlement is a separate Settlement(u64) entry; prefer the get_settlement view over raw storage. Full details are in the contract reference, and the supported way to verify leases is described in Integration.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text: See Deployment. scripts/deploy-testnet.sh runs the exact sequence and prints the values a client or indexer needs.

docs.title: Local sandbox walkthrough
docs.text:
The unit suite proves the contract logic inside a simulated ledger. This runs the same lifecycle against a real local network using the Wasm you just built, so you can watch one lease move value end to end.

scripts/sandbox-local.sh automates the walkthrough below: it connects to (or starts) the local network, funds three identities, deploys the registry and the mock token, registers one demo service and writes .env.sandbox. The manual sequence remains the reference for what the script runs and for stepping through a lifecycle by hand.

docs.title: Quick start with the sandbox script
docs.text:
./scripts/sandbox-local.sh              # connect or start, deploy, write .env.sandbox
./scripts/sandbox-local.sh --dry-run    # print every command; send nothing
./scripts/sandbox-local.sh --connect    # require an already running network
./scripts/sandbox-local.sh --force      # replace an existing .env.sandbox
./scripts/sandbox-local.sh --teardown   # stop the container, remove identities and .env.sandbox

The script has no NETWORK variable: every command passes --network local literally, so it cannot reach Testnet or Mainnet, and --teardown stops only the local container and removes the three kl-sandbox-* identities and .env.sandbox that it created. .env.sandbox holds public addresses and ids only — the identity seeds stay in the stellar CLI keystore — and it is gitignored.

Everything in the manual sequence below is stellar 28.1.0 syntax; if your CLI is a different version, re-read the flag with stellar <command> --help rather than assuming.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Requirement Check A running container engine (Docker, Podman or Colima). docker info answers without error. The registry Wasm built. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all Port 8000 free on localhost. stellar container start local maps 8000:8000 by default; pass -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT to move it.

docs.title: 1. Start a local network
docs.text:
stellar container start local

This runs the stellar/quickstart image with the node, Soroban RPC, Horizon and a friendbot in one container. The command has no detached mode — note that -d is --docker-host, not Docker's detach flag — so run it in its own terminal and leave it up for the rest of the walkthrough.

local is a built-in CLI network — stellar network ls already lists it, so you do not need stellar network add. It resolves to:

Network passphrase Standalone Network ; February 2017 Soroban RPC http://localhost:8000/rpc Horizon http://localhost:8000 Friendbot http://localhost:8000/friendbot?addr=<ACCOUNT>

You can confirm the RPC is up before going further:

stellar network health --network local
stellar ledger latest --network local

docs.title: 2. Create and fund three identities
docs.text:
Three separate accounts, not one: settle_lease checks service.provider == provider and revoke_expired_lease checks the lease owner. A single account for every role hides exactly the authorisation bugs a sandbox is for.

for who in kl-admin kl-provider kl-consumer; do
  stellar keys generate "$who" --network local --fund
done

--fund works on local too — the CLI posts to the container's own friendbot, the same code path as Testnet. Read a balance back to be sure the account exists:

stellar token balance --id native --account "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" --network local

docs.title: 3. Deploy the registry
docs.text:
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all

REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account kl-admin --network local | tail -n1)

docs.title: 4. Initialise, set the escrow token, publish a service
docs.text:
Each step reads what the previous one wrote, which is why the order is fixed.

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin \
  --network local --send=yes -- init --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)"

TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network local --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin \
  --network local --send=yes -- set_token \
     --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)" --token "$TOKEN"

ENDPOINT_HASH=$(printf '%s' "$(stellar keys address kl-provider):local-demo" \
  | shasum -a 256 | awk '{print $1}')

SERVICE_ID=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider \
  --network local --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 --endpoint_hash "$ENDPOINT_HASH" | tail -n1)

rate_per_call is in stroops, so 1000000 is 0.1 XLM per call.

The native SAC address is derived from the network passphrase, not assigned. On the standalone passphrase it is CDMLFMKMMD7MWZP3FKUBZPVHTUEDLSX4BYGYKH4GCESXYHS3IHQ4EIG4 — re-derive it with the command above rather than copying that value, because your own stellar network add passphrase would give a different address.

docs.title: 5. Create one lease
docs.text:
100 calls at 0.1 XLM escrows 10 XLM:

LEASE_ID=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" \
     --service_id "$SERVICE_ID" \
     --requested_calls 100 \
     --duration_secs 120 | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local -- get_lease --lease_id "$LEASE_ID"
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local -- remaining_calls --lease_id "$LEASE_ID"

Do not approve an allowance first — there is none to grant. create_lease calls transfer(consumer, contract, amount) itself under the consumer's own auth, so the consumer needs a balance, not a permission.

duration_secs is a wall-clock number, and the ledger still advances in real time. 120 seconds is enough to settle an expired lease without leaving the terminal; a day-long lease is not a sandbox demo.

docs.title: 6. Settle it
docs.text:
settle_lease proposes a payout when the lease has expired, or when the provider reports full consumption — whichever comes first. It does not move funds: the consumer has a 24-hour challenge window, after which finalize_settlement releases them. Reporting everything immediately is the fastest path through the happy case:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider \
  --network local --send=yes -- settle_lease \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
     --lease_id "$LEASE_ID" --verified_calls 100

Payout and refund must sum to the deposit, so 100 verified of 100 allocated pays the provider 10 XLM and refunds 0 once the challenge window closes and anyone calls finalize_settlement --lease_id "$LEASE_ID". Create a second lease and settle it partially before it expires to see the guard refuse:

OTHER=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" \
     --service_id "$SERVICE_ID" --requested_calls 100 --duration_secs 120 | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider \
  --network local --send=yes -- settle_lease \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
     --lease_id "$OTHER" --verified_calls 30
# Error(LeaseNotSettleable) — the lease is live and under-consumed

Wait past duration_secs and the same call succeeds, paying 3 XLM and refunding 7 XLM to the consumer. Verify it with the read views and the token itself:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  -- locked_balance --lease_id "$OTHER"      # 0 once settled
stellar token balance --id native --account "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
  --network local

docs.title: 7. Read the events
docs.text:
Note the ledger sequence before you deploy, then read the whole lifecycle out of the chain afterwards:

stellar ledger latest --network local          # write down the sequence
# ... run steps 3 to 6 ...
stellar events --id "$REGISTRY" --network local --start-ledger <that sequence> -c 50

Expect RegistryInitialized, EscrowTokenSet, ServiceRegistered, LeaseCreated, LeaseSettled. Use -c generously: the default is 10 events, and a full lifecycle plus the token transfers is more than that. Event payloads and their fields are in the contract reference.

docs.title: 8. Keep an entry alive
docs.text:
A local network is the only place this costs nothing to try. Reads never extend a storage entry, so an entry that is looked at but not written ages toward eviction until somebody bumps it explicitly.

# Both are permissionless — any account can pay for any entry's rent.
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider --network local \
  -- bump_service --service_id "$SERVICE_ID"

A successful bump is silent: no event, no field changes, and the only effect is a later liveUntilLedgerSeq plus the rent charged into the caller's fee. Lease entries need a lease that can still be acted on, because bump_lease refuses a settled one — so create a third lease and leave it unsettled:

LIVE=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" \
     --service_id "$SERVICE_ID" --requested_calls 10 --duration_secs 3600 | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer --network local \
  -- bump_lease --lease_id "$LIVE"

Then try the two refusals, because they are the reason these calls are safe to leave open to anyone. $LEASE_ID was settled in step 6, so its funds have already moved and extending it would only grow state:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider --network local \
  -- bump_lease --lease_id "$LEASE_ID"         # Error(LeaseAlreadySettled)

# A miss is an error, so nobody pays rent for an entry that is not there.
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider --network local \
  -- bump_service --service_id 404             # Error(ServiceNotFound)

bump_lease takes only a lease_id: the horizon comes from the lease's own expires_at and the contract's ceiling, never from the caller. The policy, the per-lease arithmetic and what eviction costs a consumer are in Storage classes and TTL policies.

docs.title: What differs from Testnet
docs.text:
Only the network is different; the contract, its ABI and the step order are not.

Testnet Local sandbox Network flag --network testnet --network local Who operates the network SDF you, in a container you start RPC https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org http://localhost:8000/rpc Friendbot https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=… http://localhost:8000/friendbot?addr=… Funding an identity stellar keys generate x --network testnet --fund stellar keys generate x --network local --fund — same flag Native SAC address derived from Test SDF Network ; September 2015 derived from Standalone Network ; February 2017; different address Deploy script ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh ./scripts/sandbox-local.sh, or the sequence above Contract id lifetime until the next Testnet reset until you stop the container Wiping the ledger 2–4× a year, on SDF's schedule whenever you like: stellar container stop local Value at risk fake XLM none

The commands that are identical are worth stating, because contributors expect to rewrite them: stellar contract deploy, upload, invoke, contract id asset and the --send=yes form all take the same arguments with a different --network. Nothing in contracts/ is network-aware.

docs.title: Teardown
docs.text:
stellar container stop local

# optional: the identities are only seeds on your machine
for who in kl-admin kl-provider kl-consumer; do
  stellar keys rm --force "$who"
done

stellar keys rm takes one name at a time and asks for confirmation unless you pass --force.

stellar container start uses --rm, so stopping the container discards the ledger. Starting it again gives you an empty network with the same passphrase — which means the redeploy you must now do is the same one described in After a Testnet reset, including register_service returning 1 again because ServiceCount lives in instance storage.

docs.title: Using contracts/mock_token instead of the native SAC
docs.text:
The mock token exists so a sandbox does not depend on lumens at all. It has an unlimited mint and must never be configured on a network that holds value — see contract reference.

MOCK=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_mock_token.wasm \
  --source-account kl-admin --network local | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$MOCK" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  --send=yes -- init --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)"

# Mint 1000 tokens (7 decimals) to the consumer, then point the registry at it.
stellar contract invoke --id "$MOCK" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  --send=yes -- mint --to "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" --amount 10000000000

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  --send=yes -- set_token --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)" --token "$MOCK"

From here the lease steps are unchanged: every money path goes through the token address that set_token stored, so swapping the asset changes nothing else. That indirection is also how you exercise a misbehaving token by hand — point the registry at a contract that reverts or re-enters on transfer. The automated version of exactly that attack is test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice in contracts/registry/src/test.rs.
