docs.title: Mainnet deployment and key-custody runbook
docs.text: Status: intentionally deferred. Do not deploy or execute a mainnet transaction until the maintainer-approved gate below is complete.

docs.title: Design approval gate
docs.text:
Implementation and deployment are separate decisions. Maintainer approval must record all of the following in the tracking issue or PR:

  • approved architecture and threat model;
  • completed independent security audit;
  • remediation and maintainer re-review;
  • pinned release commit and Wasm SHA-256;
  • named admin, provider, operator, signer, and recovery accounts;
  • signed mainnet transaction plan and rollback owner.

The audit/review gate passes only when all code and configuration is final, cargo fmt, cargo clippy, cargo test, and the Wasm build pass, no unresolved critical/high findings remain, and a maintainer has linked approval to the deployment ticket. "Audited" means independent review of the exact commit and Wasm, not merely review of a branch that later changed.

docs.title: Key custody
docs.text:
Use Stellar CLI identities backed by the Stellar CLI keystore. Never place seeds in .env, shell history, source files, CI logs, or deployment scripts.

Role Authority Minimum custody Admin init, token configuration, upgrade proposal/cancellation/execution Mainnet multisig account, threshold 2-of-3 or stronger Provider service registration, rates, active status, attestor and settlement Dedicated provider account Operator optional settlement-only role Separate hot wallet with no rate or ownership authority Deployer Wasm upload/deploy transactions Dedicated low-value account Recovery replace lost signer, rotate multisig, emergency upgrade/cancel Offline 2-of-3 recovery multisig, geographically separated

The admin is a Stellar account configured by init --admin; the contract stores that account and all admin entry points require it to sign. Configure the account as a multisig with named signer IDs, a low security threshold for deploy/review transactions, and a high threshold for signer replacement and recovery. Store one signing key offline and one in an independently managed HSM or secure enclave. The second operator key is not an emergency admin.

Provider and operator keys must be rotated by revoking the old operator or replacing provider-controlled service configuration. For provider-key loss, disable new leases, revoke affected operators, halt payouts if implemented, and migrate services through the maintainer-approved service-transfer procedure. For admin signer loss, use the recovery quorum to remove the signer and raise thresholds; if the admin key itself is lost, recovery requires the original admin account's multisig recovery process and the deployed contract cannot be made to trust a new address without an upgrade.

docs.title: Pre-deployment checklist
docs.text:
1. Pin the release commit and verify a clean worktree.
  2. Run all gates and archive complete outputs:
git rev-parse HEAD
git status --porcelain
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --all
rustup target add wasm32v1-none
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm
  1. Independently reproduce the Wasm hash from a clean checkout.
  2. Confirm RPC, network passphrase, native SAC/token id, multisig threshold, provider address, endpoint hash, and planned service id.
  3. Dry-run every command and obtain recorded maintainer approval.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Set public values only. Signing identities remain in the Stellar CLI keystore.

export NETWORK=mainnet
export RPC_URL=https://<approved-mainnet-rpc>
export DEPLOYER=keylease-mainnet-deployer
export ADMIN=G<MAINNET_MULTISIG_ADDRESS>
export PROVIDER=G<DEDICATED_PROVIDER_ADDRESS>
export TOKEN=C<APPROVED_SEP41_TOKEN_ADDRESS>
export ENDPOINT_HASH=<64-HEX-CHARACTERS>
export RATE_PER_CALL=<STROOPS_PER_CALL>

stellar network add mainnet \
  --rpc-url "$RPC_URL" \
  --network-passphrase "Public Global Stellar Network ; September 2015"

stellar contract upload \
  target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account "$DEPLOYER" --network "$NETWORK"

REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account "$DEPLOYER" --network "$NETWORK")

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" --send=yes -- \
  init --admin "$ADMIN"

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" --send=yes -- \
  set_token --admin "$ADMIN" --token "$TOKEN"

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$PROVIDER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" --send=yes -- \
  register_service --provider "$PROVIDER" \
  --rate_per_call "$RATE_PER_CALL" --endpoint_hash "$ENDPOINT_HASH"

Expected:

  • upload output is the Wasm hash and it equals the pinned SHA-256;
  • deploy output starts with C and is the new contract id;
  • init, set_token, and register_service each return success and emit registry_initialized, escrow_token_set, and service_registered;
  • no mock token or test identity is used.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run reads and record transaction hashes, ledger numbers, contract id, and output:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- version
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- get_token
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- get_service --service_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- service_count

Expected: version() equals the workspace release version; get_admin() equals $ADMIN; get_token() equals $TOKEN; service 1 has $PROVIDER, $RATE_PER_CALL, and $ENDPOINT_HASH; service_count equals 1. Independently verify contract metadata, Wasm hash, events, and live balances in a block explorer. A maintainer must sign off the verification record before any consumer funds are advertised.

docs.title: Monitor
docs.text:
Run 24/7 alerting for:

  • every lease_created, lease_settled, lease_revoked, and lease_cancelled event;
  • aggregate payout increase or circuit pause event;
  • payout/refund conservation mismatch;
  • unexpected admin, token, provider, operator, upgrade, or rate change;
  • RPC or ledger lag, failed authentication, and contract balance anomalies;
  • consumer or provider token balances diverging from published settlement totals.

Example event query:

stellar events --id "$REGISTRY" --network "$NETWORK" --start-ledger "$START_LEDGER"

Only an RPC endpoint whose event window is documented may be used. If the window does not cover the deployment ledger, restore an independently managed indexer and retain signed query results. Alerts require a human acknowledgement; indexing alone is not sufficient.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
Upgrades require the 24-hour proposal delay and an approved maintenance window.

NEW_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account "$DEPLOYER" --network "$NETWORK")

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" --send=yes -- \
  propose_upgrade --admin "$ADMIN" --new_wasm_hash "$NEW_HASH"

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- get_pending_upgrade

Wait until execute_after plus at least 24 hours and re-run audit diff, verification, Wasm hash, and signer approval. To execute:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" --send=yes -- \
  execute_upgrade --admin "$ADMIN"

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" -- version

Expected execute_upgrade to return success and emit contract_upgraded; version() must equal the pinned release. To cancel before execution:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account "$DEPLOYER" \
  --network "$NETWORK" --send=yes -- \
  cancel_upgrade --admin "$ADMIN"

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If verification fails or anomalous payouts occur:

  1. Do not send a new lease or payout transaction.
  2. Pause the service, revoke operators, or raise/circuit-break per the approved incident runbook.
  3. If an upgrade was proposed, execute cancel_upgrade from the multisig and verify no pending proposal remains.
  4. Keep the contract id and existing leases unchanged; no funds can be reclaimed globally by redeploying.
  5. If the deployed Wasm is malicious or materially defective, use the approved upgrade to a pinned remediated Wasm after re-audit; otherwise continue only the consumer revoke and documented settlement paths.
  6. Publish incident status, affected ledger range, token balances, transaction hashes, and a recovery decision.

Rollback is not "deploy the old Wasm" unless the old Wasm hash was built from an audited, storage-compatible revision and the proposal delay/maintainer gate has passed. Never overwrite the contract id or migrate balances manually.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: KeyLease is deployed per Stellar network. Everything that differs between environments is a network name, an RPC endpoint and a network passphrase — the contract and its ABI are identical.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
Network Passphrase RPC Notes Testnet Test SDF Network ; September 2015 https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org SDF-hosted; resets 2–4× per year Futurenet Test SDF Future Network ; October 2022 https://rpc-futurenet.stellar.org SDF-hosted; previews protocol changes Mainnet Public Global Stellar Network ; September 2015 third-party only, e.g. https://mainnet.sorobanrpc.com SDF does not host a mainnet RPC Local standalone Standalone Network ; February 2017 http://localhost:8000/rpc stellar container start local — see the local sandbox walkthrough

The CLI resolves these names from its config:

stellar network ls
stellar network use testnet

Read calls need a source account. stellar contract invoke builds a simulation transaction, so even read-only functions need a funded --source-account (any identity works; it only pays simulation fees). Contract events are fetched without a signer:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

docs.title: Escrow asset: the native SAC
docs.text:
On Testnet the usual escrow asset is the native Stellar Asset Contract for XLM. Its address is derived from the network passphrase, not invented:

stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native

Any SEP-41 token can be configured instead with set_token; the derive command above is only for the native asset. The admin must call set_token before any lease can be created (TokenNotSet otherwise).

docs.title: Native SAC vs. Custom SEP-41 Token
docs.text:
KeyLease accepts any contract implementing the SEP-41 token standard. Operators evaluating which asset to configure should consider the architectural and operational trade-offs:

Characteristic Native SAC (XLM) Custom SEP-41 Token / Classic SAC Issuance Native protocol asset built into the Stellar consensus layer Minted by an issuer account (classic asset wrapper) or custom token contract Trustlines None required; every funded Stellar account natively holds XLM Classic assets require explicit trustlines (ChangeTrust); contract-native tokens manage balances internally Decimals Fixed at 7 decimals (1 stroop = 0.0000001 XLM) Configurable (commonly 7 for classic wrapped assets, 6 for USDC, or 18 for EVM-style tokens) Admin controls None. No freeze, no clawback, no issuer key, no upgradeability Issuer may configure clawback, authorization flags (auth_required), pausing, or contract upgradeability Escrow guarantees Escrow lock and transfer are guaranteed by host runtime; zero re-entrancy or transfer-failure risk Follows identical SEP-41 contract interface, but subject to issuer freeze, clawback, or contract bugs

docs.title: Escrow guarantees and risk profile
docs.text:
From KeyLease's perspective, both token types interact through the same standard interface (token::Client). Escrow invariants (payout + refund == locked_deposit) hold equally across both.

However, external contract risk differs:

  • Native SAC: The transfer cannot be blocked, paused, or redirected by any third party.
  • Custom Token: If a custom token contract fails, pauses, or blacklists a participant, calls to settle_lease or revoke_expired_lease will revert. KeyLease uses checks-effects-interactions (lease.settled = true persisted before transfer) to prevent double-spend or re-entrancy attacks, but cannot force a failing external token to execute transfers.

docs.title: Deployment recommendations
docs.text:
• Testnet: Use the Native SAC (XLM). It requires zero setup, is automatically derived from the network passphrase, and accounts can be funded immediately via Friendbot.
  • Mainnet: Use USDC via SAC for commercial API and RPC leases where price volatility between fiat costs and crypto balances is undesirable. Use Native SAC (XLM) for network infrastructure services, peer-to-peer compute, or micro-metered telemetry where native settlement is preferred.

docs.title: Funding accounts
docs.text:
Friendbot funds accounts and contracts with 10,000 fake XLM on Testnet:

stellar keys generate consumer --network testnet --fund
# or, for an address you already have:
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address consumer)"

The CLI's --fund flag and the HTTP endpoint above are for networks with a friendbot: Testnet, and the local container's own friendbot at http://localhost:8000/friendbot (stellar keys generate x --network local --fund hits it). Mainnet has neither and requires real XLM for fees and for the escrowed asset. See Developer guide → Local sandbox walkthrough.

docs.title: Testnet resets
docs.text:
Testnet resets wipe all ledger entries, including the deployed contract, services and leases, 2–4 times per year at 17:00 UTC.

After a reset, the contract id changes. Re-run scripts/deploy-testnet.sh and update docs/deployments.md.

docs.title: What a reset actually takes
docs.text:
A reset is not a data purge of the deployment — it is a purge of the whole ledger, so plan for these to be gone:

Gone Survives The registry contract instance, its Wasm reference and its contractmeta!. Your local Stellar CLI identities. Seeds are stored on your machine, so KEYLEASE_ADMIN / KEYLEASE_PROVIDER / KEYLEASE_CONSUMER keep the same G… addresses. All instance storage: Admin, Token, ServiceCount, LeaseCount. The native SAC address. It is derived from the network passphrase, which a reset does not change — re-derive it with stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native and expect the same value. All persistent storage: every Service(id) and Lease(id) entry. The repository, its CI, and your built Wasm. Every funded account, including the SAC balances and any open lease's escrow. Nothing on-chain that identifies your old deployment.

Open leases are the expensive part: their Lease entries, and therefore their refund paths, are gone. Testnet escrow is fake XLM, so the loss is nuisance rather than damage, but any indexer or provider middleware that caches lease state has to be rewound too.

docs.title: After a Testnet reset
docs.text:
Redeploy in dependency order — the same order scripts/deploy-testnet.sh enforces, because each step reads what the previous one wrote.

cd keylease-core && git fetch origin && git switch main && git pull --ff-only

# 1. Re-create and re-fund the signing identity (Friendbot creates the account
#    if it is missing; the address is the same as before the reset).
stellar keys generate keylease-admin --network testnet --fund
#    Reusing an existing seed instead of generating one:
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)"

# 2. Build, deploy, init, set_token and register_service in one pass.
SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

The script's steps 2–5 are the redeploy, re-init, token-set and re-register steps. Run them individually only if you need to interpose something:

REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)"

TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token \
     --admin "$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)" --token "$TOKEN"

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)" \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 --endpoint_hash <64_HEX_CHARS>

register_service returns 1 again. That is expected, not a collision: ServiceCount lived in instance storage, and the instance is new. Lease ids restart the same way. Consumers holding a service_id from before the reset must re-read it from Deployments or from the script output.

docs.title: After a reset: update the record and the config
docs.text:
1. .env — copy the values the script prints. The three that change every reset are KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID, KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID and, if you rebuilt, nothing else; KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS, KEYLEASE_NETWORK, KEYLEASE_RPC_URL and the account addresses do not change. Restart anything that reads the file — clients pick the contract id up at construction.
  2. docs/deployments.md — replace the Testnet row's KeyLeaseRegistry id, contract version, Wasm hash, the Contract created ledger and the four tx links for init / set_token / register_service. Leave the "Escrow token (native SAC)" row alone unless you switched assets. Follow Recording a deployment, and tag the revision so a reader can tie the new ids to a commit.
  3. Cursors — an indexer following the old contract id has nothing to read and will not error loudly. Point it at the new id and start it at the deployment ledger; see Integration.

docs.title: Check the old contract id is dead
docs.text:
Do this before announcing the new id, so a stale pointer cannot be mistaken for a working one. Both commands must fail, because no ledger entry backs the old id:

OLD=CCEZYHUJUICXVPLH6UC2OFZL2RG23QQ7EMZOWE32WVQPT25DCTIAFH62   # from git history

stellar contract info fetch --id "$OLD" --network testnet
stellar contract invoke --id "$OLD" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- version
stellar events --id "$OLD" --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger just after the reset>

info fetch reports the entry is missing and the invoke fails during simulation — there is no instance to load. stellar events answers with an empty list, not an error: absence of history is the same fact stated quietly.

If version() answers, you are not looking at a reset network. Either the reset has not happened yet, or the RPC you are pointing at is a different network — check stellar network ls and the passphrase above before publishing anything.

docs.title: Explorer links
docs.text:
Each network has a contract explorer. Substitute the id from Deployments:

Network Contract URL Testnet https://stellar.expert/explorer/testnet/contract/<CONTRACT_ID> Mainnet https://stellar.expert/explorer/public/contract/<CONTRACT_ID>

docs.title: RPC production notes
docs.text:
• Testnet and Futurenet public RPCs are rate-limited. They are fine for demos and reads, not for a busy provider.
  • For production, use an authenticated RPC provider and pass its URL through KEYLEASE_RPC_URL.
  • A provider's verification path fails closed when RPC is unreachable: it must reject requests rather than admit unverified ones. No funds move either way, and settlement/revocation remain possible directly through the contract.

docs.title: Read next
docs.text:
• Deployment — the ordered sequence.
  • Integration — how to read leases and events from a service.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
Actor Address Can do Admin one Stellar account init once, set_token, propose_upgrade/execute_upgrade/cancel_upgrade (24h delay), propose_admin / cancel_admin_transfer. Cannot move escrowed funds. Provider per service (account or contract address) Register/pause services, settle leases it owns. Consumer per lease (account or contract address) Create leases, revoke expired unsettled leases. Delegate optional, any account Sponsor create_lease_for for a consumer. Pays the transaction fee only — never the deposit, and holds no claim on the lease.

The admin is a deployment role. It can point the registry at a token address and install a new Wasm, and nothing else. It has no path to user funds. The role is rotated in two steps: the admin proposes a successor with propose_admin, and the successor takes over by calling accept_admin within seven days. Both signatures are required, so neither party (nor anyone else) can move the role alone.

Because every actor is a Soroban Address, the same protocol works for classic Stellar accounts (G…), multisig accounts and smart contracts (C…).

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
pub struct Service {
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub provider: Address,
    pub rate_per_call: i128,   // smallest unit of the escrow token
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
}

A service is not an endpoint URL and not a credential. It is a price and a commitment. endpoint_hash is a 32-byte digest of the provider's off-chain descriptor, so the on-chain record proves what the endpoint should be without publishing anything secret.

docs.title: Lease
docs.text:
pub struct Lease {
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub consumer: Address,
    pub allocated_calls: u32,
    pub used_calls: u32,
    pub created_at: u64,       // unix seconds, ledger time of create_lease
    pub expires_at: u64,       // created_at + duration_secs
    pub locked_deposit: i128,  // rate_per_call * allocated_calls
    pub settled: bool,
}

created_at and expires_at are both ledger timestamps, so a lease's age, remaining term and original duration (expires_at - created_at) can be derived from the stored lease alone. A created_at of 0 marks a lease written by a release that predates the field; such leases remain settleable and report an unknown creation time (see the contract reference).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active: create_lease / create_lease_for<br/>(escrow rate × calls)
    Active --> Expired: now ≥ expires_at
    Active --> SettlementPending: settle_lease<br/>(verified_calls == allocated_calls)
    Expired --> SettlementPending: settle_lease<br/>(provider, within grace)
    Expired --> Revoked: revoke_expired_lease<br/>(consumer, after 24h grace)
    SettlementPending --> Challenged: challenge_settlement<br/>(consumer, inside 24h)
    Challenged --> SettlementPending: cancel_challenge
    SettlementPending --> Settled: finalize_settlement<br/>(window closed)
    Challenged --> Settled: resolve_challenge<br/>(admin)
    Settled --> [*]
    Revoked --> [*]

A settlement is a two-phase flow. settle_lease proposes a payout and refund but moves nothing; the consumer has 24 hours to dispute the reported call count; only after that window closes do the funds leave escrow. A raised dispute is decided by the registry admin. A lease the provider never settles can be reclaimed after the 24-hour expiry grace, ending as Revoked instead of Settled.

lease_status derives the state from settled, expires_at and the lease's revocation marker:

Status Discriminant Condition Active 0 not settled, now < expires_at Expired 1 not settled, now ≥ expires_at Settled 2 settled == true, provider was paid or a settlement is committed Revoked 3 settled == true, consumer reclaimed the deposit

Discriminants are stable on the wire. They will never be renumbered, and Revoked was appended as 3 rather than replacing Settled, so a client written before the change still decodes every pre-existing lease. The two closed states share the same stored settled flag — Lease layout is frozen — and are told apart by the LeaseRevoked(lease_id) marker the registry writes when a consumer reclaims.

docs.title: Two ways to close a lease, one stored flag
docs.text:
settled records that escrow has left the contract — it does not record why. Both terminal transitions set it: settle_lease after paying the provider, and revoke_expired_lease after refunding the consumer in full. Error::LeaseAlreadySettled (7) keeps that combined meaning: either way the escrow is gone, so neither path may run twice.

Why it left is recorded separately, in the LeaseRevoked(lease_id) marker that revoke_expired_lease writes before the refund. It is a second key rather than a Lease field because the stored struct is part of the decoding ABI: a new field would stop live leases from decoding. lease_status reads the flag, the marker and the clock, and so answers "did the provider earn?" directly:

Lifecycle event settled used_calls lease_status create_lease false 0 Active settle_lease(320) of 500, after expiry true 320 Settled settle_lease(0) of 500, after expiry true 0 Settled revoke_expired_lease after the grace window true 0 Revoked

One row still needs the event to be read fully: settle_lease(0) — the provider's legitimate way of refunding a lease it could not serve — is Settled with used_calls == 0, so the status says "no revenue" without naming it as a refund. lease_settled carries payout = 0 and refund for that lease, and it is the record an accountant should trust anyway.

The full state-by-event table, including remaining_calls and locked_balance, is in LeaseStatus and the settled flag, and how to consume the two events is in Following the event stream.

lease_status reports Settled as soon as a settlement is proposed, because the lease itself can no longer change. Read get_settlement to distinguish a pending or challenged settlement from funds that have actually been released (SettlementState::Finalized).

docs.title: When can a lease be settled?
docs.text:
settle_lease reverts with LeaseNotSettleable unless either:

  • the lease has expired (now ≥ expires_at), or
  • verified_calls == allocated_calls.

The second clause is the "consumer got what it paid for" fast path: if every allocated call was consumed, the provider should not have to wait for expiry to be paid.

Settlement itself does not pay out. It writes a Settlement entry with state = Pending and challengeable_until = now + CHALLENGE_WINDOW_SECS (24 hours). During that window the consumer may challenge the reported call count with an evidence commitment; otherwise anyone can call finalize_settlement once the window closes.

docs.title: The consumer challenge window
docs.text:
Timestamp challenge_settlement finalize_settlement now < challengeable_until allowed ChallengeWindowStillOpen now ≥ challengeable_until ChallengeWindowClosed allowed if Pending
  • A challenge stores a 32-byte evidence hash and freezes the settlement. While it is active, finalize_settlement returns SettlementChallenged.
  • The consumer may cancel a challenge. The settlement returns to Pending; the original deadline is unchanged and cancellation never pays early.
  • The admin resolves an active challenge. Upholding it refunds the entire deposit to the consumer and pays the provider nothing; rejecting it releases the original proposal. Resolution may happen before or after the window closes.
  • Once finalized, the settlement is immutable and the lease can never be settled or revoked again.

The lease is marked settled at proposal time, so the consumer cannot revoke while a proposal is pending. The challenge window, not the revoke path, is the consumer's remedy from that point.

docs.title: Transferring a lease
docs.text:
The current consumer may hand a lease to another address with transfer_lease(consumer, lease_id, new_consumer). The transfer is an assignment — the recipient does not accept — and it moves both the access right and the refund path, because every path reads the single Lease.consumer field.

  • Only an unsettled, unrevoked lease can be transferred (LeaseNotTransferable).
  • Self-transfers are rejected (InvalidConsumer).
  • An expired but unsettled lease may be transferred: access has lapsed, but the refund claim still belongs to the consumer and can change hands until the provider settles or the consumer revokes.
  • A transfer emits lease_transferred { lease_id, from, to }, which indexers use to keep an ownership projection current.
  • Providers must treat lease.consumer as mutable: a stale cache can keep admitting the previous owner, so re-read on an ownership mismatch.

A proposed settlement sets settled, so ownership freezes when the provider proposes a split: the new consumer of record is the one who can challenge and receive the refund.

docs.title: Early cancellation with provider consent
docs.text:
A consumer that stops using a service does not have to wait for expiry plus the 24-hour grace window. They can ask the provider to end the lease early:

  1. request_early_cancel(consumer, lease_id) — consumer auth; requires an unsettled, unexpired lease and no pending request. Moves no funds.
  2. The provider either reject_early_cancel(provider, lease_id) (request cleared, lease unchanged) or approve_early_cancel(provider, lease_id, verified_calls) (report served calls and release funds immediately).
  3. The consumer may withdraw_early_cancel(consumer, lease_id) at any time.

Approval is a consented early settlement. The refund is defined exactly:

payout = rate_per_call × verified_calls
unused_calls = allocated_calls − verified_calls
refund = rate_per_call × unused_calls

Every step uses checked arithmetic and payout + refund must equal locked_deposit. The rate is an integer price per whole call, so there is no division and no rounding: the refund is the exact value of the unused calls.

Approval settles the lease, emits lease_cancelled { lease_id, provider, consumer, verified_calls, payout, refund }, and removes the request. The lease can no longer be settled or revoked. A request cannot be filed after expiry — the post-expiry revoke path remains the fallback when a provider is unresponsive — but a request filed before expiry may be approved after it.

docs.title: The 24-hour grace window
docs.text:
After expiry there is a 24-hour window (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400) during which only the provider can settle. Once it elapses, the consumer may call revoke_expired_lease and reclaim the entire deposit.

expires_at ────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬──────────────▶ time
                               │                             │
                        expiry reached              expires_at + 24h
                               │                             │
        provider may settle for the whole window    consumer may revoke
                               │                             │
                        ───────┴──── provider grace ─────────┘

Why a grace window at all? Without it, a provider that was offline for a minute at expiry would lose a legitimate payout to a consumer racing to revoke. The window gives providers a guaranteed settlement period while keeping the consumer's exit bounded at 24 hours.

docs.title: Exact grace-window boundaries
docs.text:
The contract evaluates time against ledger timestamp (env.ledger().timestamp()). The exact inclusive and exclusive boundary conditions are:

Condition / Interval Status (lease_status) settle_lease (Provider) revoke_expired_lease (Consumer) Allowed Transitions now < expires_at Active (0) Allowed only if verified_calls == allocated_calls; otherwise reverts (LeaseNotSettleable) Reverts (LeaseNotExpired) Early full-consumption settlement only now == expires_at Expired (1) Allowed for any verified_calls <= allocated_calls Reverts (RevokeWindowNotElapsed) Provider settlement begins expires_at <= now < expires_at + 86_400 Expired (1) Allowed for any verified_calls <= allocated_calls Reverts (RevokeWindowNotElapsed) Exclusive provider settlement window now >= expires_at + 86_400 Expired (1) Allowed if not yet revoked; reverts (LeaseAlreadySettled) once revoked Allowed; refunds 100% of locked deposit to consumer Consumer revocation enabled (first revocable second is expires_at + 86_400)

docs.title: Boundary verification tests
docs.text:
These boundary conditions are unit-tested and asserted in contracts/registry/src/test.rs:

  • test_revoke_before_expiry_is_rejected: verifies that when now < expires_at, revoke_expired_lease returns Err(Error::LeaseNotExpired).
  • test_full_usage_can_settle_before_expiry: confirms early settlement when verified_calls == allocated_calls even when now < expires_at.
  • test_provider_can_settle_within_grace_window: confirms provider payout at expires_at + GRACE / 2 (12 hours into grace).
  • test_revoke_during_grace_window_is_rejected: asserts revoke_expired_lease reverts with Err(Error::RevokeWindowNotElapsed) at expires_at + GRACE - 1 (the final second of provider grace).
  • test_expired_unsettled_lease_is_fully_reclaimed: verifies consumer revocation succeeds at exactly expires_at + GRACE, returning 100% of escrowed deposit.
  • test_lease_ttl_ask_floors_once_the_grace_window_is_past: ensures storage rent bumps clamp gracefully after the grace period has elapsed.

docs.title: Who may act, and what each path writes
docs.text:
The arrows themselves — including the two transfers on the settlement path — are drawn in Architecture — The money paths in order. What the timing needs alongside it is the pairing of authorization and state write, because that pairing is what makes the deadline safe to race: every transition is recorded before money moves, so the actor that arrives second reverts instead of paying twice.

Transition Authenticates Timing required Written before any token call Money moved Error if too early settle_lease provider, and it must own the service expired, or verified_calls == allocated_calls used_calls, settled = true payout + refund LeaseNotSettleable (8) revoke_expired_lease consumer, and it must be the lease's now ≥ expires_at + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS settled = true only full locked_deposit LeaseNotExpired (9), then RevokeWindowNotElapsed (10)

Two consequences worth stating plainly:

  • A revoke leaves used_calls at 0, so a revoked lease is book-keeping-wise a lease that was never paid for; a settlement always satisfies payout + refund == locked_deposit. The same ambiguity, with the read that separates the two paths, is tabulated in LeaseStatus and the settled flag.
  • The grace window ends the provider's guarantee, not the provider's option: settle_lease has no upper deadline, so after expires_at + 24h either actor can still finish the lease and the first transaction to land wins. That is why consumers are told to act, not to assume the refund is automatic.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Every transition publishes a typed Soroban event. Event names are the first topic, followed by the id fields marked #[topic]; the payload is a map of the remaining fields. Each payload also carries schema_version, so a stream that spans a contract upgrade stays decodable (see Integration → Event schema version).

Event Topics Data registry_initialized — schema_version, admin escrow_token_set — schema_version, admin, token service_registered service_id schema_version, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash service_status_changed service_id schema_version, provider, is_active lease_created lease_id schema_version, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit lease_transferred lease_id schema_version, from, to lease_settlement_proposed lease_id schema_version, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund, challengeable_until lease_challenged lease_id schema_version, consumer, evidence_hash lease_challenge_cancelled lease_id schema_version, consumer lease_challenge_resolved lease_id schema_version, admin, upheld lease_cancellation_requested lease_id schema_version, consumer lease_cancellation_rejected lease_id schema_version, provider lease_cancellation_withdrawn lease_id schema_version, consumer lease_cancelled lease_id schema_version, provider, consumer, verified_calls, payout, refund lease_delegated lease_id schema_version, delegate, consumer lease_settled lease_id schema_version, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund lease_revoked lease_id schema_version, consumer, refund contract_upgraded — schema_version, admin, new_wasm_hash schema_migrated — schema_version, admin, from_version, to_version admin_transfer_proposed — schema_version, admin, new_admin, expires_at admin_transfer_canceled — schema_version, admin, new_admin admin_transfer_accepted — schema_version, previous_admin, new_admin

lease_delegated follows lease_created only for a sponsored lease, so indexers that ignore it still see every lease.

Events are the indexing contract between on-chain state and off-chain systems: a provider can settle from a projection built by subscribing to lease_created, and accounting can reconcile payouts from lease_settled without polling every lease. See Integration.

docs.title: Worked economics
docs.text:
All figures use the escrow token's smallest unit (7 decimals for the native asset, so 1 XLM = 10_000_000).

Suppose a provider registers a service at rate_per_call = 1_000_000 (0.1 XLM per call), and a consumer buys 500 calls for 1 hour.

1. create_lease

required_deposit = rate_per_call × requested_calls
                 = 1_000_000 × 500
                 = 500_000_000        (50 XLM)

The registry transfers 500_000_000 from the consumer into escrow and sets expires_at = now + 3600.

2a. settle_lease after 1 hour with 320 calls consumed

payout = 1_000_000 × 320 = 320_000_000   (32 XLM to the provider)
refund = 500_000_000 − 320_000_000
       = 180_000_000                     (18 XLM back to the consumer)

Those amounts stay in escrow for the 24-hour challenge window. If the consumer does not dispute them, finalize_settlement releases 32 XLM to the provider and 18 XLM to the consumer. If the admin upholds a challenge, the provider receives 0 and the consumer receives the full 50 XLM.

2b. Provider goes dark; consumer calls revoke_expired_lease after 24h

refund = locked_deposit = 500_000_000    (50 XLM, the full deposit)

2c. Consumer burns all 500 calls in 10 minutes

settle_lease is immediately allowed (verified_calls == allocated_calls):

payout = 1_000_000 × 500 = 500_000_000   (50 XLM)
refund = 0

docs.title: What a lease costs
docs.text:
Three different things are paid for when a lease is taken, and only one of them comes back. The table below holds the allotment fixed at the worked example — 500 calls at rate_per_call = 1_000_000 — and changes only the duration.

Lease shape duration_secs Deposit in escrow TTL the contract asks for Effective life on Testnet Short — 1 hour 3_600 500_000_000 (50 XLM) 35,280 ledgers 120,960 (the network floor, ≈7 days) Medium — 1 day 86_400 500_000_000 (50 XLM) 51,840 ledgers 120,960 (the network floor, ≈7 days) Long — 7 days 604_800 500_000_000 (50 XLM) 155,520 ledgers 155,520 (≈9 days) Longest — 30 days 2_592_000 500_000_000 (50 XLM) 552,960 ledgers 552,960 (≈32 days)

The deposit column never moves. The deposit is rate_per_call × requested_calls, and duration_secs does not appear in it: the same 500 calls cost the same 50 XLM whether the window is an hour or a month, and they are refundable in exactly the same proportions. The deposit is only bounded above, by MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT = 1_000_000_000_000 base units — two thousand times the example above — so an ordinary lease never meets the cap.

Duration changes the rent line. save_lease extends the lease entry for its remaining term, the 24-hour settlement grace window and a one-day read buffer, which is the lease_ttl_extend column. At creation the remaining term is the whole duration, so the ask is (duration + 86_400) / 5 + 17_280 ledgers, clamped to min(MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS, network maxEntryTtl). The clamp never binds a legal lease: the longest one asks for 552,960 ledgers against a 1,555,200-ledger ceiling. The first two rows land under the Testnet minimum persistent TTL, so an hour and a day cost the same here — buying a longer window only starts to cost more once it exceeds the floor.

Bumping a lease later is a smaller ask, because the same formula is applied to the time still remaining rather than to the original term; see bump_lease.

Counting transactions. A normal lifecycle is two of them: create_lease and settle_lease. The refund path is also two: create_lease and revoke_expired_lease. There is no per-call transaction — the provider settles with a single verified_calls figure, which is what makes small allotments worthwhile.

docs.title: Which of those costs come back
docs.text:
Cost Paid by Paid when Refundable Token deposit consumer create_lease Partly: locked_deposit − payout on settlement, payout being what the provider actually served Token deposit, undisbursed consumer create_lease Fully, 100%: on revoke_expired_lease after the grace window, and on a settlement with verified_calls = 0 Soroban transaction fee whoever sends the call every transaction No. It pays for block space and goes to the network Soroban storage rent whoever makes the write that extends the entry create_lease, then again at settle or revoke No, and it is prepaid. Settling an hour into a thirty-day lease does not refund the ledgers you will never use

So the consumer's token exposure is always reversible — the protocol's whole point — while the network's fees are spent the moment the transaction lands. Rent is charged again at settlement because settling rewrites the lease entry, which is one reason the provider, not the consumer, is expected to call it.

docs.title: What this page will not tell you
docs.text: Rent in XLM is not a contract constant. It is the entry's byte size times the number of ledgers it is kept alive, times a per-ledger price the network sets, and that price differs between Testnet and mainnet. The only figures in this repository that were actually measured are the Testnet ones in deployments, and they include a minimum-TTL floor that mainnet does not share. Size a real allotment against the fees of the network you deploy to — stellar network settings, or your RPC provider — before quoting a per-call price.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
These must hold for every reachable state. They are asserted in tests.

  1. Conservation. For every settlement, payout + refund == locked_deposit.
  2. Single release. A settled lease can never be settled or revoked again (LeaseAlreadySettled), and a finalized settlement is persisted before any token call.
  3. Bounded claim. A provider can never receive more than allocated_calls × rate_per_call, and only for a service it owns.
  4. Locked while disputed. No payout leaves escrow while a challenge is active; only the admin can resolve it.
  5. Consented early exit. An early cancellation releases rate × served_calls to the provider and rate × unused_calls to the consumer, with payout + refund == locked_deposit, and only after the provider approves.
  6. Guaranteed exit. Every lease has a consumer path to a full refund, through the revoke path, the challenge path or an approved early cancellation.
  7. Checked math. Deposit, payout and timestamp arithmetic abort on overflow rather than truncating.
  8. Claimable storage. A lease's persistent entry outlives its term plus the grace window (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS = 30 days), so does the revocation marker recorded against it, and settlement entries are kept for the standard persistent horizon.
  9. Funded, computable prices. register_service rejects rate_per_call above MAX_RATE_PER_CALL, and create_lease rejects a rate_per_call × requested_calls above MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT. The two bounds are the same number, so every listed price can fund at least a one-call lease and no accepted lease can quote a deposit i128 cannot hold.
  10. Refund ownership. Whoever created a lease — consumer or delegate — the consumer is debited, is the refund recipient, and is the only address that can revoke.
  11. Distinct closure. A lease closed by the provider reads Settled; one reclaimed by the consumer or ended by a cancellation the provider declined reads differently from revenue. Only finalized settlements that paid the provider enter service_stats.
  12. Single owner. Lease.consumer is the only ownership record, so a transfer moves access and the refund path in one save. A proposed settlement freezes that field until the dispute is resolved.

docs.title: Storage and lifetime
docs.text:
Key Storage Notes Admin, Token instance configuration; instance TTL is bumped on every state change PendingAdmin instance at most one admin hand-over awaiting acceptance; cleared on accept or cancel ServiceCount, LeaseCount instance monotonic id counters SchemaVersion instance storage schema the data conforms to; state-changing calls stop while it differs from the running Wasm's Service(u64) persistent TTL extended on save, on create_lease and by bump_service, never by a read Lease(u64) persistent TTL extended on save and by bump_lease, never by a read ProviderServices(Address) persistent service-id index per provider; extended by save_service, never by a read Settlement(u64) persistent keyed by lease id; extended on save to the ~30-day horizon CancelRequest(u64) persistent pending early-cancellation request; cleared on withdraw/reject/approve

LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD = 17_280 ledgers (~1 day at 5s ledgers) and LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND = 518_400 ledgers (~30 days). For leases, save_lease and bump_lease extend to (expires_at − now + 24h) / 5s + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD ledgers, so the escrow stays claimable for the whole lease, the provider's grace window and a one-day read buffer — without paying rent for unused storage time. Once a lease is past its term and grace window that ask settles at about two days, so keeping a dead lease alive costs rent per bump rather than per month.

Rent scales with that ask: at the ledger where an extension is due, bump_lease estimates 48,684 stroops of persistent rent for a 30-day-term lease against zero for get_lease, which is why reads do not extend. MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS (1,555,200 ledgers ≈ 90 days) caps any single extension, and the cap is also taken against the network's live maxEntryTtl, so an entry's horizon is never derived from stored expires_at alone.

docs.title: The provider index
docs.text:
ProviderServices(provider) holds that provider's service_ids, oldest first. Its lifetime rules are the service rules, not a new third policy:

  • Written with the record. save_service appends to the index and extends it in the same step it stores the Service, with the same clamped horizon, so an entry and the index row that points at it cannot drift apart in rent terms.
  • Refreshed by any write to the catalogue, not by reading it. save_service also runs on set_service_active, whose id is already in the index, so pausing or resuming one service keeps the whole catalogue alive. Nothing on the read path extends anything, this entry included — see the module doc in contracts/registry/src/storage.rs for the rent measurement behind that rule.
  • Never bumped for the listed services. Paging reads each Service record to re-check ownership but does not extend it: a page is a discovery read over entries somebody else owns, so their rent stays with their owner. A caller cannot keep another provider's records alive, nor evict them.
  • Append-only, pruned on read. The index is derived state; Service.provider is the authority. If a service is later transferred, its id stays in the old owner's row and the read path drops it, while save_service puts it in the new owner's row. An index can therefore only ever make a page shorter — never disclose a service that belongs to someone else. The stale id costs one ledger read to skip, and a provider that re-registers does not duplicate it.

If the index entry expires while its services live on, the provider's pages go empty until the next write to any of its services recreates the row. That is a discovery-availability failure, not a loss of funds or of ownership, which is why the index is safe to treat as cache. bump_service does not refresh it: that call takes a service_id and extends one record without loading it, and finding the index key means reading the record — the cost it exists to avoid. A provider that needs a durable index across months of inactivity is the case an explicit index bump would serve, and it is not implemented here.

docs.title: Provider guide
docs.text: You run an API or RPC endpoint. This guide shows how to sell metered access to it with KeyLease instead of handing out a static key, using only Stellar tooling and the Soroban contract.

docs.title: What you are agreeing to
docs.text:
• You publish a price per call and a 32-byte endpoint_hash commitment.
  • Consumers escrow price × calls in a SEP-41 token before they can make a request.
  • You settle a lease once, reporting how many calls were consumed.
  • If you never settle, the consumer reclaims the full deposit 24 hours after expiry. That guarantee is what makes consumers willing to prepay.

You never publish a secret on-chain. endpoint_hash is a commitment, not a credential. It must digest the descriptor's actual content; an all-zero hash is rejected with InvalidEndpointHash, because a placeholder commits to nothing and gives consumers nothing to verify against.

docs.title: 1. Register a service
docs.text:
export REGISTRY=<your registry contract id>
export PROVIDER=$(stellar keys address provider)

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider $PROVIDER \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 \
     --endpoint_hash $(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER:my-api" | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}')

rate_per_call is in the escrow token's smallest unit (7 decimals for the native asset, so 1000000 = 0.1 XLM per call). It must be positive and no more than MAX_RATE_PER_CALL, which is MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT — 1,000,000,000,000 base units, 100,000 XLM per call. A higher rate reverts with RateTooHigh and registers nothing. The two bounds are the same number on purpose: the cheapest lease is a single call, so a price above the deposit cap would advertise a service no consumer could ever rent.

Your rate still decides how large a lease can be, because MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT caps the rate_per_call × requested_calls product: at your rate, the largest lease a consumer can open is MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT ÷ rate_per_call calls. A rate of 1000000 leaves room for 1,000,000 calls; a rate of 100000000 caps them at 10,000. Price the whole allotment your typical customer wants before you pick one. The command prints the new service_id — record it.

The registration emits service_registered { service_id, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash }, so your own indexer can pick it up without a separate query.

To read your catalogue back from the chain instead of your own database, page through services_for_provider(provider, after, limit) — pass next back as after until done, and keep limit at or below MAX_PAGE_SIZE (100). See contract reference.

docs.title: 2. Pause or resume a service
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- set_service_active --provider $PROVIDER --service_id 1 --is_active false

Deactivation blocks new leases only. Existing leases stay valid and must still be settleable — you remain obligated to settle or let them expire. The change emits service_status_changed.

docs.title: 3. Verify leases and meter calls
docs.text: The contract cannot see your HTTP traffic, so verification and metering happen in your request path. The credential is the on-chain lease; there is no session token to mint.

docs.title: Verify against Soroban RPC
docs.text:
1. Authenticate the caller as a Stellar address (SEP-10 challenge–response is the standard approach).
  2. Read the lease with get_lease(lease_id) over Soroban RPC and cache it briefly.
  3. Reject if settled, if now ≥ expires_at, if the caller is not lease.consumer, or if your counter has consumed allocated_calls. consumer is mutable: the owner can transfer the lease, so refresh your cache when the authenticated address does not match instead of rejecting forever.
  4. Count the call, return the response.
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

Reads need no secret key: a verifier can run without any signing authority.

docs.title: Or project the event stream
docs.text:
If you would rather not call RPC per request, subscribe to lease_created and keep a local table of active leases. The on-chain allocated_calls and expires_at remain the bound; your projection is an optimisation.

The full pipeline, including the Stellar SDK read example and cache guidance, is in Integration.

docs.title: 4. Settle
docs.text:
Settle when the lease expires, or immediately once the consumer has used every allocated call. One settlement covers the whole lease — never one per request.

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- settle_lease --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

That call moves no funds. It records verified_calls × rate_per_call as your payout, records the rest as the consumer's refund, and emits lease_settlement_proposed { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund, challengeable_until }. The funds stay in escrow for a 24-hour consumer challenge window. After it closes, anyone (including you, or a keeper) can release them:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- finalize_settlement --lease_id 1

Finalization emits lease_settled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund } and transfers the payout to you and the refund to the consumer.

Settle with verified_calls = 0 to propose a full refund for a lease you could not serve.

docs.title: Settling rules
docs.text: Situation Result now ≥ expires_at, any verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls settle allowed verified_calls == allocated_calls, any time settle allowed now < expires_at and verified_calls < allocated_calls LeaseNotSettleable verified_calls > allocated_calls InvalidCalls lease already settled or proposed LeaseAlreadySettled you don't own the service Unauthorized finalize before challengeable_until ChallengeWindowStillOpen finalize while the consumer's challenge is active SettlementChallenged finalize/resolve after payout SettlementFinalized

docs.title: 5. Early cancellation requests
docs.text:
A consumer who stops using the service early can ask you to release the unused balance without waiting for expiry + 24 hours. The request moves no funds:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- approve_early_cancel \
     --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

Approving reports the calls you actually served. You receive verified_calls × rate_per_call, the consumer is refunded rate_per_call × (allocated_calls − verified_calls), and the lease ends in the same transaction. There is no rounding: the rate is a per-call integer, so the refund is the exact value of whole unused calls.

Approval is valid even if the lease has passed expires_at, as long as the consumer requested it before expiry. If you decline, reject the request instead; the lease is untouched and settles normally later:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- reject_early_cancel --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1

The consumer may withdraw the request at any time. A lease that is already settled cannot be cancelled early.

docs.title: 6. Accounting
docs.text:
finalize_settlement pays you from escrow. Nothing else does. The registry never holds funds on your behalf after finalization, and there is no yield or custody to manage.

  • Revenue recognised: verified_calls × rate_per_call per settlement, published in the lease_settled event at finalization.
  • Lifetime totals: service_stats --service_id <id> returns settled_leases, settled_calls and total_payout for one service without replaying history. It counts every path that pays the provider — a finalized settlement and an approved early cancellation — and nothing else: a lease the consumer revoked contributed nothing, so a reclaimed lease never inflates reported revenue. Treat it as a convenience view and lease_settled as the book of record: the aggregate is stored with a TTL, so an entry nothing has settled or read for a long stretch can age out and read back as zero.
  • Unused consumer balance: refunded to the consumer at finalization, on an approved early cancellation, or by the consumer via revoke_expired_lease after the 24h grace window if you never settled.
  • Early cancellation: lease_cancelled publishes verified_calls, payout and refund. It is a consented early settlement; the same conservation rule holds (payout + refund == locked_deposit).
  • Disputes: the consumer can challenge your reported count inside the 24-hour window with an evidence hash. The registry admin resolves it; an upheld challenge refunds the whole deposit and pays you nothing. Report honestly and keep the evidence that supports your count.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• Watch expiry. A lease you forget to settle becomes revocable 24 hours after it expires. Subscribe to lease_created and settle from that queue.
  • Ownership moves. A consumer can transfer an unsettled lease; the refund then goes to the new consumer at settlement. Re-read consumer rather than caching it for the whole term. Watch lease_transferred if you project events.
  • Changing your rate. Today you register a new service; an update entry point is a wave-medium issue. In-flight leases keep their original escrow.
  • Rotating your key. A service is bound to the registering address; key rotation/transfer is a wave-medium issue. Register from an account you can keep — a Stellar multisig account works today.
  • Upgrades. Watch contract_upgraded and check version() after a release. Storage and balances are preserved across upgrades.
  • Testnet resets wipe your service. Re-register after each reset.

docs.title: Read next
docs.text:
• Integration — the verification pipeline in detail.
  • Consumer guide — what your customers do.
  • Networks — RPC endpoints and resets.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
KeyLease escrows funds on Stellar. This page states exactly what the Soroban contract guarantees, what it assumes, and what is not yet hardened. For reporting a vulnerability, see SECURITY.md.

No mainnet deployment may begin until the maintainer-approved mainnet runbook audit gate is complete. The runbook requires independent audit evidence, an exact release/Wasm hash, multisig custody, verification, monitoring, upgrade, and rollback records.

docs.title: Trust assumptions
docs.text:
Assumption Consequence if violated The admin configures a well-behaved SEP-41 token. A malicious token contract could revert transfers and stall settlement. It cannot be paid twice: settled is persisted before the transfer, and a re-entrant token is rejected (LeaseAlreadySettled). The admin does not upgrade to a malicious Wasm. An upgrade can change the contract logic. The admin key should be cold or multisig. Upgrades now require a 24h on-ledger delay and emit upgrade_proposed with the hash and execution ledger, so consumers can exit; execution emits contract_upgraded. The provider reports verified_calls honestly, or the consumer and admin can correct it. It can under-report (it gets paid less) and can over-report up to allocated_calls; the consumer has 24h to challenge the report, and the admin resolves the dispute. The admin adjudicates challenges honestly. A compromised admin can zero a legitimate payout by upholding a challenge, or refuse to resolve one. It cannot redirect funds to itself. Use a cold or multisig admin. Soroban ledger time is monotonic and honest. Validity windows would be unreliable. Consumers keep their own key safe. Anyone with the consumer key can create leases that spend its balance.

The provider is explicitly untrusted in the direction that matters: it cannot take more than it is owed, and it cannot prevent the consumer's refund.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
1. The provider is paid at most allocated_calls × rate_per_call. The payout is computed from the stored rate_per_call and the lease allotment; an over-claim reverts with InvalidCalls.
  2. Only the owning provider can settle. settle_lease checks service.provider == provider after authenticating provider (Unauthorized).
  3. Only the consumer can revoke, and only after the grace window. Combined checks for ownership, expiry and elapsed grace (Unauthorized, LeaseNotExpired, RevokeWindowNotElapsed).
  4. Early cancellation needs the provider's consent. Only the consumer can request or withdraw, only the owning provider can approve or reject, and only approval moves funds (Unauthorized, CancellationNotRequested). A request never blocks use, settlement or revocation and expires with the lease.
  5. A lease releases funds once. A settlement is proposed once (settled is persisted at proposal time), its state is persisted as Finalized before any token call, and every payout path rejects an already-finalized settlement (LeaseAlreadySettled, SettlementFinalized). Checks-effects-interactions is enforced by test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice; the service's running totals are written before the transfers, so a re-entrant token cannot inflate them either.
  6. The payout is locked during a dispute. A pending settlement cannot be finalized before challengeable_until, and a challenged one cannot be finalized at all until the admin resolves it (ChallengeWindowStillOpen, SettlementChallenged).
  7. Overflow aborts. Deposit, payout, refund and expiry arithmetic use checked_mul/checked_add/checked_sub and revert with Overflow.
  8. Lease durations are storage-safe. Durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) revert with DurationTooLong, and the persistent entry is extended for the term plus the grace window, so escrow cannot be evicted while it is claimable.
  9. A single lease cannot escrow an unbounded amount. A deposit that fits i128 but exceeds MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT reverts with DepositTooLarge, before the lease id is allocated and before the token is called. Checked arithmetic alone cannot catch this: a product can be perfectly representable and still be three orders of magnitude more than the consumer meant to lock.
  10. Listed prices are leasable. register_service rejects rate_per_call above MAX_RATE_PER_CALL, which equals MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT. A service can therefore never be listed at a price that cannot fund even the smallest (one-call) lease, and the worst legal rate × calls product stays far inside i128, so a consumer's quote is always the amount that moves.
  11. The admin cannot redirect user funds. It can call set_token, the upgrade entry points, the admin-rotation entry points and resolve_challenge. Resolution only chooses between the provider's proposal and a full consumer refund; there is no path that pays an arbitrary recipient.
  12. Every mutation is authenticated. No state-changing entry point trusts its caller without require_auth(). finalize_settlement is permissionless by design: it can only release the exact split already recorded on chain.
  13. A sponsor cannot spend your balance. create_lease_for calls require_auth() on the delegate and the consumer, and the deposit is transferred from the consumer; the refund and revoke paths stay bound to the consumer alone. Missing either signature reverts before any state changes.
  14. Revocation is not settlement. A reclaimed lease reports LeaseStatus::Revoked, keeps used_calls == 0, pays the provider nothing, and is excluded from service_stats, so revenue reporting cannot be confused with a refund. An approved early cancellation is the opposite case: the provider was paid for served calls, so it is counted like any other settlement.
  15. Every mutation is observable. Each transition emits a typed Soroban event with no secret material in it.
  16. Only the current consumer can transfer, and never after settlement. transfer_lease rewrites the single Lease.consumer field, so access and the refund path always belong to the same address (Unauthorized, LeaseNotTransferable, InvalidConsumer). A pending early-cancellation request is cleared so the previous owner cannot trigger a payout.
  17. The admin role changes hands only with both signatures. propose_admin needs the current admin, accept_admin needs the proposed address, and a proposal expires after ADMIN_TRANSFER_WINDOW_SECS (7 days).

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
Asserted in contracts/registry/src/test.rs. The contract reference lists the exact error code for each violation.

  • payout + refund == locked_deposit for every settlement and every approved early cancellation.
  • A settled lease never transitions again.
  • settled is true on-chain before any value leaves the contract.
  • A settlement is Finalized on-chain before any value leaves the contract.
  • No settlement can release more value than was escrowed.
  • A challenged settlement moves no value until the admin resolves it.
  • Every lease has a consumer path to a full refund, for its entire TTL.
  • service_stats advances only on provider settlement, and only by exactly verified_calls and the payout the transfers performed.
  • A revoked lease and a settled lease are distinguishable through lease_status alone.
  • Every lease has exactly one consumer, and it owns both access and the refund path for its entire TTL; a proposed settlement freezes that ownership.

docs.title: Threats considered
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Provider claims more calls than allocated InvalidCalls Provider over-reports within the allotment Consumer challenges inside the 24h window; admin can uphold a full refund Provider settles a lease twice settled flag persisted before transfers + LeaseAlreadySettled Payout released while a challenge is open SettlementChallenged; only the admin can resolve Finalize races the challenge deadline now < challengeable_until → ChallengeWindowStillOpen; at the boundary challenges are closed Admin upholds every challenge to deny payouts On-chain lease_challenge_resolved events; admin should be cold/multisig; consumer and provider can both observe Attacker settles someone else's lease service.provider == provider check Attacker revokes someone else's lease lease.consumer == consumer check Attacker transfers someone else's lease lease.consumer == consumer check + require_auth on the current consumer Consumer transfers, then revokes as the old owner Ownership is one field; the revoke/refund path reads the new consumer Lease changes hands after payout settled check in transfer_lease (LeaseNotTransferable) Consumer cancels early without paying for served calls Provider approval reports verified_calls; no unilateral path reduces the payout Provider approves a cancellation that was never requested CancellationNotRequested Cancellation bypasses the grace window at expiry Requests are rejected at/after expires_at (LeaseExpired) Re-entrant token pays a lease twice checks-effects-interactions; adversarial test Provider strands funds by never settling 24h grace, then full consumer refund Consumer races the provider at expiry 24h grace window reserved for the provider Rate overflow creates a cheap lease checked_mul → Overflow, and RateTooHigh blocks the price before it can ever be leased Typo locks a consumer into an enormous deposit MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT → DepositTooLarge Escrow token has more decimals than assumed MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT is in base units, so the ceiling tightens as the scale grows Provider lists a price no consumer can rent MAX_RATE_PER_CALL = MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT, so the cheapest lease of any listed service is fundable Duration overflow wraps expiry checked_add → Overflow Delegate locks a consumer's deposit unilaterally create_lease_for requires the consumer's require_auth() as well; no state changes without both Delegate claims a refund it sponsored refunds and revocation are keyed to lease.consumer, and the delegate is never stored on the lease Provider inflates reported revenue revoked leases are excluded from service_stats; totals use checked_add and revert on overflow Long lease is evicted from storage DurationTooLong + duration-aware TTL extension Fake "KeyLease" contract id Only ids in Deployments are ours Third party takes over the admin role accept_admin requires the proposed address's auth and a proposal made by the sitting admin; adversarial tests with real auth Admin role handed to a mistyped or unreachable address Two-step hand-over: nothing changes until the successor signs accept_admin Forgotten proposal accepted months later Proposals expire after 7 days (AdminTransferExpired); the admin can cancel at any time Silent logic change on upgrade 24h delay + admin-only execution, emits upgrade_proposed/contract_upgraded, contractmeta! exposes the version Upgrade installs code that misreads the stored layout Storage schema stamp; docs.title: Running with a multisig admin
docs.text: KeyLease stores the admin as a standard Soroban Address. In production, operators should avoid using a single hot keypair for the admin role. Instead, the admin can be a native Stellar multi-signature account (G...) or a multisig smart contract.

docs.title: Host-enforced authentication
docs.text:
When admin.require_auth() is called inside set_token or upgrade:

  • If admin is a Stellar account, Soroban's runtime delegates authentication to Stellar's native account signing engine.
  • If the account is configured with multi-signature weights and operation thresholds (e.g., medium threshold for contract invocations), the Stellar host requires signatures that satisfy the threshold before the invocation transaction can execute.
  • The contract does not need special multisig code; multi-signature security is enforced natively at the protocol host layer.

docs.title: What the contract can and cannot enforce
docs.text: Scope Contract capability Details Can enforce Execution authority (require_auth) Ensures that the admin account legitimately approved the call based on Stellar's consensus rules Cannot enforce Signer composition The contract cannot inspect individual signers, public keys, or individual weights Cannot enforce Minimum threshold The contract cannot verify whether the admin account is 1-of-1, 2-of-3, or 3-of-5 Cannot enforce Signer set immutability Signers and thresholds can be modified on the Stellar account via standard SetOptions operations without contract interaction

docs.title: Audit status
docs.text: No external audit of this contract has been performed. As of v0.2.1 no third party has reviewed, formally verified or signed off on contracts/registry. No firm is engaged and no report exists. Everything on this page is the project's own claim about its own code: read Guarantees as a specification of what the authors intended, not as an independent finding.

docs.title: Coverage that exists
docs.text:
What How much Where Contract tests 63 contracts/registry/src/test.rs, run by cargo test --all Documented guarantees 10 Guarantees Invariants asserted in tests 5 Invariants Threats modelled 14 Threats considered CI gates 9 Format, Clippy, Test, Build (wasm32v1-none), Secret Scan (gitleaks), Spell Check, Markdown Lint, Dependency Policy (cargo-deny) and Malware Scan (ClamAV) in .github/workflows/ci.yml

The counts are as of the revision this page is written against; each one is mechanically checkable from the file it names.

Two of the 63 tests matter more than the rest, because they attack the contract instead of exercising it:

  • test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice registers a hostile token whose transfer calls back into settle_lease while the first settlement is still paying out. The attack is attempted once, and the test asserts the re-entrant call errored and the lease ended up settled exactly once. This is the only executable proof of the checks-effects-interactions ordering, and it is the property that makes a malicious token non-exploitable rather than merely inconvenient.
  • the full lifecycle test escrowed with the real Stellar Asset Contract (env.register_stellar_asset_contract_v2) rather than contracts/mock_token, so the money paths are checked against a token this project does not control.

docs.title: What that coverage does not establish
docs.text:
A green suite is easy to over-read, so the limits are stated explicitly.

  • The threat model may be incomplete. The 14 rows are the threats the authors thought of. The main value of an audit is the rows it adds, and by definition none of those are here yet.
  • Arbitrary tokens are out of scope. set_token accepts any SEP-41 address. The suite proves the registry survives a re-entrant token; it cannot prove anything about a token that deviates from the interface in ways the registry does not expect.
  • Only simulated-ledger behaviour is tested. The tests run against the soroban-sdk Env, not a deployed network, so instruction-footprint limits, eviction under real storage pressure, and consensus-timing edges are not covered here. The soroban-sdk test host does not enforce maxEntryTtl on extend_ttl at all, so the TTL clamp is asserted from the policy value rather than demonstrated as a host rejection. Read the TTL rules in the contract reference as analysis, not as measurement.
  • State growth is bounded per call, not in aggregate. bump_service and bump_lease are permissionless and each one charges its rent to the caller, which is what makes them safe to expose — but nothing here bounds how many entries may be kept alive or by whom. Persistent state that outlives its usefulness is an operational cost, and the suite does not price it.
  • Client code and provider middleware are not this contract. Anything integrating per Integration is outside the audited surface, and outside the surface these guarantees describe.
  • The documentation itself is unaudited. A page that describes behaviour the code does not have is precisely the defect an audit catches and a test suite cannot.

docs.title: What a mainnet deployment would require
docs.text:
Deployments records Mainnet as ⛔ not deployed, and Deployment → Mainnet gives the reason: deployment is deferred until the contract is audited. Audited is a process, not a badge, so the gate list a mainnet launch would have to clear first is:

  1. An independent audit by a contract-security firm, with the report published and linked from the release notes and SECURITY.md. A private report that stays private does not count as clearing this.
  2. Findings fixed and re-proved. Every High and Medium with a code fix and a test in contracts/registry/src/test.rs that fails without the fix. Per the developer guide, each security-sensitive change gets an adversarial case, not just a happy path.
  3. Upgrade trust bounded. Today a single admin key can swap the Wasm and rewrite the escrow rules. Before mainnet value is in range, that key should be multisig or timelocked, and the timelock itself reviewed (see Known limitations).
  4. A live operation path. Someone watching the event stream, a named owner for the deployment, and a written response procedure. There is no protocol-wide pause: set_service_active(provider, service_id, false) blocks new leases on one service and leaves in-flight leases valid, and upgrade is admin-only. That is a throttle, not a kill switch.
  5. A staged value ramp. Deploy, cap total escrow to something you would accept losing, run real lease cycles against the cap, and only then raise it.
  6. A verifiable record. The mainnet contract id, Wasm hash and version in docs/deployments.md, each confirmed on-chain through version(), get_admin() and get_token() rather than taken from the page.

Until 1 through 4 are done, this contract is for Testnet and for limited-value evaluation. On Testnet every failure mode above costs an afternoon of redeploying fake XLM; on Mainnet it costs someone's deposit.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
These are real and tracked as Drips Wave issues rather than hidden.

  • Upgrade trust. The admin can replace the contract Wasm. While using a multisig admin prevents a single compromised key from executing an unauthorized upgrade, adding an on-chain timelock to upgrades remains future work.
  • No provider key rotation. A service is bound to the address that registered it. Transferring a service is a wave-medium issue.
  • No rate updates. Changing rate_per_call requires registering a new service; in-flight leases keep their original escrow.
  • Settlement disputes are adjudicated, not proven. The contract trusts the provider's verified_calls unless the consumer challenges it. The challenge is a 32-byte evidence commitment, and the admin decides off chain; the contract cannot verify usage or evidence. Consumers are still protected by the fixed allotment and the refund path.
  • Resolution depends on the admin. A challenged settlement stays locked until the admin acts. Settlement entries live for the standard ~30-day persistent TTL, so disputes should be resolved well inside that horizon.
  • Early cancellation depends on the provider. A consumer cannot exit early unilaterally; if the provider never approves or rejects, the lease runs to expiry and the normal revoke path applies. There is no penalty scheme yet.
  • Transfers are final. transfer_lease is a direct assignment: the recipient does not accept, and there is no protocol-level reversal. A mistyped address hands the lease (and its refund right) to an unreachable account.
  • Settlement is a single report. The contract trusts the provider's verified_calls; it cannot independently observe HTTP usage. Consumers are protected by the fixed allotment and the refund path, not by proof of non-delivery.
  • Not audited, and nothing on this page substitutes for it. See Audit status.

docs.title: Secret scanning
docs.text:
Pull requests are scanned for committed secrets with gitleaks in CI (Secret Scan job). The scan uses a pinned gitleaks version, fails on findings, and reads allowlist entries only from .gitleaks.toml. Add allowlist entries only for documented false positives and include a comment explaining why the match is not a secret.

Run locally before opening a PR:

gitleaks detect --source . --redact --verbose --config .gitleaks.toml

docs.title: Deployment hygiene
docs.text:
• Only trust contract ids in docs/deployments.md.
  • The admin key should be a cold or multisig Stellar account. It can change the escrow token and propose/cancel upgrades, but execution waits 24h on-ledger. Rotate it with propose_admin followed by accept_admin from the new account; a key that is already lost cannot propose, so rotate before retiring a key, and prefer a multisig admin whose signers can be replaced at the account level.
