  • Verify the deployed metadata and configuration after deploy:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_token
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

Testnet resets (2–4 times a year, at 17:00 UTC) wipe all ledger entries and change the contract id. Redeploy after a reset. See Networks.

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text: Report vulnerabilities privately per SECURITY.md. We will credit reporters in the release notes unless asked not to.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Every failure this contract can return, grouped by who is holding the error. Each entry names the fix and the command that proves the state you are about to act on. Error codes link to the contract reference table, which is the authoritative list.

Nothing here moves funds. settle_lease pays a provider and revoke_expired_lease refunds a consumer, and both can only be called once per lease — so verify first, then call.

docs.title: Three commands first
docs.text:
Most "the contract is broken" reports are a wrong contract id, a wrong network or an unconfigured token. These three answers cost one simulation each:

export REGISTRY=<contract id from docs/deployments.md>
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_token
What you see What it means Go to version returns the release you deployed the id is live and initialised keep reading any call returns Error(WasmNotInstalled) or the ledger says the entry does not exist wrong id, or the network was reset The network moved under you get_admin returns NotInitialized this contract was never initialised NotInitialized and AlreadyInitialized get_token returns TokenNotSet leases can be read but never funded TokenNotSet

Read calls still need a funded --source-account, because the CLI builds a simulation transaction: see the note on read calls in Networks.

docs.title: LeaseNotExpired
docs.text:
Cause: revoke_expired_lease ran before expires_at. The lease is still inside its term, so the provider may still be paid.

Fix: wait for the term to end, or use the calls you paid for and let the provider settle.

Verify the term:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- lease_status --lease_id 1

Reference: error code 9.

docs.title: RevokeWindowNotElapsed
docs.text:
Cause: the lease is expired, but fewer than SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS (24 hours) have passed since expires_at. That window belongs to the provider: they can still settle for the calls they served.

Fix: wait until expires_at + 24h. The refund is the whole locked_deposit — revocation is all-or-nothing and pays the provider nothing, which is why the window exists.

Verify how much is still yours:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- locked_balance --lease_id 1

Reference: error code 10.

docs.title: Unauthorized on revoke_expired_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the lease belongs to a different address than the one that authorised. A lease is not transferable, and the refund path follows lease.consumer, not the caller.

Fix: re-run with the account that created the lease. If you lost that key, there is no recovery path on chain — that is a trust assumption, not a bug.

Verify who owns it: compare consumer in the get_lease output with stellar keys address <your-seed-name>.

Reference: error code 3.

docs.title: InvalidCalls, InvalidDuration, DurationTooLong on create_lease
docs.text:
Code Cause Fix InvalidCalls requested_calls is 0 ask for at least one call InvalidDuration duration_secs is 0 the lease must have a term DurationTooLong term exceeds MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) renew instead of lengthening: the storage TTL is only guaranteed for the bounded term

create_lease escrows rate_per_call × requested_calls before anything else, so a rejected lease moves no funds. To check the price before you buy:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

docs.title: ServiceNotFound or ServiceInactive on create_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the id is from another deployment, or the provider paused the service. Testnet resets restart service_id from zero, so an id you saved last week can point at a different service — or at nothing.

Fix: re-read the ids for the network you are on:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- service_count

ServiceInactive is the provider's set_service_status(false). Nothing is stuck: your funds never left your account.

docs.title: Overflow on create_lease
docs.text:
Cause: rate_per_call × requested_calls does not fit in i128. All deposit math is checked and a failed multiplication returns this instead of a cheaper lease.

Fix: request fewer calls. If a provider's rate is large enough that a normal order overflows, that is a pricing bug on their side — quote it as rate_per_call × calls before you escrow.

docs.title: DepositTooLarge on create_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the deposit fits in i128 but exceeds MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT (1,000,000,000,000 base units, so 100,000 XLM at seven decimals). Overflow means the multiplication does not fit; this means it fits and is still more than one lease is allowed to escrow.

Fix: split the order into several leases of fewer calls each. The bound is deliberate: it caps what a single lease can put at risk, so raising it is a contract change, not a client setting.

docs.title: Your balance did not move but the lease exists
docs.text:
Cause: the transaction was not sent. stellar contract invoke simulates by default and prints the result without submitting.

Fix: add --send=yes, then confirm the lease landed:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

A lease_created event is the record that the escrow happened; see Following the event stream.

docs.title: LeaseNotSettleable on settle_lease
docs.text:
Cause: neither settlement condition holds yet. A lease settles when it has expired, or when the consumer used every call it paid for (verified_calls == allocated_calls).

Fix: settle at expiry with the real number of served calls — an under-report refunds the consumer and is not recoverable later, because a lease settles once.

Verify what you may claim:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- remaining_calls --lease_id 1

remaining_calls returns 0 for an expired lease, so use used_calls for the quota, not for the payout.

Reference: error code 8.

docs.title: InvalidCalls on settle_lease
docs.text:
Cause: verified_calls exceeds allocated_calls. Settlement cannot pay out more than the consumer escrowed.

Fix: pass at most allocated_calls. If your counter is higher than the allotment, your local count and the lease disagree — the on-chain record wins.

docs.title: Unauthorized on settle_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the authorising account is not service.provider for that lease.

Fix: settle with the key that registered the service. Two things make this surprisingly common:

  • a service was registered by one key and the settlement daemon runs with another
  • keys cannot be rotated yet; a service is bound to its registering address forever (known limitation)

Verify the binding:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

docs.title: Your funds never arrived after settling
docs.text:
Cause: the settlement paid verified_calls × rate_per_call, and the rest went back to the consumer. A settle with verified_calls = 0 pays you nothing.

Fix: check the amounts against the event, not your logs:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

A lease_settled event carries payout and refund. If the event is absent, the transaction was simulated and never sent (--send=yes).

docs.title: 429 / 403 from your own service, not the chain
docs.text: The contract only escrows; the HTTP layer is yours. The verification pipeline fails closed at each step, so the causes are: lease expired or settled (403), the caller is not lease.consumer (403), or the allotment is exhausted (429). A lease id that is not in docs/deployments.md's network is 403 with a LeaseNotFound on chain.

docs.title: NotInitialized and AlreadyInitialized
docs.text: Code Cause Fix NotInitialized init never ran on this id, or you are pointed at an old one check version above, then run init or correct REGISTRY AlreadyInitialized init ran twice, usually a re-run of the deploy script against an id that already exists stop; deploy a fresh contract instead. The admin cannot be changed by re-initialising

docs.title: TokenNotSet
docs.text:
Cause: the escrow asset was never configured. create_lease refuses to store a lease it cannot fund.

Fix: set the token, then verify it resolved to the address you meant:

stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token --admin $ADMIN --token <TOKEN_ID>
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_token

Changing the token while leases are in flight strands their payouts against the old asset. Settle or revoke first: see set_token.

docs.title: Unauthorized on set_token or upgrade
docs.text:
Cause: the caller is not the stored Admin.

Fix: stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account <whoever> --network testnet -- get_admin prints the only address that can authorise. If that key is lost, the token and the Wasm are frozen — escrow can still be refunded by consumers through revoke_expired_lease.

docs.title: upgrade succeeded but behaviour did not change
docs.text:
Cause: the hash you uploaded is not the build you think it is, or the version() string was not bumped before building.

Fix: compare what is on chain with what you built:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- version

version is embedded from Cargo.toml by contractmeta!, so it proves which release is live. Upgrades must keep the storage layout and must never renumber error codes (upgrading).

docs.title: The network moved under you
docs.text:
Testnet and Futurenet are reset by SDF 2–4 times a year, at 17:00 UTC. A reset deletes every ledger entry: the contract, its services, its leases and the account that funded them. The contract id changes, so the symptom is not one error but all of them at once — LeaseNotFound for ids that worked yesterday, ServiceNotFound for ids in Deployments, and clients that look like they are reading a broken protocol.

# Is this network a fresh one? Its ledger is near zero after a reset.
curl -s -X POST "$KEYLEASE_RPC_URL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"getLatestLedger","params":{}}'

# Is this the network you think it is?
curl -s -X POST "$KEYLEASE_RPC_URL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"getNetwork","params":{}}'

The passphrase in the getNetwork reply must match the row for your network in Networks. After a reset: redeploy with scripts/deploy-testnet.sh, re-issue set_token and register_service, fund accounts again, then update KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID and Deployments.

docs.title: Reads work, then start failing with 429
docs.text:
Cause: the public Testnet and Futurenet RPC endpoints are rate-limited and are not meant for a busy provider (production notes).

Fix: move to an authenticated provider and point KEYLEASE_RPC_URL at it. Back off on 429 rather than retrying immediately, and cache get_lease for a few seconds instead of re-reading per request.

docs.title: Your service rejects requests while RPC is down
docs.text: That is correct. The contract is not reachable during an RPC outage, so a provider cannot verify a lease and must not serve it (verification pipeline, step 2). No funds move: settlement and revocation still work as soon as any RPC responds, and a consumer's refund path never depends on a provider's infrastructure.

docs.title: Events are missing after a restart
docs.text:
Cause: the start ledger predates the contract's creation, or is ahead of the events you need.

Fix: re-read from the deploy ledger and check the count:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

Event names, topics and payloads are part of the ABI and only ever gain fields; decode by position-tolerant lookup, and treat a settled lease as final (Integration).

docs.title: Storage reads return nothing
docs.text:
Cause: raw getContractData needs the exact wire key. #[contracttype] enums encode as a vector whose first element is the variant symbol, so DataKey::Lease(7) is Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)].

Fix: prefer the read views (get_lease, get_service, lease_status) over raw storage. If you must read the key directly, the mapping table is in Reading contract state and events.

docs.title: Error code index
docs.text: The full table, with the precondition each code guards, is in the contract reference. Codes are part of the ABI: they are appended and never reused, so a number you see today is the same number after an upgrade.

docs.title: Read next
docs.text:
• Contract reference — entry points, events, error codes.
  • Integration — the verification path a provider should ship.
  • Networks — endpoints, passphrases, resets.
  • Security model — what the contract does not promise.

docs.title: Design note — Two-step admin transfer (#121)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design; the accompanying PR implements it so the review can happen against working code and tests.

Issue: #121 — Make admin transfer a two-step, accept-based operation Touches: lib.rs, storage.rs, types.rs, events.rs, errors.rs

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text:
init stores the admin once and nothing can change it. The admin is the only account that can call set_token and the upgrade entry points, so a key that has to be rotated (a departing operator, a suspected leak, a move from a single key to a multisig) cannot be rotated: the deployment must keep trusting the old key forever, or be abandoned along with its contract id and in-flight escrow.

A naive set_admin(admin, new_admin) would fix rotation but introduce a worse failure: one typo, or an address nobody holds the key for, permanently strands upgrade and token control.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
After this change the following must hold:

  1. The stored admin changes only in accept_admin, and only to the address that the sitting admin proposed.
  2. A hand-over needs authorization from both the outgoing admin (propose_admin) and the incoming admin (accept_admin). No other address can complete, start or cancel one.
  3. At most one proposal exists at any time, and it can be accepted only before its expires_at.
  4. A proposal made by an admin who is no longer in office is never acceptable.
  5. On acceptance the previous admin loses every admin right in the same transaction; there is no window with two admins.
  6. Escrow, services and leases are untouched by any admin-rotation call.
  7. Existing storage keys, event payloads and error codes are unchanged.

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text: Entry point Auth Effect propose_admin(admin, new_admin) -> u64 current admin Store PendingAdmin, replacing any earlier one; return expires_at. cancel_admin_transfer(admin) current admin Remove PendingAdmin, expired or not. accept_admin(new_admin) proposed admin Check proposal, set Admin, remove PendingAdmin. get_pending_admin() -> Option<PendingAdminTransfer> — Pure read.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
pub struct PendingAdminTransfer {
    pub proposed_by: Address, // admin at proposal time
    pub new_admin: Address,
    pub proposed_at: u64,     // ledger timestamp
    pub expires_at: u64,      // proposed_at + ADMIN_TRANSFER_WINDOW_SECS
}

Stored under a new DataKey::PendingAdmin in instance storage. It is a single bounded value tied to the configuration it would change, every rotation call extends the instance TTL, and so it needs no TTL policy of its own. The new variant is additive, so existing keys keep decoding across the upgrade.

docs.title: Expiry
docs.text: ADMIN_TRANSFER_WINDOW_SECS = 7 days, a compile-time constant. That is long enough for a multisig successor to gather signatures, and short enough that a forgotten proposal does not stay live as a hand-over to an address whose key may since have leaked. Acceptance requires now < expires_at. An expired proposal stays in storage (and visible through get_pending_admin) until the admin cancels or replaces it, because an erroring accept_admin reverts and cannot clean up after itself.

docs.title: Events and errors
docs.text:
New events (no topics, matching the other admin events; payloads carry schema_version): admin_transfer_proposed { admin, new_admin, expires_at }, admin_transfer_canceled { admin, new_admin }, admin_transfer_accepted { previous_admin, new_admin }. Adding events does not change any existing payload, so EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION stays at 1.

New errors are appended: NoPendingAdminTransfer = 40, AdminTransferExpired = 41, InvalidAdmin = 42 (proposing the current admin).

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text:
• Single-step set_admin. One call, but a typo or unreachable address permanently loses admin control. This is the failure the issue is about.
  • Requiring both signatures on accept_admin. That would make acceptance a coordinated multi-party transaction and add nothing: the outgoing admin already authorized the exact successor in propose_admin, and can cancel until acceptance.
  • Caller-chosen expiry. More flexible, but a long or unbounded window brings back the stale-proposal risk. It can be added later if operators need it.
  • Persistent storage with its own TTL. More rent policy for a value that is only ever one entry and naturally belongs with the configuration.
  • Lost-key recovery (guardian, timelocked override). Out of scope. Two-step rotation needs the current key. Recovery from a key that is already lost is what a multisig admin account is for, since Stellar lets the account replace its own signers.

docs.title: 4. Threat model
docs.text: Adversarial case Handling A third party calls accept_admin for itself Not the proposed address → Unauthorized. A third party calls accept_admin(new_admin) with its own signature new_admin.require_auth() fails in the host. The outgoing admin accepts on the successor's behalf Same: only the successor's signature satisfies require_auth. A third party proposes or cancels require_admin → Unauthorized; with real auth, require_auth on the admin fails first. The proposed admin cancels or re-proposes Not the stored admin → Unauthorized. A superseded successor accepts after a new proposal Only the latest proposal exists → Unauthorized. A proposal is replayed after the role moved on Acceptance clears it → NoPendingAdminTransfer. A proposal survives an upgrade or admin change proposed_by must equal the sitting admin → Unauthorized. A months-old proposal is accepted after the successor's key leaked Expired → AdminTransferExpired. Admin rotation is used to reach escrow Rotation calls never call the token or touch lease state.

docs.title: 5. Test plan
docs.text:
All in contracts/registry/src/test.rs:

  • Happy path: propose → accept, with an exact event for each step, the single authorizer for each step, and get_pending_admin before and after.
  • Every admin right moves: the old admin is rejected by set_token, propose_upgrade, execute_upgrade, cancel_upgrade and propose_admin; the new admin can set the token and rotate again.
  • Third-party, outgoing-admin and no-proposal accept_admin calls are rejected.
  • Real-auth adversarial test (mock_auths, not mock_all_auths): an attacker's signature cannot propose for the admin, and neither the attacker's nor the outgoing admin's signature can accept for the successor. The successor's own signature succeeds.
  • Cancel: event, proposal gone, later accept fails; cancel is admin-only (third party and proposed admin both rejected); cancel with nothing pending fails.
  • Expiry: accept at expires_at fails, at expires_at - 1 succeeds; an expired proposal can still be cancelled.
  • A new proposal replaces the old one; an accepted proposal cannot be replayed; a proposal recorded under a previous admin is rejected.
  • Rotation does not move escrow, and a lease still settles afterwards.
  • Propose and accept extend the instance TTL.

docs.title: Design note — Storage schema versioning and safe upgrades (#123)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design; the accompanying PR implements it so the review can happen against working code and tests.

Issue: #123 — Version the storage schema and reject unsafe upgrades Touches: storage.rs, lib.rs, errors.rs, events.rs, scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text: execute_upgrade replaces the Wasm but keeps every stored entry. The code assumes the DataKey variants and the Service / Lease shapes never change, but nothing records which layout a deployment holds, and nothing checks it after an upgrade. An upgrade that renames a variant or retypes a field silently orphans or misreads live escrow (LeaseNotFound on a funded lease, or a locked_deposit decoded as something else). A rollback after new data has been written has the same effect in reverse.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
1. The registry always knows which storage schema its data conforms to.
  2. Code never writes through a state-changing entry point unless its compiled schema equals the stored one. A mismatch fails closed.
  3. Older data reaches the new schema only through an explicit, admin-authorized and bounded migrate, applied atomically.
  4. Newer data is never migrated "down" and never written by older code.
  5. The upgrade entry points (propose_upgrade, cancel_upgrade, execute_upgrade) are always reachable by the admin, so a bad install can be reverted. The 24h upgrade time lock still applies to that revert.
  6. Existing deployments are not stranded. Their data is schema 0, and 0 → 1 only adds the stamp.
  7. Existing keys, event payloads and error codes are unchanged (additive only).

docs.title: Version record
docs.text:
• storage::SCHEMA_VERSION: u32 = 1 is the layout this Wasm reads and writes. It is mirrored in the storageSchemaVersion contractmeta! entry, so a reviewer can read it from the uploaded artifact before installing it. A test fails if the two diverge.
  • DataKey::SchemaVersion (instance storage, u32) is the layout the stored data conforms to. init stamps it.
  • An initialized registry without a stamp reports LEGACY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 0. An uninitialized one has no data to misread and is not gated.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• init: writes the stamp. It refuses (AlreadyInitialized) if a stamp already exists without an admin, since that is state this contract did not write.
  • After an upgrade: the old code cannot inspect the new Wasm (the swap takes effect after the invocation), so the check runs in the new code on every state-changing call. storage::check_schema is called by set_token, register_service, set_service_active, create_lease, settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease:
  • stored == code: run normally.
  • stored < code: SchemaMigrationRequired (29).
  • stored > code (a downgrade): SchemaVersionUnsupported (30).

This puts the registry into a stopped state from the upgrade transaction until migrate succeeds, without needing a separate pause flag. - Not gated: the upgrade entry points (so a rollback is always possible), migrate, bump_service / bump_lease (which change no stored value and keep entries alive during the stop) and every view.

docs.title: migrate(admin) -> u32
docs.text:
Admin only. If the stored version equals the code's, it is a silent no-op and returns the version, so the deploy script can always call it. If the stored version is newer, it returns SchemaVersionUnsupported. Otherwise it applies storage::migrate_step(v) for each v in stored..SCHEMA_VERSION, writes the stamp, extends the instance TTL and emits schema_migrated { admin, from_version, to_version }, all in one transaction. migrate_step is a match on the source version. A version with no arm has no path and is rejected. Today the only arm is 0 => Ok(()).

Steps must be bounded. They may rewrite instance storage but never iterate over services or leases. A change to persistent entries is migrated lazily by an accessor that reads both shapes and writes the new one, and the step only marks that those readers are live.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text: How a migration is proposed, reviewed and executed is documented in Deployment → Storage schema migrations. In short: the PR that changes the layout bumps the constant and the metadata, adds the migrate_step arm, a stopped → migrate → running test and a design note. The reviewer checks the arm is bounded and verifies storageSchemaVersion on the uploaded Wasm. The operator runs execute_upgrade and then migrate in the next transaction. deploy-testnet.sh --execute-upgrade now does both.

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text:
• Check the new Wasm inside execute_upgrade. Soroban gives the running contract no way to read another Wasm's metadata or code, so the old code cannot validate the new one. The check has to live in the new code.
  • A separate admin pause flag. This would duplicate the stop the schema gate already provides, and it relies on the operator remembering to pause. The gate stops the registry automatically in exactly the window that matters. A general pause (open in other PRs) composes with this design and is not required by it.
  • Run the migration inside the new code's first call. That is implicit and unauthorized, a migration failure would surface in an unrelated user's transaction, and there would be no single reviewed event marking the switch.
  • Version each Service / Lease entry. This makes every entry larger and doesn't detect a wholesale layout mismatch. Lazy per-entry migration remains available inside a step when it is needed.
  • Treat the absent stamp as 1. That would skip the stop on the first upgrade, but leave legacy deployments indistinguishable from stamped ones. Using 0 makes the first rollout exercise the full procedure once, at no risk, because the 0 → 1 step is a no-op.

docs.title: 4. Threat model
docs.text:
Case Handling Upgrade to code with a new layout, migrate forgotten Every state-changing call reverts with SchemaMigrationRequired. No value moves. Downgrade after new data was written SchemaVersionUnsupported everywhere, migrate refuses, and only a re-upgrade resumes. A third party triggers a migration migrate requires the admin's auth and identity (Unauthorized). A migration with no defined path migrate_step rejects it, and the whole transaction reverts. A migration runs out of budget halfway Steps are bounded, and a failure reverts atomically with no partial stamp. Bad upgrade blocks its own fix The upgrade entry points are not gated. Stopped registry lets entries expire bump_service and bump_lease stay available. Foreign or corrupted state before init init refuses a pre-existing stamp.

Trade-off: while stopped, consumers cannot revoke_expired_lease either. That is deliberate, because code that may misread a lease must not pay one out. The window is one transaction long when the procedure is followed, and the 24-hour grace window already exceeds it by orders of magnitude.

docs.title: 5. Test plan
docs.text:
In contracts/registry/src/test.rs, under Storage schema versioning:

  • SCHEMA_VERSION is pinned and matches the storageSchemaVersion metadata.
  • init stamps the version. schema_version before init is NotInitialized. init refuses a pre-existing stamp.
  • Newer stored schema: all fourteen gated entry points return SchemaVersionUnsupported, migrate refuses, and escrow is unchanged.
  • Older (legacy) stored schema: all fourteen return SchemaMigrationRequired. migrate emits schema_migrated and stamps the version, then a pre-upgrade lease settles and new services register.
  • migrate is admin-only (even as a no-op), requires init, and is a silent no-op when the schema is current. An undefined step is rejected.
  • propose_upgrade, cancel_upgrade and execute_upgrade are not blocked by a mismatch, but still enforce admin.
  • TTL bumps and views keep working while stopped.

docs.title: Design note — Revenue splits across multiple providers (#133)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. No contract code is changed by this note. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design before implementation begins.

Issue: #133 — Allow revenue splits across multiple providers Target release: v0.3.0 · Touches: lib.rs, types.rs, storage.rs, events.rs, errors.rs

docs.title: 1. Problem statement
docs.text:
A service has exactly one provider address, and settle_lease pays that address the whole payout. Teams that share operational and infrastructure costs — an API owner plus an RPC operator, a marketplace front end plus an upstream data source — have to route money off-chain after settlement, which is manual, opaque to indexers and outside the protocol's accounting.

This note proposes a bounded revenue split stored per service: an ordered list of recipients with basis-point shares that always sums to 10 000. A service with no split configured keeps the current single-provider behaviour exactly.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Pay multiple recipients atomically in the settlement transaction.
  • Keep the existing single-provider layout and settlement flow as the default, with no migration and no change to Service or Lease.
  • Bound the work per settlement: fixed maximum recipients, no unbounded loop.
  • Make the split and every per-recipient payout observable off-chain.
  • Guarantee the distributed total never exceeds the settlement payout and that rounding never strands or creates value.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Changing who may settle a lease (service.provider remains the only settler).
  • Transferring service ownership or splitting governance rights; recipients get revenue only.
  • Per-lease split snapshots or recipient-level escrow accounts.
  • Splitting the consumer refund (it always goes to the consumer).

docs.title: 2.1 Representation
docs.text:
/// One entry in a service's revenue split.
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct RevenueShare {
    pub recipient: Address,
    /// Share of every payout, in basis points. All shares sum to 10_000.
    pub share_bps: u32,
}
  • Basis points: 1 bps = 0.01 %, and 10_000 bps = 100 %.
  • Recipient count: 1..=MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS, with MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS = 10 (see §6 for why 10).
  • Sum: sum(share_bps) == 10_000 exactly, computed with checked_add.
  • Non-zero: every share_bps > 0; a zero-share recipient is rejected rather than silently paid nothing.
  • Duplicates: the same recipient address may appear once. A duplicate is rejected at configuration time, which also prevents duplicate payments at settlement.
  • Self-payment: a recipient equal to the registry's own address is rejected, because a transfer to self would be a no-op that breaks the distributed == payout accounting story.

The split is stored outside Service:

Key Storage Value TTL RevenueSplit(u64) persistent Vec<RevenueShare> extended on write and read, 30-day horizon, matching Service

Service keeps exactly its current five fields. That is what makes the change upgrade-safe: existing Service entries decode unchanged, and the split key is simply absent for every service that never configures one.

docs.title: 2.2 Backward compatibility: the single-provider default
docs.text:
An absent RevenueSplit(service_id) key is the legacy configuration:

no split stored  =>  pay 100 % to service.provider, as today

Consequences:

  • register_service is unchanged; a provider does not have to configure anything.
  • Existing services continue to settle with one transfer and the exact same lease_settled event payload.
  • Existing leases are unaffected; the split is read at settlement time, and a service without a split behaves identically to v0.2.x.
  • A provider that wants the old behaviour back can call set_revenue_split with a single entry { provider, 10_000 }, or clear_revenue_split to remove the key entirely. Both produce the same payout; the event differs.

docs.title: 2.3 Settlement
docs.text:
settle_lease keeps all of its current checks, ordering and refund logic. Only the payout step changes:

payout = service.rate_per_call * verified_calls      // unchanged, checked
refund = lease.locked_deposit - payout               // unchanged, checked

persist lease.used_calls, lease.settled = true       // unchanged, before transfers

if a split is stored for lease.service_id:
    distributed = 0
    for i in 0 .. shares.len():
        amount[i] = (payout * shares[i].share_bps) / 10_000    // floor, checked
        distributed += amount[i]                               // checked
    amount[last] += payout - distributed                       // remainder
    for each non-zero amount[i]:
        transfer(contract -> shares[i].recipient, amount[i])
else:
    transfer(contract -> service.provider, payout)             // unchanged

Rounding rule. The first n-1 recipients receive floor(payout * share_bps / 10_000); the last recipient in the configured list receives its own floor plus the entire remainder payout - sum(floors). Because the shares sum to 10 000,

sum(floor(payout * bps_i / 10_000))  <=  payout  <  sum(floors) + n

so the remainder is in 0..n, and the last payment remains at most payout plus a few stroops of rounding. Total distributed is exactly payout; nothing is stranded in the contract and nothing is minted. The rule is deterministic and depends only on the stored order, so any indexer can reproduce every amount from lease_settled plus the stored split. If payout == 0, no transfers occur.

Ordering and atomicity. The split is read before the first transfer and is not re-read afterwards, so a re-entrant token cannot change recipients mid-settlement. settled = true is still persisted before any transfer, so a re-entrant settle_lease reverts. If any transfer fails, the whole Soroban invocation reverts: no recipient is paid, the lease stays unsettled, and the refund does not happen either.

Refund. The consumer refund is unchanged and is paid once, after the payout distribution. It is never split.

docs.title: 2.4 Changing the split
docs.text:
set_revenue_split is callable only by the current service.provider. It replaces the entire list atomically; there is no per-entry editing, so a partial write can never leave the shares summing to something other than 10 000.

The split applies to settlements that happen after the change. In-flight leases are paid under the split in force at settlement time. This is deliberate: the escrow is owed to the provider, and routing that revenue among the provider's own recipients is the provider's commercial decision. The consumer's refund and the total payout are unaffected, so no consumer is harmed by a mid-lease change. The trade-off against snapshotting per lease is discussed in §8.

docs.title: 3. Storage changes
docs.text:
Key Storage Value Notes RevenueSplit(u64) persistent Vec<RevenueShare> new, additive; TTL extended on save and read

No existing key changes, no field is added to Service or Lease, and the DataKey discriminants keep their wire names. A v0.3.0 Wasm can be installed over a deployment that holds live services and leases; services without the new key settle exactly as before.

The stored vector is bounded by MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS, so a split entry has a fixed maximum encoded size (about ten address+bps pairs) and a predictable rent cost.

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text:
Entry point Auth Description set_revenue_split(provider, service_id, shares: Vec<RevenueShare>) provider (must own the service) Validate and store a complete split. Emits revenue_split_updated. clear_revenue_split(provider, service_id) provider (must own the service) Remove the split and fall back to 100 % to service.provider. Emits revenue_split_cleared. get_revenue_split(service_id) — Option<Vec<RevenueShare>>; None means the single-provider default.

Read-only helper (optional, recommended for indexers):

View Returns payees(service_id) Vec<Address> — the configured recipients, or [service.provider] when no split is stored

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Topics Data revenue_split_updated service_id provider, shares: Vec<RevenueShare>, recipient_count, total_bps revenue_split_cleared service_id provider lease_split_paid lease_id total_payout, recipients: Vec<Address>, amounts: Vec<i128>
  • revenue_split_updated carries the full configured list, so an indexer can reconstruct every future payment from one event without extra RPC reads. total_bps is included (always 10 000) as a self-check for consumers.
  • lease_split_paid is emitted only when a split is configured and carries the exact per-recipient amounts actually transferred (including the remainder assignment). Indexers therefore never have to re-implement the rounding rule to reconcile balances. It is emitted alongside the unchanged lease_settled; the two share the lease_id topic, and lease_settled.payout equals lease_split_paid.total_payout.
  • For the legacy single-provider path neither new settlement event is emitted, so the existing event stream is unchanged.
  • Neither event carries secret material: recipients and shares are already public on-chain configuration.

docs.title: Error codes (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text:
Code Variant Meaning 33 EmptySplit Zero recipients supplied 34 TooManyRecipients More than MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS 35 InvalidShares A share is zero, or the total is not exactly 10 000 36 DuplicateRecipient The same address appears twice 37 InvalidRecipient A recipient is the registry itself

(17–32 are reserved by the #137 proposal; the final numbers are assigned when both designs are approved so the two changes never collide.)

docs.title: 5. Authorization and governance model
docs.text:
Actor Can do Cannot do service.provider Set/clear the split for its service Change another service's split Recipient Receive its share at settlement Change the split, settle, or claim outside settlement Admin set_token, upgrade Change a split or move payouts Consumer Create/revoke leases Change the split or redirect the refund

No new governance role is introduced. Setting a split is an ordinary provider-signed transaction, exactly like set_service_active, and the service owner remains the only account that can settle, so the payer and the person choosing the payees are the same actor.

docs.title: 6. Security considerations
docs.text:
Unauthorized changes. set_revenue_split / clear_revenue_split call require_auth() on provider and then check service.provider == provider. A third party cannot redirect a service's revenue, and the admin cannot either.

Invalid or excessive allocations. Validation happens before any write: non-empty, <= 10 entries, every share_bps > 0, checked_add sum exactly 10_000, no duplicates, no self-recipient. A rejected call leaves the stored split untouched. The store-then-overwrite design is atomic per call, so there is never an intermediate sum other than the old or the new valid list.

Duplicate payments. Rejected at configuration time, and the settlement loop walks each vector index exactly once. Because the payout is computed and validated before the loop, no recipient can be paid more than its stored share (plus the single remainder allocation to the last entry).

No value creation or loss. sum(amounts) == payout, enforced by the remainder assignment and checked arithmetic; payout + refund == locked_deposit still holds. payout and every amount[i] use checked_mul/checked_add; an overflow reverts the transaction rather than truncating a recipient's payment.

Reentrancy and atomicity. settled = true is persisted before any transfer, and the split vector is read once, before the transfers, so a hostile recipient or token contract cannot alter the list or settle twice. All payments and the refund happen in one transaction; a failure reverts the entire distribution and the refund. The adversarial re-entrant-token test is extended to a split with two recipients.

Resource limits. MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS = 10 bounds the settlement to at most ten payout transfers plus one refund. That is the main cost driver: each SEP-41 transfer is a cross-contract call, and Soroban charges instructions and ledger entries per call. Ten keeps a split settlement comfortably within a standard transaction while covering realistic team structures. The trade-off against a larger bound is in §8; the implementation must include a test that settles a 10-recipient split so the budget is measured, not assumed.

Griefing and storage. The list is provider-owned and bounded, so no one can inflate a service's storage through the split. RevenueSplit is persistent with the same 30-day TTL policy as Service; it cannot be evicted while the service is being read or settled, and a split costs its provider a bounded rent.

Rounding edge cases. payout < number of recipients produces zeros for some entries; zero-amount transfers are skipped and the last entry receives the few stroops of remainder. A single-recipient split at 10 000 bps is mathematically identical to the legacy path; a one-recipient split at any other value is rejected by the sum check. payout == 0 emits no split payments but still emits lease_settled and the refund.

Interaction with #137. A stake is attached to service.provider, not to split recipients. Slashing debits the provider's stake, never a recipient's payout, and the revenue split does not affect stake availability or dispute resolution. Only the provider can settle and therefore only the provider can trigger a distribution.

docs.title: 7. Testing strategy
docs.text:
New tests in contracts/registry/src/test.rs, keeping the existing suite green:

Configuration

  • a service with no split settles exactly as before: one transfer to the provider, unchanged lease_settled payload, no lease_split_paid;
  • set_revenue_split with one entry {provider, 10_000} behaves like the default and emits revenue_split_updated;
  • two and three recipients with valid shares are stored and readable through get_revenue_split / payees;
  • the full event payload (topics + shares + count + total) is asserted with assert_single_event;
  • invalid totals (9 999, 10 001), a zero share, an empty list, eleven recipients, a duplicate address and a self-recipient each revert with the documented error and leave the previous split intact;
  • a non-owner, an impostor and the admin all fail to set or clear a split (Unauthorized);
  • clear_revenue_split restores the legacy behaviour and emits the event.

Settlement

  • a two-recipient split (e.g. 7 000 / 3 000) pays each the right amount and the consumer gets the correct refund; escrow == 0 afterwards;
  • three recipients with a payout that does not divide evenly (e.g. payout 100, shares 3 333 / 3 333 / 3 334) pays 33 / 33 / 34 and emits matching lease_split_paid.amounts;
  • a rounding case where every floor truncates (payout 1, two recipients) gives the remainder to the last recipient, and the total still equals the payout;
  • verified_calls == 0 (full refund) performs no payout transfers and emits no lease_split_paid;
  • a 10-recipient split settles successfully (resource-limit test) with the total exactly equal to payout;
  • the real-SAC lifecycle test is repeated with a split token, proving the distribution works against the SAC;
  • the re-entrant token cannot settle twice when a split is configured and the first recipient is hostile;
  • a recipient that is a contract is paid exactly once.

Invariants asserted after every settlement test

  • sum(recipient payments) + refund == locked_deposit;
  • lease.locked_deposit, lease.settled and the provider's stake (when #137 is present) are unchanged by the split;
  • the registry's token balance returns to zero.

docs.title: 8. Open questions and trade-offs
docs.text:
1. Recipient bound. 10 covers most teams and bounds settlement to 11 cross-contract calls. A larger bound (e.g. 20) is more flexible but raises the fee of every settlement and the chance of exceeding the transaction budget. Question for maintainers: is 10 right, or should it be 5?
  2. Snapshot vs live split. Reading the split at settlement lets a provider re-route revenue mid-lease; snapshotting it into the lease would require a new Lease field (breaking the stored encoding) or a new per-lease key and more storage. This note chooses live configuration because only the payer's own routing changes and the consumer's refund is untouched. Alternative: LeaseSplit(lease_id) written at create_lease for full per-lease determinism.
  3. Remainder policy. Paying the remainder to the last configured entry is the simplest deterministic rule and easy to reproduce. Alternatives: the largest share, or largest-remainder (Hamilton) apportionment, which is marginally fairer but more code and more subtle to test.
  4. Dust when all shares floor to zero. With payout < n, early recipients can receive 0 while the last receives the whole payout. That is exact and harmless, but a provider may be surprised. Alternative: reject settlements whose payout is smaller than the recipient count — rejected here because it would couple settlement to the split and could block a refund.
  5. Recipients as contracts. Paying a contract recipient is allowed; whether it should require the recipient to implement a specific interface (or be rejected) is a policy question. This note allows any Address, consistent with the rest of the protocol.
  6. Per-recipient events. One lease_split_paid carrying parallel arrays is compact and cheap; n separate events would be easier for naive indexers but costs n event emissions per settlement. This note prefers the single event; the schema should be documented before release.
  7. Split plus future service transfer. If service transfer ships (#issue for key rotation), the new owner inherits the split. The design should state that explicitly, and whether a transfer must clear or re-confirm the split.
  8. Versioning. The change is additive, but the workspace version should move to 0.3.0 with the #137 work and the release notes must describe the split semantics and rounding rule.

docs.title: 9. Review request
docs.text:
Per CONTRIBUTING.md, this note needs maintainer approval before code:

  • Confirm MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS (10 vs 5) and the one-event-with-arrays shape.
  • Confirm that the split is read at settlement time rather than snapshotted per lease.
  • Confirm the rounding rule (remainder to the last configured recipient).
  • Confirm the error-code range so it does not collide with #137.

Once approved, implementation lands on the same feature branch as #137, with the tests above and the full four-command validation from CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Design note — Optional oracle attestation for metered usage (#136)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. No contract code is changed by this note. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design before implementation begins.

Issue: #136 — Add optional oracle attestation for metered usage Target release: v0.3.0 · Touches: lib.rs, types.rs, storage.rs, events.rs, errors.rs, test.rs, docs/security.md

docs.title: 1. Problem statement
docs.text:
settle_lease(provider, lease_id, verified_calls) trusts one number supplied by the provider. The allotment bounds the damage — a provider can never be paid for more than allocated_calls — but within that bound the provider is the only witness to usage. A consumer that was served 120 of 500 calls and a provider that reports 400 cannot be distinguished on-chain, and the consumer's only recourse is to stop using the service.

Some providers and consumers already operate an independent usage oracle: a gateway, an RPC operator, a metering service or a co-signed receipt log. This note proposes an optional per-service attestor that must approve a settlement before it pays out. A service that never configures one keeps the current trust model and the current settle_lease path exactly.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Let a service bind settlement to an independent attestation of usage.
  • Define a small, explicit attestor interface rather than one signature scheme.
  • Bind every attestation to the registry deployment, lease id, service id and exact call count, so it cannot be replayed or retargeted.
  • Make the opt-in per lease at creation time, so a provider cannot silently drop the requirement for an in-flight lease.
  • Reject a missing, stale, mismatched or otherwise invalid attestation without touching escrow.
  • Keep the consumer's refund and revocation path completely unchanged.
  • Add no unbounded loops, no new trusted key inside the registry, and no change to the Service or Lease stored encoding.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Proving that an HTTP request actually happened. The registry cannot observe traffic; it enforces whose answer is required, not that the answer is true.
  • Making attestation mandatory, protocol-wide, or retroactive to existing leases.
  • Verifying one specific signature algorithm inside the registry. An attestor is a contract, so it may use ed25519, secp256k1, a quorum, its own storage or anything else.
  • Multiple attestors, threshold policies or per-call attestations. A single attestor per lease is the smallest useful unit.
  • A dispute process for a lying attestor. That is #137 (staking and slashing) territory.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
These must hold after the change, in both attestor and no-attestor modes:

  1. payout + refund == locked_deposit for every settlement.
  2. settled is persisted before any token transfer, and a settled lease never transitions again.
  3. A settlement pays at most allocated_calls × rate_per_call.
  4. No attestation, no payout for a lease created on an opted-in service.
  5. The consumer's right to revoke after expires_at + 24h is never gated by an attestor, an attestor outage or an attestor configuration change.
  6. An attestation is accepted only for the lease, service and call count it was created for, in this registry deployment, inside its validity window.
  7. A lease's attestation requirement is fixed when the lease is created. Later provider configuration changes affect new leases only.
  8. The no-attestor mode is byte-for-byte the current behaviour: same entry point, same event, same errors, same storage shape.

docs.title: 3.1 The attestor interface
docs.text:
An attestor is a Soroban contract address. The registry expects exactly one method, declared next to the other contract types:

/// Payload the registry asks an attestor to approve at settlement time.
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct UsageAttestation {
    /// Registry deployment this attestation is valid for.
    pub registry: Address,
    /// Lease whose usage is being attested.
    pub lease_id: u64,
    /// Service the lease belongs to.
    pub service_id: u64,
    /// Calls the provider reports as consumed.
    pub verified_calls: u32,
    /// Ledger timestamp the attestor observed the usage.
    pub issued_at: u64,
    /// Ledger timestamp after which the attestation is no longer valid.
    pub valid_until: u64,
}

/// The interface an attestor contract must implement.
#[soroban_sdk::contractclient(name = "UsageAttestorClient")]
pub trait UsageAttestor {
    /// Return `true` only if `payload` is a genuine attestation for this
    /// registry. Implementations must check `payload.registry` (or the calling
    /// contract) and reject payloads they did not produce.
    fn attest(env: Env, payload: UsageAttestation) -> bool;
}

The interface is deliberately thin:

  • The registry owns the schema of what is attested. An attestor cannot redefine what verified_calls means.
  • The attestor owns the proof. It may verify an ed25519 signature, read its own stored observation, check a quorum, or return false unconditionally during an incident.
  • The registry never verifies a signature itself. Soroban's env.crypto().ed25519_verify aborts the invocation on an invalid signature, which would turn a malformed attestation into an opaque host error rather than the documented InvalidAttestation. Keeping verification in the attestor gives callers a typed result and lets a provider rotate or replace the attestor's internals without a registry upgrade.

An attestor is configured per service:

/// Attestation requirement snapshotted for new leases of a service.
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct AttestationConfig {
    /// Contract that must approve settlements for leases created under it.
    pub attestor: Address,
    /// Maximum accepted age of an attestation, in seconds.
    pub max_age_secs: u64,
}

docs.title: 3.2 Opt-in and per-lease snapshot
docs.text:
The requirement lives in two additive persistent keys:

Key Written by Read by Meaning ServiceAttestor(service_id) set_service_attestor create_lease, get_service_attestor Template for new leases. Absent means the legacy trust model. LeaseAttestor(lease_id) create_lease both settlement paths, get_lease_attestor Immutable requirement for this lease.

create_lease reads ServiceAttestor(service_id) after the service is loaded. If it exists, it writes the same AttestationConfig into LeaseAttestor(lease_id) in the same transaction that writes the lease. If it does not, no per-lease key is written and the lease is a legacy lease.

Why snapshot instead of reading the service config at settlement time:

  • A provider cannot opt out of attestation for leases it has already sold.
  • A consumer can read get_lease_attestor(lease_id) immediately after create_lease and know exactly which attestor must approve the payout.
  • Clearing or replacing a service's attestor only changes the requirement for future leases, so it cannot strand a lease whose attestor has since been removed.
  • Existing Lease and Service values do not change, so an upgrade does not rewrite live entries.

The per-lease entry costs one write per opted-in lease and is removed when the lease settles or is revoked.

docs.title: 3.3 Settlement paths
docs.text:
The existing entry point keeps its exact signature:

pub fn settle_lease(env: Env, provider: Address, lease_id: u64, verified_calls: u32)
    -> Result<(), Error>

It gains one check, after the lease and service have been loaded and before any state is written:

if LeaseAttestor(lease_id) exists:
    return Err(AttestationRequired)

Everything else in settle_lease is unchanged, so every service without an opt-in behaves exactly as today.

The attested path is a new entry point, not a new argument on the old one:

pub fn settle_lease_attested(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    attestation: UsageAttestation,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Adding an Option<UsageAttestation> argument to settle_lease would break the ABI for every existing client and indexer; a new function is additive.

settle_lease_attested performs, in order:

  1. provider.require_auth().
  2. Reject attestation.registry != env.current_contract_address() with AttestationMismatch.
  3. Load the lease by attestation.lease_id; reject if settled (LeaseAlreadySettled) or missing (LeaseNotFound).
  4. Load LeaseAttestor(lease_id); if absent, reject with AttestationNotConfigured (the caller used the wrong entry point).
  5. Reject attestation.service_id != lease.service_id with AttestationMismatch.
  6. Reject attestation.verified_calls > lease.allocated_calls with InvalidCalls.
  7. Load the service and require service.provider == provider (Unauthorized).
  8. Apply the unchanged settleability rule: the lease must be expired or verified_calls == allocated_calls (LeaseNotSettleable).
  9. Validate freshness against config.max_age_secs:
  10. now >= issued_at, otherwise AttestationStale;
  11. now - issued_at <= max_age_secs, otherwise AttestationStale;
  12. valid_until > issued_at and now < valid_until, otherwise AttestationStale.
  13. Compute payout and refund with the same checked arithmetic.
  14. Call UsageAttestorClient::new(&env, &config.attestor).attest(&attestation). A false return is InvalidAttestation. A revert inside the attestor reverts the whole settlement; the registry does not retry or ignore it.
  15. Persist used_calls and settled = true, remove LeaseAttestor(lease_id), then perform the payout and refund transfers.
  16. Publish the unchanged lease_settled event plus a new lease_attested event.

Step 11 happens after every registry check and before any registry state write or token call. The attestor is untrusted code, but at that point it can only return a boolean or revert. It cannot observe a half-written settlement, and a re-entrant call into the registry fails because the nested invocation has no provider authorization. The token transfers still happen only after settled = true is persisted, so the re-entrant-token guarantee is unchanged.

revoke_expired_lease is untouched except that it also removes LeaseAttestor(lease_id) when it refunds. It never reads or calls the attestor, so a dead or hostile attestor cannot block the consumer's exit.

docs.title: 3.4 Configuring and reading the requirement
docs.text:
pub fn set_service_attestor(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    service_id: u64,
    attestor: Address,
    max_age_secs: u64,
) -> Result<(), Error>

pub fn clear_service_attestor(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    service_id: u64,
) -> Result<(), Error>

pub fn get_service_attestor(env: Env, service_id: u64) -> Option<AttestationConfig>
pub fn get_lease_attestor(env: Env, lease_id: u64) -> Option<AttestationConfig>
  • Only service.provider may set or clear, after require_auth() and the same ownership check as set_service_active (Unauthorized).
  • attestor must not be the registry itself, otherwise settlement would recurse into attest; this is InvalidAttestationConfig.
  • max_age_secs must be in MIN_ATTESTATION_MAX_AGE_SECS (60) to MAX_ATTESTATION_MAX_AGE_SECS (7 * 24 * 60 * 60). Zero would make every attestation stale, and an unbounded window defeats the staleness check.
  • Setting replaces the template atomically. Clearing removes it. Neither touches existing LeaseAttestor snapshots.
  • Both writers emit an event (see §5); both views are read-only and do not extend a TTL.

There is no admin override. The provider is the party that chooses its own attestor, exactly as it chooses rate_per_call; the consumer's protection is the snapshot and the unchanged refund path, not an admin promise.

docs.title: 4. Storage and resource changes
docs.text:
All keys are additive DataKey variants; Service, Lease and every existing key keep their exact encoding.

Key Storage Value TTL policy ServiceAttestor(u64) persistent AttestationConfig Extended when create_lease snapshots it; 30-day horizon, matching Service. LeaseAttestor(u64) persistent AttestationConfig Extended with the lease: term + 24h grace + 1-day buffer, clamped to MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS and the network maxEntryTtl. Removed on settle/revoke.
  • settle_lease gains one persistent read (LeaseAttestor) and one delete on the attested path.
  • create_lease gains one read and, only for opted-in services, one write plus a TTL extension.
  • No entry point iterates a user-supplied collection; the attestor call is a single cross-contract call.
  • bump_lease also extends LeaseAttestor when present, so a long-lived lease cannot lose its requirement to eviction while its escrow is still claimable. bump_service also extends ServiceAttestor when present.

The attestor contract's own storage is outside this contract's rent model. A provider choosing an attestor is choosing that dependency.

docs.title: 5. Events
docs.text:
New events follow the existing schema_version convention; no existing topic or payload changes.

Event Topics Data service_attestor_set service_id schema_version, provider, attestor, max_age_secs service_attestor_cleared service_id schema_version, provider lease_attested lease_id schema_version, service_id, attestor, verified_calls, issued_at, valid_until

lease_attested is emitted immediately after the unchanged lease_settled, in the same transaction. It carries the attestor address and the exact validity window, so an indexer can reconcile the payout with the attestation without a second RPC read. Neither event contains secret material.

LeaseCreated is intentionally unchanged. The per-lease requirement is discoverable through get_lease_attestor(lease_id), and changing LeaseCreated would force every indexer to handle a new payload version for a field they can already read.

docs.title: 6. Errors (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text:
Code Variant Meaning 38 AttestationRequired settle_lease called for a lease that requires attestation 39 AttestationNotConfigured settle_lease_attested called for a lease with no attestor snapshot 40 AttestationMismatch Payload registry, lease or service does not match the stored lease 41 AttestationStale issued_at is in the future, older than max_age_secs, or valid_until has passed 42 InvalidAttestation The attestor returned false 43 InvalidAttestationConfig Zero/out-of-range max_age_secs, or the registry itself as attestor

17–32 are proposed for #137 and 33–37 for #133. This note appends 38–43 so the three proposals do not collide; the final numbers are assigned when the designs are approved and before any of them becomes ABI.

docs.title: 7. Backward compatibility
docs.text:
• Default mode. No ServiceAttestor key means no LeaseAttestor key, settle_lease unchanged, lease_settled unchanged, no new transfers, no new errors. This is the path every current service takes.
  • Existing services and leases. Neither has the new keys, so both are legacy. An upgrade to a v0.3.0 Wasm does not migrate or rewrite them.
  • Existing clients. settle_lease keeps its signature. A client that never calls set_service_attestor cannot observe the feature at all.
  • Existing events. lease_created, lease_settled and lease_revoked keep their topics and payloads. The new events are additional names.
  • Opting out. clear_service_attestor stops requiring attestation for leases created afterwards. Leases already created keep their snapshot and must still be settled through settle_lease_attested; that is the point of the snapshot.
  • Consumer exit. revoke_expired_lease never requires an attestation, so opting in cannot trap escrow.

docs.title: Added trust assumption
docs.text:
Choosing an attestor means trusting that address's code and operator to return true only for genuine usage of that lease. The registry enforces that the attestor approved this exact lease, service, deployment and call count, recently and once; it cannot enforce that the approval is truthful. If the provider controls the attestor, the opt-in is an operational integrity control, not a trustless guarantee. Consumers should treat get_lease_attestor as the description of who they must trust.

Two operational assumptions come with it:

  • Liveness. If the attestor stops answering, an opted-in lease cannot be settled. The escrow is not stuck: after expiry plus the 24h grace the consumer can still revoke in full, and the provider loses the payout it failed to attest. Providers should choose an attestor with an availability story and should not opt in leases they cannot attest.
  • Code safety. A malicious attestor can return false (denying the provider's payout) or revert. It cannot move escrow: the registry makes no token call before the attestor answers, and the attestor is never approved to spend the registry's balance.

docs.title: Adversarial cases
docs.text: Attack / failure Handling Provider bypasses attestation with settle_lease LeaseAttestor exists, so AttestationRequired. Provider settles on a legacy lease through the attested path No snapshot, so AttestationNotConfigured. Attestation from another lease or service lease_id/service_id are checked against stored state; AttestationMismatch. Attestation from another registry deployment attestation.registry must equal current_contract_address; AttestationMismatch. Call count differs from the attested count The exact verified_calls is part of the payload; the attestor must approve it. A different count fails InvalidAttestation, an over-count fails InvalidCalls. Replay after settlement settled is checked first; LeaseAlreadySettled. Replay on a second lease Lease id is bound into the payload; the attestor should reject, and the registry rejects a mismatched lease. Stale or future-dated attestation AttestationStale on issued_at, valid_until and max_age_secs. Provider rotates or clears the attestor mid-lease Snapshot is immutable; the lease keeps its original requirement. Provider configures a different attestor before settlement Ignored for existing leases; only new leases see it. Malicious attestor re-enters the registry All checks precede the call, no registry write or transfer precedes it, and a nested settlement lacks provider auth. The settlement either gets one boolean or reverts. Malicious attestor reverts Whole settlement reverts; escrow stays in place; consumer revocation still available. Attestor returns true for a false count Not preventable on-chain. This is the declared trust assumption, not a bug. Consumer cannot exit because attestation is missing revoke_expired_lease is unchanged and attestor-independent. Storage eviction removes the requirement LeaseAttestor inherits the lease TTL policy and is extended by bump_lease.

docs.title: 9. Rejected alternatives
docs.text:
1. Add Option<UsageAttestation> to settle_lease. Breaks the published ABI and forces every client, CLI invocation and indexer to change even when no attestor exists. Rejected; a new entry point is additive.
  2. Verify an ed25519 signature directly in the registry. The host's ed25519_verify panics on an invalid signature, so the registry cannot return InvalidAttestation; it would also hard-code one algorithm and one key format into the money path. A contract attestor can still verify ed25519 internally and return false.
  3. Store a public key instead of an attestor contract. Simpler storage, but it makes key rotation a provider transaction that can silently change the meaning of an already-created lease, and it cannot express a quorum or an oracle that keeps its own observation log.
  4. Read the service config at settlement time (no snapshot). Lets a provider remove the requirement after selling the lease. Rejected because it defeats the consumer-visible guarantee.
  5. Attestor as a Stellar account with require_auth(). The attestor would have to co-sign every settlement transaction, and there is no payload to carry issued_at/valid_until. Operationally worse and less expressive than a pre-issued attestation.
  6. Add an attestor field to Service or Lease. Changes the stored value encoding and forces a migration of every live entry. Additive keys avoid that.
  7. Mandatory attestation for all services. Changes the default trust model, which the issue explicitly excludes.

docs.title: 10. Test plan
docs.text:
New tests in contracts/registry/src/test.rs, with a small test-only attestor contract defined in the test module (never deployed):

// Test-only: returns a configurable verdict and records the last payload.
#[contract]
pub struct MockAttestor;

Configuration and views

  • set_service_attestor by the provider stores the config, extends the TTL and emits service_attestor_set with the exact topics and payload.
  • a non-owner, an impostor and the admin all fail with Unauthorized.
  • max_age_secs of 0, 59, or above 7 days fails InvalidAttestationConfig; the registry address as attestor fails the same way.
  • clear_service_attestor removes the template, emits service_attestor_cleared, and leaves existing lease snapshots intact.
  • get_service_attestor / get_lease_attestor return None for legacy and the stored config for opted-in entries.

Lease snapshot

  • create_lease on an opted-in service writes LeaseAttestor with the config in force at creation;
  • a later set_service_attestor / clear_service_attestor does not change that lease's snapshot;
  • a lease created before the opt-in has no snapshot and is legacy;
  • create_lease on a legacy service writes no LeaseAttestor key.

The four acceptance cases

Case Setup Expected Missing Opted-in lease; call settle_lease(provider, id, calls) AttestationRequired; no transfer, lease unsettled Stale issued_at older than max_age_secs, issued_at in the future, or valid_until in the past AttestationStale; no transfer, no state change Mismatched Wrong registry, wrong service_id, or an attestation for another lease AttestationMismatch (or the other lease, if that is the lease being settled) Valid Attestor returns true inside the window Settlement succeeds: exact payout/refund, lease_settled and lease_attested emitted

Settlement and failure paths

  • a valid attestation settles exactly once; a second call is LeaseAlreadySettled;
  • settle_lease_attested on a legacy lease is AttestationNotConfigured;
  • the attestor returning false is InvalidAttestation and moves nothing;
  • verified_calls > allocated_calls is InvalidCalls before the attestor is called;
  • settling before expiry with fewer than allocated_calls remains LeaseNotSettleable, even with a valid attestation;
  • a lease whose attestor was cleared after creation still requires its snapshot and settles through the attested path;
  • revoke_expired_lease ignores the attestor and refunds in full after the grace window; it also removes the snapshot.

Adversarial and Stellar-specific

  • a hostile attestor that reverts makes the settlement revert and leaves escrow intact;
  • a hostile attestor that re-enters settle_lease_attested cannot settle twice or move funds (auth failure);
  • the real-SAC lifecycle test is repeated with an attested settlement;
  • the existing re-entrant-token test still proves a lease cannot settle twice.

Invariants asserted after every settlement test

  • payout + refund == locked_deposit, and locked_balance == 0 afterwards;
  • the registry token balance returns to zero;
  • a revoked or settled lease never transitions again;
  • LeaseAttestor is gone after settlement or revocation.

docs.title: 11. Rollout and documentation
docs.text:
• Workspace version moves to 0.3.0 with the #133/#137 work; this change is additive and needs no migration.
  • docs/security.md gains the new trust assumption and a known limitation: attestation binds who may report usage, not whether the usage happened, and a provider-controlled attestor does not remove the provider's incentive to over-report.
  • docs/contract-reference.md and README.md gain the new entry points, events, error codes and views once the code lands.
  • Release notes describe the opt-in, the per-lease snapshot and the liveness risk.
  • cargo fmt --all -- --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test --all and cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all are the acceptance gate.

docs.title: 12. Open questions
docs.text:
1. Attestor bound. One attestor per service/lease is the smallest useful unit. Question for maintainers: is a single attestor enough, or should the first version allow a small Vec with an "all must approve" rule?
  2. Default max_age_secs. The note proposes provider-chosen between 60s and 7 days with no protocol default, because the useful window depends on the oracle. A shorter cap (for example 24h, matching the grace period) is safer but constrains outage recovery.
  3. Snapshot storage cost. One extra persistent entry per opted-in lease. The alternative — a Lease field — avoids the key but breaks the stored encoding; this note keeps the additive key.
  4. Event schema. No existing payload changes, so EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION stays at 1. New events are new names, not new versions.
  5. Error numbering. 38–43 assumes #133 and #137 keep their proposed ranges. If either changes, these move before implementation.
  6. Attestation evidence. The payload carries no usage digest or receipt hash. If maintainers want off-chain verifiability, a future version can add a commitment to the attested usage log without changing the settlement semantics.

docs.title: 13. Review request
docs.text:
Per CONTRIBUTING.md, this note needs maintainer approval before code:

  • Approve the contract-attestor interface (attest(payload) -> bool) over a registry-verified signature.
  • Confirm the per-lease snapshot so later config changes cannot downgrade an in-flight lease.
  • Confirm the new entry point (settle_lease_attested) rather than an optional argument on settle_lease.
  • Confirm the max_age_secs bounds and the 38–43 error range.

Once approved, implementation lands on the same feature branch as the #133 and #137 work, with the tests above and the full four-command validation from CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Design note — Provider staking and slashing (#137)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. No contract code is changed by this note. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design before implementation begins.

Issue: #137 — Add provider staking and slashing for proven over-reporting Target release: v0.3.0 · Touches: lib.rs, storage.rs, types.rs, events.rs, errors.rs

docs.title: 1. Problem statement
docs.text:
settle_lease trusts the provider's verified_calls. The allotment caps the damage per lease, and the consumer can reclaim an unsettled deposit after the grace window, but a provider that reports more calls than it actually served keeps the over-payment. The only penalty is that the consumer does not come back. There is no on-chain cost to over-reporting within allocated_calls, so the protocol's central trust assumption — "the provider reports honestly" — has no economic backstop.

This note proposes an opt-in provider stake that a service must post before it accepts leases, plus a bounded, evidence-based slashing process for proven over-reporting.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Give consumers a recourse that is funded by the provider, not by other users.
  • Make the penalty proportional to the over-report and hard-capped, so the mechanism cannot be used to confiscate a provider's business.
  • Keep staking opt-in: existing services and deployments keep working unchanged, and unstaked services continue to be leaseable.
  • Never delay, block or alter settlement or the consumer refund path.
  • Add no unbounded loops, no new trust in off-chain data, and no change to the existing Service/Lease storage layout.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Proving real HTTP usage on-chain. The contract cannot observe traffic; the design constrains who may accuse, how much may be slashed and where the money goes, and relies on a public evidence hash plus an arbiter.
  • Insuring consumers for non-delivery. That remains the refund path plus, now, a stake.
  • A general arbitration court, appeals beyond one challenge round, or slashing for anything other than over-reporting.

docs.title: 2.1 Stake custody
docs.text:
Stake is held by the registry in the same SEP-41 token as escrow, but accounted for separately. Escrow accounting is per lease (locked_deposit); stake accounting is per provider. The contract must never infer one from the token balance — sum(locked deposits) + sum(stakes) == token balance is an invariant the tests assert; the token balance itself is never used as a source of truth.

Stake is associated with the provider address (Service.provider), not the service id. One pool covers every service that provider opts in, which avoids duplicating capital across services and keeps the slash/withdraw bookkeeping bounded. Revenue-split recipients (#133) are payees only; they are not stakers and cannot be slashed.

docs.title: 2.2 Opt-in per service
docs.text:
A provider opts a service into staking with opt_in_service_stake. The opt-in is a separate storage key (ServiceStake(service_id)) rather than a new field on Service, so existing Service entries keep decoding and the storage layout is upgrade-safe. Opting out only blocks new leases.

create_lease enforces the invariant for opted-in services:

if service is staked:
    provider stake must exist and available_stake >= min_stake
    the provider must not have a withdrawal pending

If either check fails the lease reverts (InsufficientStake / StakeWithdrawalPending). Existing services that never opt in are unaffected; no new lease on an unstaked service ever requires stake.

docs.title: 2.3 Minimum and configurable requirements
docs.text:
The admin configures a single StakeConfig in instance storage:

Field Meaning Default Bound min_stake Minimum available stake an opted-in service needs at lease creation — > 0 dispute_bond Bond an accuser posts to open a dispute — > 0 dispute_window_secs How long after a lease's dispute anchor a dispute may be opened — 1 h – 30 days challenge_period_secs Provider response window before resolution — 1 h – 7 days unbonding_period_secs Delay between withdrawal request and release — >= dispute_window + challenge_period, max 30 days max_slash_bps Hard cap on the share of a provider's stake one dispute may slash — 1 – 10 000 bps

Staking is disabled until the admin sets a config; opt_in_service_stake and open_dispute revert with StakeNotConfigured before then. This means an upgraded deployment behaves exactly like today until the operator opts the protocol in. The admin can raise/lower min_stake later; lowering it takes effect immediately for new leases, raising it never invalidates existing leases.

docs.title: 2.4 Evidence and slashing authority
docs.text:
The contract cannot validate usage data, so "proven" is defined procedurally. A dispute may only be opened by the lease's consumer — the party that paid and therefore has standing — and only against a settled lease of a staked service, within the dispute window.

Admissible evidence. The contract stores only a 32-byte commitment (evidence_hash) and emits it. The evidence bundle is published off-chain in a documented format so any third party can reproduce the verdict:

  • the lease id, service id and settlement transaction hash,
  • the provider's reported verified_calls,
  • per-call records the provider signed or that the consumer can verify (signed request logs, provider receipts, or the provider's own metering export),
  • a manifest hash over those artifacts, which is the evidence_hash.

The provider may answer once with contest_dispute, supplying its own counter_evidence_hash. Both hashes and the final verdict are permanent event data.

Who may slash.
