  1. The consumer opens the dispute and posts dispute_bond.
  2. The provider may contest during challenge_period_secs.
  3. The arbiter — a dedicated role, defaulting to the admin and rotatable by the admin — resolves after the challenge period with resolve_dispute.
  4. Only then, and only if approved, is stake moved.

Bounds that prevent arbitrary confiscation.

  • Only a consumer with a settled lease can accuse; the arbiter cannot open a dispute against a provider it dislikes.
  • The disputed amount is bounded by the on-chain over-report: overreported_calls * rate_per_call, where overreported_calls <= lease.allocated_calls.
  • The slash is additionally capped at stake_total * max_slash_bps / 10_000 and can never exceed the provider's remaining stake.
  • Slashed value is paid to the accusing consumer, never to the admin, the arbiter or the registry. The arbiter therefore cannot profit from a ruling.
  • A rejected dispute returns nothing to the accuser: the bond is paid to the provider as compensation for the false accusation, and the provider's stake is untouched.
  • Every step emits an event with the evidence hashes and amounts; the arbiter role and config are admin-visible and rotatable.

A single challenge round is deliberately the whole procedure. It is a bounded governance process, not a court: the cap, the consumer-only standing and the "proceeds to the accuser" rule are what make it safe to keep small.

docs.title: 2.5 Withdrawal rules
docs.text:
Stake leaves in two steps:

  1. request_stake_withdrawal(provider, amount) requires:
  2. the provider has opted out of every service (staked_services == 0),
  3. no unsettled leases are attributable to the provider (open_leases == 0),
  4. no dispute against the provider is pending (pending_disputes == 0),
  5. amount <= available, and amount > 0. It moves amount from available to unbonding and sets unbonding_until = now + unbonding_period_secs. A withdrawal request also makes create_lease revert with StakeWithdrawalPending for that provider's services, so no new exposure can be created while capital is leaving.
  6. withdraw_stake(provider) requires now >= unbonding_until, open_leases == 0 and pending_disputes == 0, then transfers the unbonding amount to the provider.

Because unbonding_period_secs >= dispute_window_secs + challenge_period_secs, every settlement that could still be disputed has either been disputed or is past its window before the capital is released, and unbonding stake remains slashable until the transfer happens. A new deposit_stake during unbonding cancels the request (unbonding returns to available, the timer clears), which is safe because the funds never left the contract.

pending_disputes and open_leases are per-provider counters, incremented and decremented on the paths that create and close them, so withdrawal never scans a collection.

docs.title: 2.6 Settlement and service lifecycle
docs.text:
• Settlement and revocation are unchanged: stake never gates settle_lease or revoke_expired_lease, and the consumer's exit remains guaranteed. A provider that has been slashed can still settle leases it already sold.
  • Slashing is paid from the provider's stake, not from lease escrow, so payout + refund == locked_deposit still holds for every lease.
  • If a slash drops available below min_stake, the service is effectively deactivated without writing to Service: the next create_lease reverts InsufficientStake. This avoids iterating a provider's services to flip is_active, keeps Service layout-compatible, and makes topping the stake up an immediate recovery. set_service_active(false) remains available for an explicit pause, and a provider can always opt out.
  • A provider's opt-in/opt-out never changes the terms of an existing lease; those leases settle under the rules in force when they were created.

docs.title: 3. Storage changes
docs.text:
All additions are new DataKey variants. Service, Lease, LeaseStatus and every existing key keep their exact wire encoding.

Key Storage Value TTL policy StakeConfig instance StakeConfig instance TTL, bumped on every state change Arbiter instance Address instance TTL Stake(Address) persistent StakeAccount extended on read/write, 30-day horizon ServiceStake(u64) persistent bool extended with the service, 30-day horizon DisputeCount instance u64 instance TTL Dispute(u64) persistent Dispute extended on read/write; retained through resolution + 30 days 
pub struct StakeAccount {
    pub available: i128,
    pub unbonding: i128,
    pub unbonding_until: u64,
    pub open_leases: u32,      // leases of this provider not yet settled/revoked
    pub staked_services: u32,  // services currently opted in
    pub pending_disputes: u32, // disputes not yet resolved
}

pub struct Dispute {
    pub dispute_id: u64,
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub accuser: Address,       // lease.consumer
    pub provider: Address,      // service.provider
    pub evidence_hash: BytesN<32>,
    pub counter_evidence_hash: BytesN<32>, // zeroed until contested
    pub overreported_calls: u32,
    pub slash_amount: i128,     // computed and frozen at open time
    pub bond: i128,
    pub opened_at: u64,
    pub status: DisputeStatus,  // Open = 0, Contested = 1, Approved = 2, Rejected = 3
}

pub struct StakeConfig {
    pub min_stake: i128,
    pub dispute_bond: i128,
    pub dispute_window_secs: u64,
    pub challenge_period_secs: u64,
    pub unbonding_period_secs: u64,
    pub max_slash_bps: u32,
}

slash_amount is frozen at open_dispute so topping up the stake, or a second dispute, cannot change what the first one may take. The bounded cap is re-evaluated against the balance at resolution and the payout is the smaller of the frozen amount and the remaining stake.

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text: Entry point Auth Description set_stake_config(admin, config) admin Set/update the staking configuration. Emits stake_config_set. set_arbiter(admin, arbiter) admin Rotate the dispute arbiter. Emits arbiter_set. deposit_stake(provider, amount) provider Transfer amount from the provider into the stake pool; cancels a pending withdrawal. Emits stake_deposited. request_stake_withdrawal(provider, amount) provider Start unbonding. Emits stake_withdrawal_requested. cancel_stake_withdrawal(provider) provider Return unbonding to available before release. Emits stake_withdrawal_cancelled. withdraw_stake(provider) provider Release unbonding stake after the delay. Emits stake_withdrawn. opt_in_service_stake(provider, service_id) provider Require stake for new leases of the service. Emits service_stake_changed. opt_out_service_stake(provider, service_id) provider Stop requiring stake for new leases. Emits service_stake_changed. open_dispute(consumer, lease_id, evidence_hash, overreported_calls) consumer Post the bond and open a dispute on a settled lease. Emits dispute_opened. contest_dispute(provider, dispute_id, counter_evidence_hash) provider Answer once inside the challenge period. Emits dispute_contested. resolve_dispute(arbiter, dispute_id, approve: bool) arbiter After the challenge period, slash or reject. Emits dispute_resolved and provider_slashed. get_stake(provider) — Result<StakeAccount, Error> get_stake_config() — Result<StakeConfig, Error> get_dispute(dispute_id) — Result<Dispute, Error> is_service_staked(service_id) — bool stake_requirement(service_id) — Result<Option<i128>, Error>: min_stake when staked, otherwise None

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Topics Data stake_config_set — admin, min_stake, dispute_bond, dispute_window_secs, challenge_period_secs, unbonding_period_secs, max_slash_bps arbiter_set — admin, arbiter stake_deposited provider amount, available, unbonding stake_withdrawal_requested provider amount, unbonding_until stake_withdrawal_cancelled provider amount stake_withdrawn provider amount, available service_stake_changed service_id provider, staked dispute_opened dispute_id lease_id, service_id, accuser, evidence_hash, overreported_calls, slash_amount, bond dispute_contested dispute_id provider, counter_evidence_hash dispute_resolved dispute_id approved, slash_amount, bond_to_provider, evidence_hash provider_slashed provider amount, remaining_available, remaining_unbonding

service_registered, service_status_changed, lease_created, lease_settled and lease_revoked keep their exact payloads; the stake checks add no field to a lease.

docs.title: Error codes (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text: Code Variant Meaning 17 StakeNotConfigured Staking has not been enabled by the admin 18 InvalidStakeAmount Zero/negative stake, bond or config value 19 InsufficientStake Provider's available stake is below min_stake 20 StakeWithdrawalPending Withdrawal unbonding; no new leases 21 WithdrawalNotReady Unbonding period has not elapsed 22 PendingDispute A pending dispute blocks the action 23 ServiceNotStaked Dispute against a service that did not opt in 24 ServiceAlreadyStaked Opt-in on an already-staked service 25 OutstandingLeases Unsettled leases block withdrawal 26 NoStake No stake account for the provider 27 DisputeWindowClosed Dispute opened too late (or lease not settled) 28 ChallengePeriodActive Resolution attempted before the provider's window closed 29 DisputeClosed Dispute already resolved 30 InvalidDispute Wrong accuser, over-report bound, or duplicate contest 31 InvalidStakeConfig Config outside the documented bounds 32 NothingToWithdraw No unbonding stake to release

docs.title: 5. Authorization and governance model
docs.text:
Role Can do Cannot do Provider Deposit, opt in/out, request/cancel/complete withdrawal, contest a dispute, settle its leases Slash, resolve disputes, withdraw while exposed Consumer Open a dispute on its settled lease after posting the bond Open disputes on others' leases, slash directly Arbiter Resolve a dispute after the challenge period Open disputes, change config, touch escrow, keep slashed value Admin Set config, rotate the arbiter, upgrade the Wasm Slash, resolve disputes, move stake or escrow

The admin and arbiter should be separate keys (both cold/multisig) in production; the default of "arbiter = admin" exists so a fresh deployment works without a second key, and the role is rotatable and announced by arbiter_set. Governance is deliberately narrow: the only discretionary decision in the protocol is the one-bit approve in resolve_dispute, and its consequences are capped, recipient-fixed and permanently logged.

docs.title: 6. Backward compatibility
docs.text:
• Storage: only new keys. Service and Lease are untouched, so a v0.3.0 Wasm can be installed over a v0.2.x deployment with live services and leases.
  • Existing services: remain unstaked and continue to accept leases with no stake requirement. Nothing becomes mandatory.
  • Existing leases: unchanged terms; settlement, refund and revocation do not consult stake.
  • ABI: all new entry points, events and error codes are additive. No error number is reused and no event payload changes.
  • Default state: staking is inert until set_stake_config is called, so an upgraded deployment behaves identically to v0.2.x.
  • Events: the existing event stream for lease lifecycle is byte-identical; stake and dispute events are new names.

docs.title: 7. Security considerations
docs.text:
Re-entrancy and ordering. Every money path follows checks-effects-interactions. open_dispute persists the dispute and the bond before transferFrom-style movement (the consumer transfer happens after the counter and bond are recorded). resolve_dispute sets the dispute to Approved/Rejected, decrements pending_disputes and debits stake before any token transfer, so a malicious recipient contract cannot re-enter for a second slash or a second bond refund. withdraw_stake zeroes the unbonding balance before the transfer. A re-entrant token would see terminal state and revert the whole transaction.

Storage integrity. open_leases and pending_disputes are counters, not collections, and are maintained on both sides of each transition (create/settle/revoke, open/resolve). The tests assert they return to zero after a full lifecycle. Dispute records are immutable after resolution except for status. All persistent additions carry explicit TTL extensions; a stake entry is read/written on every path that needs it, and a dispute entry is extended when opened, contested and resolved.

Economic attack vectors.

Attack Mitigation Provider over-reports and withdraws before a dispute Unbonding ≥ dispute window + challenge period; unbonding remains slashable; withdrawal requires zero open leases and zero pending disputes; new leases are blocked while unbonding Consumer grieves a provider with disputes Bond forfeited to the provider on rejection; bounded cap; one contest round; evidence hash makes frivolous claims auditable Arbiter colludes with a consumer Slash proceeds go to the consumer, not the arbiter; per-dispute cap; admin-rotatable role; every ruling is event-logged with evidence hashes Provider keeps too little stake relative to revenue min_stake is admin-set and enforced on every new lease of a staked service; raising it never invalidates existing leases Slash is used to seize a business Only settled leases, consumer standing, over-report bound, max_slash_bps cap, one round, provider keeps all un-slashed stake and future revenue Double slash on one lease At most one dispute per lease (open_dispute rejects a lease that already has one, checked through a per-lease dispute index), and a terminal status Stake/escrow accounting confusion Separate internal ledgers; the token balance is never read as a source of truth; tests assert escrow + stake == balance Griefing by never contesting Resolution is permissionless in time but arbiter-driven; an uncontested dispute resolves on schedule

Governance and upgrade implications. StakeConfig, Arbiter and the new keys must keep their meaning across upgrades; the implementation must never renumber errors or change the Service/Lease encoding. A malicious upgrade can already change any rule, so the arbiter/admin keys deserve the same cold-storage treatment as the existing admin key. Because min_stake and max_slash_bps are live parameters, changes to them should be announced and are visible in stake_config_set.

Resource limits. Every new path is O(1) in storage reads/writes and does a constant number of token calls (at most two transfers in a resolution). No entry point iterates a user-controlled collection; recipient and service lists are never walked to enforce stake.

docs.title: 8. Testing strategy
docs.text:
New tests in contracts/registry/src/test.rs (plus the existing suite kept green):

Stake lifecycle

  • deposit credits available, moves tokens, emits stake_deposited, extends TTL;
  • deposit with zero/negative amount reverts InvalidStakeAmount;
  • opt-in requires a config and an account; opt-in/opt-out emit service_stake_changed;
  • create_lease on a staked service reverts InsufficientStake below min_stake and succeeds at exactly min_stake;
  • unstaked services keep leasing with no stake at all (backward compatibility).

Withdrawal

  • request moves available to unbonding, blocks new leases (StakeWithdrawalPending);
  • early withdraw_stake reverts WithdrawalNotReady;
  • withdraw succeeds after the delay and only then moves tokens;
  • request reverts while a lease is unsettled (OutstandingLeases), while a service is still opted in, and while a dispute is pending (PendingDispute);
  • deposit during unbonding cancels the request and restores available.

Disputes and slashing

  • only the lease consumer can open (InvalidDispute / Unauthorized);
  • a dispute on an unstaked service reverts ServiceNotStaked;
  • a dispute on an unsettled or out-of-window lease reverts DisputeWindowClosed;
  • the bond is transferred in and the frozen slash_amount respects both the over-report bound and max_slash_bps;
  • contest is provider-only and single-shot; resolution before the challenge period reverts ChallengePeriodActive;
  • approval pays the accuser the slash plus the returned bond, debits stake (available first, then unbonding), emits dispute_resolved and provider_slashed;
  • rejection pays the bond to the provider, leaves stake untouched, and clears the pending counter;
  • double resolution reverts DisputeClosed; a second dispute on the same lease reverts;
  • a re-entrant token cannot double-slash or double-refund a bond.

Settlement and lifecycle after a slash

  • an existing lease still settles and refunds correctly after its provider is slashed;
  • create_lease reverts InsufficientStake after the stake falls below min_stake (effective deactivation), and works again after a top-up;
  • opt_out_service_stake blocks new leases but leaves existing leases settleable;
  • payout + refund == locked_deposit and escrow + stake == token balance hold across the whole flow;
  • the real-SAC lifecycle test and the existing re-entrancy test still pass.

docs.title: 9. Open questions and trade-offs
docs.text:
1. Provider-level vs per-service stake. A single pool is capital-efficient and keeps checks O(1); a per-service pool isolates a bad service from a provider's other business. This note chooses provider-level and lets the provider opt out individual services. Rejected alternative: a stake field on Service (breaks stored-value layout) and a per-service pool (fragments capital and needs per-service withdrawal bookkeeping).
  2. Arbiter discretion. One challenge round with a capped, accuser-directed payout is cheap and bounded, but a corrupt arbiter can still approve a malicious dispute up to the cap. Alternatives: two-of-two (arbiter + admin) approval, a bonded arbiter, or a consumer/provider optimistic game with a fraud proof. Each adds interface and governance surface; we should decide before implementation whether disputes above a threshold need two approvals.
  3. Exposure-based stake. The design requires available >= min_stake, not "stake proportional to open escrow". Per-lease stake would price risk better but needs mid-lease top-ups and makes settlement conditional on stake. Question for maintainers: should a later version require min_stake >= k * open_leases?
  4. Dispute window anchor. Disputes are anchored at expires_at + grace + dispute_window, because Lease has no settled_at field and adding one would change its encoding. This grants a generous window to fully-consumed leases settled early. Alternative: add SettlementTime(lease_id) as a new key and anchor on the real settlement time.
  5. Bond size. A flat dispute_bond is simple but may be too small for large services or too large for small ones. Alternative: a bps-of-disputed-value bond with a floor and a ceiling.
  6. Who audits evidence. The on-chain record is a hash plus a verdict. If maintainers want verifiable evidence handling, the off-chain bundle format needs a documented schema and a canonical hashing rule before release.
  7. Unbonding UX. Requiring open_leases == 0 and full opt-out before a withdrawal request is conservative and can lock capital for up to a lease term plus the delay. Alternative: allow withdrawal requests with open leases by reserving the newest leases' exposure.
  8. Versioning. This is a breaking-in-behaviour (not ABI) change once a config is set; the workspace version should move to 0.3.0 and the release notes must describe the governance assumptions.

docs.title: 10. Review request
docs.text:
Per CONTRIBUTING.md, this note needs maintainer approval before code:

  • Approve or amend the arbiter model (single arbiter vs two-key approval).
  • Confirm provider-level stake and opt-in-per-service.
  • Confirm the withdrawal precondition open_leases == 0 and the unbonding bound.
  • Confirm the error-code allocation (17–32) and event names before they become ABI.

Once approved, implementation lands on the same feature branch as #133, with the tests above and the full four-command validation from CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Design note: consumer challenge window before settlement pays out
docs.text:
• Issue: #132 — Add a consumer challenge window before settlement pays out
  • Status: Implemented on fix/132-consumer-challenge-window; a maintainer must approve this note before the change is merged.
  • Scope: contracts/registry/src/{lib,storage,types,events,errors}.rs and the public documentation. No Lease layout change is required.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: settle_lease is a single trusted report: the provider submits verified_calls, and the contract immediately pays verified_calls × rate_per_call and refunds the rest. The contract cannot observe HTTP usage, so a provider can over-report up to allocated_calls and the consumer has no way to dispute it. The fixed allotment bounds the loss, but it does not give the consumer a remedy inside the protocol.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Give the consumer a bounded window to dispute a proposed settlement using an on-chain evidence commitment (no evidence bytes on chain).
  2. Keep the payout locked while a dispute is open; no party can withdraw it.
  3. Define an unambiguous resolver and the two outcomes.
  4. Preserve the existing provider and consumer guarantees:
  5. a provider that never settles can still be revoked after the grace window,
  6. a settlement can never be paid twice,
  7. a consumer always has a path to the deposit.
  8. Keep the Lease storage entry unchanged, so the upgrade is additive.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Adjudicating evidence on chain. The contract stores a 32-byte commitment; the admin evaluates the evidence off chain.
  • Partial or formula-based awards. Resolution is binary: uphold (full refund) or reject (proposal stands).
  • Changing the 24-hour post-expiry provider grace window or the revoke path.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text: Actor Power Provider Proposes a settlement split for a lease it owns. Consumer Challenges a proposal inside the window, or withdraws the challenge. Admin Resolves an active challenge: uphold (full consumer refund) or reject (proposal stands). Anyone Finalizes a proposal after the window closes when no challenge is active.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: CHALLENGE_WINDOW_SECS = 86_400 (24 hours), the same length as the existing settlement grace period. It is a protocol constant, not a per-service setting, so indexers and clients can hard-code the settlement time without reading service metadata.

docs.title: State machine
docs.text:
settle_lease (proposal)
        │
        ▼
   ┌─────────┐   challenge_settlement    ┌────────────┐
   │ Pending │ ────────────────────────▶ │ Challenged │
   └─────────┘ ◀──────────────────────── └────────────┘
        │        cancel_challenge              │
        │                                      │ resolve_challenge (admin)
        │ now ≥ challengeable_until            │
        ▼                                      ▼
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │                  Finalized                    │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • settle_lease records a Settlement with state = Pending, challengeable_until = now + 24h, and moves no funds.
  • The lease's settled flag is set at proposal time, so it can no longer be settled again or revoked. Funds remain in escrow.
  • challenge_settlement(consumer, lease_id, evidence_hash) requires consumer auth, a non-zero evidence hash, and now < challengeable_until.
  • cancel_challenge(consumer, lease_id) clears an active challenge and returns the settlement to Pending. The original deadline is unchanged, so cancellation cannot extend the window. A consumer may challenge again while the window is still open.
  • finalize_settlement(lease_id) is permissionless and requires state == Pending and now >= challengeable_until. It pays the recorded payout and refund.
  • resolve_challenge(admin, lease_id, upheld) requires the stored admin. It may run before or after the deadline while a challenge is active:
  • upheld = true: payout 0, refund locked_deposit (the proposal's payout plus refund),
  • upheld = false: the original payout and refund stand.
  • locked_balance(lease_id) reports the full deposit while a settlement is pending or challenged, and 0 once finalized or revoked.

docs.title: Boundary semantics
docs.text:
Timestamp challenge_settlement finalize_settlement now < challengeable_until allowed ChallengeWindowStillOpen now >= challengeable_until ChallengeWindowClosed allowed if Pending

challengeable_until is an exclusive deadline for challenges and an inclusive start for finalization, so there is no ledger at which both are allowed.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
A new persistent entry keeps the upgrade additive:

DataKey::Settlement(u64) // persistent, keyed by lease_id

Settlement carries lease_id, consumer, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund, proposed_at, challengeable_until, state, challenge_evidence and challenged_at. The consumer and provider are copied in, so finalization and resolution never need to read the Lease entry (whose TTL is scoped to the lease term plus grace). Settlement entries are extended to the standard ~30-day persistent TTL on every save and read.

Lease itself is unchanged.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Topics Payload lease_settlement_proposed lease_id schema_version, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund, challengeable_until lease_challenged lease_id schema_version, consumer, evidence_hash lease_challenge_cancelled lease_id schema_version, consumer lease_challenge_resolved lease_id schema_version, admin, upheld lease_settled lease_id schema_version, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund

lease_settled keeps its payload but now means funds have been released; it is emitted only by finalize and resolve, not by the proposal. Indexers that watched it as "provider was paid" remain correct; they should add lease_settlement_proposed if they need the proposal time.

docs.title: Errors (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text: Code Variant 28 SettlementNotFound 29 SettlementFinalized 30 ChallengeWindowClosed 31 SettlementChallenged 32 NoActiveChallenge 33 ChallengeWindowStillOpen 34 InvalidEvidence

docs.title: Safety analysis
docs.text:
• No double release. Lease.settled is set before the settlement entry is written, and the settlement state is persisted as Finalized before any token transfer. A re-entrant token sees a finalized settlement and cannot pay again.
  • No revocation race. Because the lease is marked settled at proposal time, revoke_expired_lease fails with LeaseAlreadySettled once a proposal exists. The consumer cannot take both the refund and the provider's payout.
  • No payout while disputed. finalize_settlement rejects Challenged regardless of the timestamp.
  • No admin theft. The admin can only choose between the proposal and a full consumer refund; it cannot direct funds to itself or to an arbitrary address. Its address is fixed at init.
  • Conservation. Every path pays payout + refund == locked_deposit (upholding sets payout = 0, refund = locked_deposit).
  • No dangling challenge. Resolution has no deadline, but settlement entries live for the ~30-day persistent TTL and are re-extended on read. A dispute should be resolved well inside that horizon; this is documented as a known operational bound.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• Settlement is slower. Providers wait 24 hours for the payout unless they settle with verified_calls = 0. This is the cost of a dispute path; it matches the existing 24-hour grace period, so the consumer's and provider's clocks are symmetric.
  • The admin becomes an adjudicator. The trust model shifts from "the provider is trusted on usage" to "the provider and the consumer can escalate to the admin". A compromised admin can zero a legitimate payout or refuse to resolve. The mitigation is the same as for upgrades: a cold or multisig admin and public on-chain events.
  • Binary resolution. There is no partial award. A future version could let the admin set awarded_calls, but that adds another trust dimension and more storage; the issue asks for a dispute path, not an arbitration engine.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
1. Challenge directly against a finalized payout (clawback). Rejected: the token has no clawback guarantee, and a provider that withdraws immediately would be outside the contract's reach.
  2. Consumer challenge with no resolver (auto-refund on any challenge). Rejected: a consumer could always avoid paying by challenging, which breaks the provider's guarantee.
  3. Optimistic challenge with an admin-settable award. Deferred: more complex and not required to close the over-reporting gap.
  4. Per-service challenge window. Rejected: adds a configuration surface and makes indexer expectations harder to reason about. A protocol constant keeps the ABI simple.

docs.title: Test matrix
docs.text:
Covered in contracts/registry/src/test.rs:

  • no-challenge fast path: funds locked before the boundary, finalized at exactly challengeable_until,
  • window boundary: challenge accepted at challengeable_until - 1, rejected at challengeable_until,
  • active challenge blocks finalization,
  • consumer cancellation returns the settlement to pending and never pays early,
  • cancellation without a challenge, double challenge, non-consumer actions,
  • zero evidence hash rejected,
  • admin uphold (full consumer refund) and admin reject (proposal stands),
  • resolution before the window closes,
  • resolver authorization and "nothing to resolve" cases,
  • events for proposal, challenge, cancellation, resolution and payout,
  • existing lifecycle, SAC, re-entrancy and revocation tests updated for the two-phase settlement.

docs.title: Rollout
docs.text:
• Deploy as a new version of the registry Wasm; the new DataKey variant is additive and Lease is unchanged, so in-flight leases remain readable.
  • In-flight leases that were settled under the old code are already finalized and have no Settlement entry; views return SettlementNotFound, which clients must handle.
  • Indexers should subscribe to lease_settlement_proposed and lease_challenge_* in addition to lease_settled.

docs.title: Design note: early consumer cancellation with a defined refund
docs.text:
• Issue: #135 — Support early consumer cancellation with a defined refund
  • Status: Implemented on fix/135-early-consumer-cancellation; a maintainer must approve this note before the change is merged.
  • Scope: contracts/registry/src/{lib,types,storage,events,errors}.rs, tests and docs.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The only consumer exit on main is revoke_expired_lease: it requires the lease to have expired and the full 24-hour provider grace window to elapse. A consumer that stops using a service early — or a provider that agrees the remaining calls will never be served — has to wait out that whole window before any funds move.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Let a consumer end a lease early and receive the value of its unused calls, with the provider's consent.
  2. Define the refund exactly, with checked arithmetic and no rounding ambiguity.
  3. Never let the consumer take funds the provider has earned: consent is the provider's, and it includes the served-call count.
  4. Keep the existing unconditional revoke path unchanged as the fallback when the provider is unresponsive.
  5. Preserve single-release accounting: a cancelled lease cannot be settled or revoked again.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• A unilateral consumer exit with a penalty. The issue allows either provider consent or a configurable penalty; consent is the smaller, safer change because it needs no new pricing parameter, no penalty treasury, and no assumption about what a fair penalty is.
  • Partial cancellation, splitting a lease, or transferring unused calls to a different service.
  • Changing the post-expiry revoke path.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
consumer                      registry                       provider
   |-- request_early_cancel ---->|                               |
   |                             |-- lease_cancellation_requested ->|
   |                             |                               |
   |                             |<-- reject_early_cancel --------|
   |                             |    (request cleared)          |
   |                             |                               |
   |                             |<-- approve_early_cancel(used) -|
   |<-- refund unused calls -----|---- payout served calls ------>|
   |                             |-- lease_cancelled ----------->|

A request is a signal, not a state change to the lease: the lease stays active and usable while the provider decides.

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text:
pub fn request_early_cancel(env: Env, consumer: Address, lease_id: u64) -> Result<(), Error>
pub fn withdraw_early_cancel(env: Env, consumer: Address, lease_id: u64) -> Result<(), Error>
pub fn reject_early_cancel(env: Env, provider: Address, lease_id: u64) -> Result<(), Error>
pub fn approve_early_cancel(env: Env, provider: Address, lease_id: u64, verified_calls: u32) -> Result<(), Error>
  • Request (consumer auth): lease exists, caller is lease.consumer, not settled, now < expires_at, and no request is already pending.
  • Withdraw (consumer auth): clears a pending request. The consumer may request again later.
  • Reject (provider auth, owns the lease's service): clears a pending request. The lease is untouched and keeps running.
  • Approve (provider auth, owns the lease's service): requires a pending request and verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls, then pays out and settles the lease in one transaction.

docs.title: Refund definition
docs.text:
Let rate = service.rate_per_call, unused_calls = allocated_calls − verified_calls, payout = rate × verified_calls, and refund = rate × unused_calls.

  • verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls is checked before the subtraction, and both multiplications use checked_mul.
  • payout + refund is asserted to equal locked_deposit with checked_add; a mismatch (only possible if the stored rate no longer matches the deposit arithmetic) reverts with Overflow instead of releasing an inconsistent split.
  • Rounding: there is none. rate_per_call is an integer price in the token's smallest unit and calls are whole units, so both the payout and the refund are exact integers. No division, basis points, or fee is applied. If a future version adds a penalty, it should be expressed in basis points with an explicit rounding rule; this design deliberately avoids that surface.

The refund is sent to lease.consumer and the payout to the service provider in the same transaction. The lease is marked settled before either transfer (checks-effects-interactions), so a re-entrant token cannot release it twice.

docs.title: Authorization and refusal
docs.text: Only the current consumer can request or withdraw; only the owning provider can approve or reject. A provider refusal is an explicit on-chain event, and the consumer still has every existing path: keep using the lease, settle normally, or wait for expiry + grace and revoke.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text:
Situation Result Request after expires_at LeaseExpired; use the revoke path after grace Request when settled or revoked LeaseAlreadySettled Request twice CancellationAlreadyRequested Approve/reject without a request CancellationNotRequested Approve with verified_calls > allocated_calls InvalidCalls Approve after expiry allowed, if the request was filed before expiry Settle after approval LeaseAlreadySettled Revoke after approval LeaseAlreadySettled

Approval is allowed after expiry so a request filed in the last seconds of the lease is not lost; the funds are still exactly the unused-call value.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
A new persistent entry, keyed by lease id, holds only the pending request:

DataKey::CancelRequest(u64)  // persistent

CancelRequest { lease_id, requested_at } is extended to the standard ~30-day persistent TTL. The Lease layout is unchanged, so the upgrade is additive. The request is removed on withdraw, reject, approve, or settlement; a stale request carries no funds and is harmless.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Topics Payload lease_cancellation_requested lease_id schema_version, consumer lease_cancellation_rejected lease_id schema_version, provider lease_cancellation_withdrawn lease_id schema_version, consumer lease_cancelled lease_id schema_version, provider, consumer, verified_calls, payout, refund

lease_cancelled is the money-moving event, so indexers can treat it like lease_settled for reconciliation.

docs.title: Errors (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text: Code Variant Meaning 25 CancellationNotRequested no pending request 26 CancellationAlreadyRequested a request is already pending 27 LeaseExpired early cancellation is only for active leases

docs.title: Safety analysis
docs.text:
• Provider consent is required. No unilateral path reduces the provider's payout; the provider signs the served-call count.
  • Conservation. payout + refund == locked_deposit is enforced before any transfer.
  • Single release. Approval sets settled = true before transfers, and both settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease reject a settled lease.
  • No expired-lease shortcut. A request cannot be filed after expiry, so the consumer cannot use approval to bypass the provider's 24-hour grace window at the last moment. A request filed before expiry may be approved after it; the provider is the one choosing that timing.
  • No grief via pending requests. The consumer can withdraw or request again, but a pending request never blocks use, settlement, or revocation. The provider can reject at any time.
  • Stale requests. Requests are cleared on every terminal path; a request with no lease value left cannot move funds because approval re-reads the lease.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
1. Unilateral cancel with a configurable penalty. Would let a consumer exit without the provider, but requires a penalty parameter (per service or protocol-wide), a rounding rule, and a policy for where the penalty goes. It also weakens the provider's guarantee. Rejected for this change; the design note records it as future work.
  2. Consumer-specified refund amount / negotiation. Adds a bid field and an acceptance rule, with no on-chain way to judge fairness. Rejected.
  3. Approve with no served-call report (full refund always). Simple, but the provider could not be paid for calls already served. Rejected.
  4. Reuse settle_lease before expiry. That would be a unilateral provider action with a different authorization story; keeping a separate consented path makes the intent and events explicit.

docs.title: Interaction with other protocol changes
docs.text:
• Consumer challenge window (#132): on that branch a settlement proposal sets settled = true, so request_early_cancel fails with LeaseAlreadySettled once a settlement is proposed. That is correct: a provider that has already reported usage should use the settlement flow, not early cancellation.
  • Transferable leases (#134): the new consumer is lease.consumer, so only they can request or withdraw a cancellation. Ownership moves the right to cancel with the rest of the lease.

docs.title: Test matrix
docs.text:
Covered in contracts/registry/src/test.rs (48 tests total):

  • consent path: request, approve with 4/10 calls served, correct payout/refund, lease settled and locked balance zero,
  • conservation at both extremes (0 served → full refund; all served → no refund),
  • refusal: request cleared, no funds release, lease still settles normally,
  • ownership/authorization for request, withdraw, approve and reject, double request, approve without request, non-provider approval,
  • cancellation after a partial settlement is rejected,
  • request at expiry is rejected; a pre-expiry request approved after expiry works,
  • events for request, reject, withdraw and approval.

docs.title: Rollout
docs.text:
• Additive DataKey; Lease and existing entries are unchanged. No migration.
  • Indexers should add the four lease_cancellation* / lease_cancelled events. lease_cancelled carries the payout and refund for accounting.
  • Consumers and providers need one extra transaction each compared with the post-expiry revoke path, but avoid the wait.

docs.title: Design Note: Admin Emergency Pause
docs.text:
• Issue: #120
  • Status: Pending Maintainer Approval
  • Author: Antigravity Agent
  • Target Contract: KeyLeaseRegistry (contracts/registry)

docs.title: 1. Context and Problem
docs.text:
KeyLease escrow holds funds on behalf of consumers and providers. In the event of an identified vulnerability, token anomaly, or external emergency, the protocol administrator needs a mechanism to halt inbound risks immediately.

However, a naive pause mechanism that freezes all contract executions would trap consumer funds locked in escrow and prevent providers from claiming earned settlements. This violates the core trust model of KeyLease.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
1. Non-blocking settlement and refunds (Core Invariant): settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease are NEVER blocked by an emergency pause. Escrowed consumer deposits and provider payouts must never be held hostage by a contract pause.
  2. Safe default for upgrades: Existing contract deployments upgraded to a Wasm containing the emergency pause logic must default to unpaused without requiring data migrations. An absent pause storage key evaluates to false (unpaused).
  3. Admin exclusivity: Only the configured contract admin can pause or unpause the contract. Unauthorized callers fail with Error::Unauthorized.
  4. Transparent observability: State transitions between paused and unpaused must emit typed Soroban contract events (EmergencyPaused and EmergencyUnpaused).

docs.title: Blocked Entry Points (Fail with Error::ContractPaused)
docs.text:
The following state-mutating entry points accept new commitments or modify service definitions, and are therefore blocked during an emergency pause:

Function Reason for Blocking register_service Halts registration of new services during an incident. set_service_active Prevents modifying service active/inactive status during an incident. create_lease Prevents consumers from depositing funds or minting new leases. create_lease_for Shares create_lease's mint path, so a delegate cannot bypass the pause.

docs.title: Available Entry Points (Never Blocked)
docs.text:
The following entry points remain fully accessible while the contract is paused:

Function Reason for Remaining Available settle_lease Invariant: Providers must always be able to claim earned revenue and disburse remaining refunds to consumers. revoke_expired_lease Invariant: Consumers must always be able to reclaim full escrow for abandoned or unserved leases after the 24h grace period. pause Admin can invoke to enter or re-affirm the paused state. unpause Admin can invoke to resume normal operations. upgrade Admin must be able to deploy bug fixes or patches during an incident. set_token Admin configuration function. init Initialization (one-time). All read views All get_*, lease_status, remaining_calls, locked_balance, version, is_paused read-only views remain accessible.

docs.title: 4. Storage Design
docs.text:
• Storage Key: DataKey::Paused placed in instance storage.
  • Data Type: bool.
  • Default Value: false (unpaused).
  • Upgrade Compatibility: an absent key reads as unpaused, so no migration is needed.
pub fn is_paused(env: &Env) -> bool {
    env.storage()
        .instance()
        .get(&DataKey::Paused)
        .unwrap_or(false)
}

Because unwrap_or(false) is used, any contract upgraded from an earlier Wasm version where DataKey::Paused was not set immediately evaluates to unpaused without data migration or re-initialization.

docs.title: 5. Event Schema
docs.text:
Typed events emitted on state transitions (in events.rs):

/// Emitted when the admin triggers an emergency pause.
#[contractevent]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct EmergencyPaused {
    /// Payload schema version; see the events module docs.
    pub schema_version: u32,
    /// Admin that authorized the pause.
    pub admin: Address,
}

/// Emitted when the admin unpauses the registry.
#[contractevent]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct EmergencyUnpaused {
    /// Payload schema version; see the events module docs.
    pub schema_version: u32,
    /// Admin that authorized the unpause.
    pub admin: Address,
}

docs.title: 6. Error Handling
docs.text:
A new error discriminant is added to errors.rs:

/// The contract is currently paused by admin emergency action.
ContractPaused = 44,

44 is the next free code after InvalidEndpointHash = 43 on main; no existing discriminant is renumbered.

docs.title: 7. Public ABI Additions
docs.text:
impl KeyLeaseRegistry {
    /// Pause new service registrations and lease creations. Admin only.
    pub fn pause(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), Error>;

    /// Resume normal operations. Admin only.
    pub fn unpause(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), Error>;

    /// Query whether the contract is currently paused.
    pub fn is_paused(env: Env) -> bool;
}

docs.title: Design note: transferable leases with consumer authorization
docs.text:
• Issue: #134 — Make leases transferable with consumer authorization
  • Status: Implemented on fix/134-transferable-leases; a maintainer must approve this note before the change is merged.
  • Scope: contracts/registry/src/{lib,events,errors}.rs, tests and docs. No storage change is required.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A lease is bound to the consumer that created it. The provider authenticates requests against lease.consumer, and revoke_expired_lease refunds that same address. A consumer that over-bought, changed accounts, or wants to resell unused access has no protocol-level way to hand the lease over. Off-chain key sharing is the only workaround, and it transfers the account's identity rather than the lease.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Let the current consumer move a lease to another Stellar address.
  2. Move the access right and the refund path atomically — one source of truth, no window where two addresses can both use or reclaim the lease.
  3. Make the change observable so providers and indexers can follow it.
  4. Refuse transfers that would corrupt accounting: settled/revoked leases, and self-transfers.
  5. Stay compatible with the consumer challenge window (issue #132).

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• An offer/accept handshake. The issue allows assignment, and assignment is the smaller surface: no pending-offer state, no expiry, no cancellation.
  • A marketplace, pricing, or fees. The protocol only moves ownership.
  • Splitting a lease across consumers.

docs.title: Entry point
docs.text:
pub fn transfer_lease(
    env: Env,
    consumer: Address,
    lease_id: u64,
    new_consumer: Address,
) -> Result<(), Error>
  • Auth: only the current consumer.
  • Preconditions: the lease exists, lease.consumer == consumer, !lease.settled, and new_consumer != consumer.
  • Effect: sets lease.consumer = new_consumer and saves the lease once. There is no second copy of ownership to keep in sync.
  • Event: lease_transferred { lease_id | schema_version, from, to }.

The new consumer does not authorize the assignment. Being given a lease is receiving an asset; requiring the recipient's signature would let a typo or a lost key strand the lease, and it would need a pending-offer state to avoid griefing. Assignment is final and the new consumer can immediately use the lease or transfer it again.

docs.title: Why no storage change
docs.text:
Lease.consumer is already the single field every path reads:

  • revoke_expired_lease checks and refunds lease.consumer,
  • settle_lease refunds lease.consumer,
  • providers authenticate callers against lease.consumer,
  • remaining_calls, lease_status and locked_balance are ownership-agnostic.

Updating that one field is the atomic move the acceptance criteria ask for. A DataKey index would add a second source of truth that could drift.

docs.title: Errors (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text:
Code Variant Meaning 35 LeaseNotTransferable lease is settled or revoked 36 InvalidConsumer new_consumer equals the current consumer

Unauthorized still covers a caller that is not the current consumer.

docs.title: Expired but unsettled leases
docs.text: Transfer is allowed after expires_at as long as the lease is unsettled. Access has lapsed (remaining_calls is 0), but the refund claim still has value and should be sellable. The new consumer owns the revoke path from then on. This is deliberate and covered by test_transfer_after_expiry_moves_refund_right.

docs.title: Interaction with the consumer challenge window (#132)
docs.text:
The challenge-window change makes settle_lease a proposal that sets lease.settled = true immediately, with the payout released later by finalize_settlement or resolve_challenge. Because transfer_lease rejects any settled lease:

  • a lease with a pending settlement cannot be transferred,
  • a lease under an active challenge cannot be transferred,
  • the settlement record keeps the consumer that owned the lease at proposal time, so a challenge always belongs to the address that filed it.

That is the correct composition: a provider's settlement proposal freezes ownership just as it freezes revocation. A consumer who wants to sell a lease must do so before the provider proposes settlement. If the challenge-window PR merges first, this entry point needs no change; its settled check already covers the new states. The design note for #132 should link here as the transfer interaction.

docs.title: After a transfer
docs.text:
• The previous consumer cannot use, revoke or transfer the lease. Their get_lease reads show the new owner.
  • The new consumer inherits both the remaining access (if unexpired) and the refund right.
  • A provider that cached lease.consumer must refresh on a mismatch: transfers are on chain, and the cached value is only an optimisation.

docs.title: Safety analysis
docs.text:
• Atomicity. One field is written in one save_lease call; there is no intermediate state where both addresses can act.
  • No refund theft. The old consumer cannot transfer and then revoke: the revoke path checks lease.consumer, which is now the recipient.
  • No post-settlement transfer. settled is set before any payout or refund, so a lease cannot change hands after funds have been released.
  • No self-transfer. Rejecting new_consumer == consumer avoids a meaningless ownership event that indexers would have to special-case.
  • Auth is not delegable. The recipient never signs; only the current owner can move the lease. A stolen consumer key can transfer the lease, which is the same authority that key already has to use or revoke it.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
1. Offer/accept handshake. Safer against typos but requires pending-offer storage, offer expiry and cancellation, and doubles the transaction count. Not required by the issue; assignment is a smaller protocol.
  2. Transfer by provider co-signature. Adds a provider liveness dependency and lets a provider block resale. Rejected.
  3. Splitting or partial transfer. Needs per-consumer accounting inside one lease and breaks the single consumer field. Out of scope.
  4. Revoke-and-recreate. The old consumer could revoke (only after expiry) and the recipient create a new lease, but that loses the term and requires the recipient to pay again. This issue exists because that is not a transfer.

docs.title: Test matrix
docs.text:
Covered in contracts/registry/src/test.rs:

  • transfer moves ownership, access and the refund right, and emits lease_transferred,
  • settlement after transfer pays the provider and refunds the new consumer,
  • unauthorized attempts by an impostor and by the provider, plus self-transfer,
  • transfer of a settled lease and of a revoked lease → LeaseNotTransferable,
  • transfer after expiry but before revocation, after which only the new consumer can revoke.

docs.title: Rollout
docs.text:
• No storage layout or Lease shape change: existing leases are transferable immediately after the upgrade.
  • Indexers should add lease_transferred to keep a consumer→lease projection in sync. lease_created alone is no longer the final word on ownership.
  • Providers must treat lease.consumer as mutable. Re-read on an ownership mismatch instead of caching it for the whole lease term.

docs.title: Design note: time-locked registry upgrades
docs.text: Status: draft for maintainer review. This note is required by CONTRIBUTING.md for a 200-point (high) issue. Implementation was requested explicitly, but merging the change is gated on a maintainer approving this design.

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text:
KeyLeaseRegistry::upgrade accepts a Wasm hash and calls deployer().update_current_contract_wasm in the same transaction. The admin can therefore replace the rules governing in-flight leases atomically with the upload, giving consumers no window to observe the change and revoke before new rules apply. Storage and balances survive an upgrade, which makes an exit window both useful and practical.

Impact: a compromised or hostile admin key can change settlement/refund logic without any warning period, defeating the consumer exit guarantee that the rest of the protocol is built around.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
1. No Wasm may be installed until a delay has elapsed since the proposal was recorded on-ledger.
  2. The admins who propose and execute may be the same key; the delay, not a second party, is the safety mechanism.
  3. There is always a cancel path, and cancellation never installs code.
  4. A proposal records the exact Wasm hash and the ledger timestamp after which it may execute, and both are readable by clients.
  5. Every state transition is authenticated by the current admin and emits a typed event; events never contain secret material.
  6. Upgrades keep the contract id, DataKey layout, stored values, token balances and in-flight leases. This change only adds an instance key.

docs.title: 3. Approach
docs.text:
• Add UPGRADE_DELAY_SECS = 86_400 (24 hours) as a public, documented constant, matching the existing settlement grace period.
  • Replace upgrade with three admin-only entry points:
  • propose_upgrade(admin, new_wasm_hash) — stores PendingUpgrade { new_wasm_hash, execute_after } under DataKey::PendingUpgrade (instance storage) and emits upgrade_proposed. A new proposal replaces a pending one and restarts the delay.
  • execute_upgrade(admin) — requires a pending proposal and ledger.timestamp() >= execute_after, installs the Wasm, clears the pending entry, and emits contract_upgraded with both the hash and the ledger timestamp. Executing early returns UpgradeDelayNotElapsed.
  • cancel_upgrade(admin) — clears the proposal and emits upgrade_cancelled.
  • Add get_pending_upgrade() -> Option<PendingUpgrade> as a read-only view.
  • Append error codes only (17, 18); never renumber existing codes.
  • Update the README interface/event tables and the deployment guide so operators use the new flow.

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text:
• Two-party approval / multisig — changes the trust model and needs a governance design outside this issue's scope.
  • Delay stored as a ledger sequence number — ledger timestamps are already how lease expiry works, and they make the delay human-readable (24h). A sequence number would couple the delay to close-time assumptions.
  • Keep the old instant upgrade for emergencies — that is exactly the unsafe path being removed; emergencies are covered by cancel_upgrade plus a fresh proposal.

docs.title: 4. Threat model
docs.text:
• Admin key compromise: the attacker can propose, but cannot install for at least 24 hours. Consumers can watch upgrade_proposed, use get_pending_upgrade, and revoke/settle before execute_after.
  • Front-running the execution: execute_upgrade re-checks the ledger timestamp at execution time; a proposal cannot be backdated.
  • Griefing by repeated proposals: an admin (or stolen key) can restart the clock, but this only ever delays an upgrade and never shortens the window.
  • Storage eviction: the pending entry lives in instance storage, whose TTL is extended to ~30 days by extend_instance_ttl; the 24-hour delay is well inside that horizon.
  • Event spoofing: events are published by the registry contract only, and the hash/ledger come from the stored proposal.

docs.title: 5. Test plan
docs.text:
• propose_upgrade stores the hash and execution ledger in the view and emits upgrade_proposed carrying both.
  • execute_upgrade before execute_after fails with UpgradeDelayNotElapsed and leaves the proposal intact.
  • cancel_upgrade removes the proposal and emits upgrade_cancelled; execution afterwards fails with NoPendingUpgrade.
  • Non-admins cannot propose, execute or cancel.
  • A proposal replaces a previous one and resets the clock.
  • Execution at/after the boundary installs the Wasm and publishes contract_upgraded with the hash and ledger. A 40-byte, hand-built module with a contractenvmetav0 metadata section is uploaded to the test host so the real update_current_contract_wasm primitive is exercised without a build-time Wasm dependency or third-party fixture.
  • Full CI gate: cargo fmt --all -- --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test --all, and cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.1.0
docs.text:
Superseded by v0.2.1. This page records the first release as it shipped; the current interface (events, upgrade, MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS) is in the contract reference.

First public release of the KeyLease registry contract.

KeyLease replaces long-lived static API/RPC credentials with time-bound, on-chain micro-leases: a consumer locks a micropayment in Soroban escrow and receives an authorization the provider can verify cheaply, with an automatic refund path if the provider goes offline.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Escrowed micro-leases. create_lease locks rate_per_call × requested_calls in a SEP-41 token and mints a lease that expires at ledger.timestamp() + duration_secs.
  • Provider settlement. settle_lease pays the provider for verified calls and refunds the remainder to the consumer. Settleable once the lease expires or once every allocated call is consumed.
  • Guaranteed consumer exit. revoke_expired_lease reclaims the full deposit 24 hours after expiry if the provider never settled — no support ticket required.
  • Service registry. Providers publish a rate and an endpoint_hash commitment instead of a secret, and can pause new leases.
  • Checked arithmetic throughout. Deposit and payout math aborts on overflow rather than truncating into a cheaper lease or a short refund.

docs.text:

MockToken has an unlimited mint and exists only for tests and local sandboxes. Never deploy it to a network holding value.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.2.0
docs.text:
Soroban-native hardening: events, upgrades, storage-safe leases and re-entrancy protection.

This release moves the protocol closer to the Stellar primitives it depends on. The escrow model and the public lease lifecycle are unchanged, but the contract is now observable, upgradeable and hardened against hostile SEP-41 tokens.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Typed Soroban events. Every transition publishes a #[contractevent]: registry_initialized, escrow_token_set, service_registered, service_status_changed, lease_created, lease_settled, lease_revoked and contract_upgraded. Topics carry service_id / lease_id, so the lifecycle is indexable without polling storage.
  • On-chain metadata. contractmeta! embeds the name, version, description and repository in the Wasm, and version() returns the running version.
  • In-place upgrades. upgrade(admin, new_wasm_hash) installs a new Wasm through the Soroban deployer, preserving the contract id, storage and balances. Admin-only, and it emits contract_upgraded.
  • Checks-effects-interactions. settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease persist settled = true before calling the token. A new adversarial test installs a re-entrant token that calls back into settle_lease and asserts the second attempt is rejected.
  • TTL-safe lease durations. create_lease rejects durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) with the new DurationTooLong (16) error, and lease storage is extended for the term plus the 24h grace window. Escrow can no longer outlive its ledger entry.
  • Real SAC coverage. The suite now escrows through register_stellar_asset_contract_v2 — the same Stellar Asset Contract that wraps native XLM — in addition to the mock token.

docs.text:

  • New restriction: duration_secs above 30 days now reverts with DurationTooLong. Existing longer leases are unaffected and remain settleable.
  • New entry point and events are additive.
  • Set the escrow token with the native SAC and confirm version() afterwards.

docs.text:
• Not audited. Pre-1.0 software. Do not escrow mainnet value you would be unhappy to lose.
  • Upgrade trust. The admin can replace the Wasm; use a cold or multisig Stellar account for the admin role.
  • No provider key rotation or rate update yet. Both are wave-medium issues.
  • Settlement trusts the provider's call count, bounded by the on-chain allotment and the consumer refund path.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.2.1
docs.text: Rent-aware lease storage. A Testnet deployment showed that extending every lease to the generic thirty-day horizon made Soroban storage rent dominate short leases: creating a 100-call, one-hour lease cost more in rent than the deposit itself. This release pays only for the storage time a lease can actually be used.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
• Lease TTL is term-aware. save_lease and get_lease extend a lease entry to (expires_at − now + 24h) / 5s + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD ledgers: the lease's remaining term, the provider's 24-hour grace window and a one-day read buffer.
  • No more month-long padding. A one-hour lease no longer rents thirty days of storage; the host still enforces its minimum persistent TTL (~7 days on Testnet), but the unnecessary padding is gone. A 30-day lease still gets the full term plus grace and buffer, under the network's maximum entry TTL.
  • Reads use the same policy. get_lease no longer bumps to a fixed thirty-day horizon, so a read near expiry does not silently pay a month of rent.
  • Verified on Testnet. CCEZYHUJ…TAFH62 runs this build; two leases were created, fully settled and partially settled on-chain. See Deployments.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• No ABI, event, storage-key or error-code changes. v0.2.0 deployments can be upgraded in place with upgrade.
  • Rust 1.84+, soroban-sdk 26, wasm32v1-none.
  • version() returns 0.2.1.
